The Qur’an, however, never says that Muḥammad did it. It does not describe his hand, his finger, a mountain between two halves, or a request from Quraysh. Those details come from hadith and tafsīr. The verse itself says only that the Hour has drawn near and that the moon has split. This article separates the Qur’anic statement from the later miracle-story, then examines the modern Apollo 11 reading with the same standard it applies to hadith: the claims must be checkable, the counting rules must be declared, and the evidence must not be exaggerated. Qur’an 54:1 · Apollo 11 · Miracle Claims The Moon Did Split — but not in the hadith story The stronger argument is not that the Qur’an copied a later NASA event in a crude way. It is that the traditional seventh-century spectacle is not required by the Qur’an, while the Apollo reading offers a tightly arranged set of numerical correspondences around Sūrat al-Qamar, the lunar module’s ascent, and the return of lunar material to Earth. Verse 54:1 “The Hour has come closer, and the moon has split.” NASA event time 17:54 UTC Apollo 11 lunar module liftoff from the lunar surface, 21 July 1969. Returned lunar material 21.6 kg First geologic samples brought back from the Moon.

sections.heading: The Qur’anic statement does not name Muḥammad
sections.text: The first thing to notice is what the verse does not say. It does not say, “Muḥammad split the moon.” It does not say the pagans requested this miracle. It does not say the event happened in Mecca, Mina, or beside a mountain. It does not say the moon was divided into two equal halves. Those are the later narrative details. The Arabic is compact: اقْتَرَبَتِ السَّاعَةُ وَانشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ “The Hour has come closer, and the moon has split.” The verb inshaqqa can mean that something split, cleaved, broke apart, or separated. The verse does not state the mechanics. The traditional hadith picture imagines a visible cosmic rupture. The Apollo reading argues for another kind of separation: part of the moon was physically removed from the lunar surface and carried away from it. That reading is not the same as saying the Moon was cracked in half. It is a narrower claim about lunar material leaving the Moon.

sections.heading: Why the hadith story is not enough
sections.text: The canonical hadith material supplies the missing story. In al-Bukhārī, Ibn Masʿūd is made to say that the moon split into two parts during the Prophet’s lifetime, one part over the mountain and the other beyond it, and that the Prophet said, “Bear witness.” Muslim preserves the same basic report and also transmits versions through Ibn Masʿūd, Anas, and Ibn ʿAbbās. That hadith tradition explains how later Sunnī memory read the verse. It does not prove that this is what the verse originally meant. The Qur’an repeatedly answers demands for physical signs by redirecting people back to God, the future, and the Book itself. The Qur’anic pattern is therefore important. When the disbelievers demand a sign, the Prophet is not presented as producing spectacle after spectacle. He is told to say that signs belong to God, that he is only a warner, and that the revealed Book should be enough. That makes the later moon-splitting miracle-story theologically awkward. It gives Muḥammad precisely the kind of public supernatural sign that the Qur’an elsewhere refuses to make the basis of his mission.

sections.heading: The Apollo 11 reading: what is actually verifiable
sections.text: The Apollo reading is often presented in a chaotic meme format. That weakens it. The professional version should separate official mission data from Qur’anic counting arguments. 20 Jul Lunar landing NASA’s lunar event table gives the lunar landing time as 20:17:43 GMT on 20 July 1969. 21:36 Surface stay NASA’s record gives the stay on the lunar surface as 21 hours, 36 minutes, and 17 seconds. 17:54 Departure from Moon The lunar module lifted off from the lunar surface at 17:54:00 GMT / UTC on 21 July 1969. 21.6 kg Lunar samples The Lunar and Planetary Institute reports 21.6 kilograms of Apollo 11 lunar material, including rocks, soil, and core tubes. The strongest external anchor is the mission record. NASA’s Apollo 11 “Record of Lunar Events” lists LM Liftoff From Lunar Surface at ground elapsed time 124:22:00 and 17:54:00 GMT on 21 July 1969. The same table gives the lunar surface stay as 21:36:17. The Lunar and Planetary Institute’s Apollo 11 sample page reports 21.6 kg of material collected and returned from the Moon. Important correction: many online versions say “17:54:01.” The official NASA event table gives 17:54:00. Other mission-timeline data give liftoff ignition at 124:22:00.79, which can be rounded toward the next second, but the clean public-source match is the minute: 17:54 , not a universally stated NASA “17:54:01.” This should be admitted openly. It makes the presentation more credible, not weaker.

sections.heading: The numerical correspondences
sections.text: The numerical argument becomes stronger when the counting rules are stated rather than hidden. The following ledger gives the cleaner form of the case. Qur’anic datum Apollo datum Rule / note 54:1 اقْتَرَبَتِ السَّاعَةُ وَانشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ 17:54 UTC LM liftoff from lunar surface The chapter number appears as the minute in universal time. The verse number is often linked to the rounded second, but official NASA tables normally display 17:54:00. 1,389 verses after 54:1 to the end of the Qur’an 1389 AH / 1969 CE Using the standard 6,236-verse count, there are 1,389 verses after 54:1. The year 1389 AH began in March 1969, so Apollo 11 occurred in 1389 AH. al-Qamar / moon count 20 or 21 before/in 54:1; 7 after 20/21 July landing and lunar departure dates Verse-text qamar counting gives 54:1 as the 20th qamar occurrence if 41:37 is counted twice. Including the sūrah title “al-Qamar” gives the symbolic 21st. Seven qamar occurrences follow after 54:1. 22 letters in 54:1 without spaces or diacritics 21.6 kg ≈ 22 kg lunar material; also a 21:36 surface stay The verse has 22 Arabic letters under the common no-diacritic count. The rock/sample number is not exactly 22 kg in NASA sources, but 21.6 kg rounds to 22 kg. 11 words in 54:1–2 combined Apollo 11 54:1 has four Arabic words; 54:2 has seven if conjunction-attached forms such as wa-in and wa-yaqūlū are counted as single written words. Together they produce eleven written words. This is the version of the argument that deserves to be published. It does not pretend that every datum has the same force. Some correspondences rest on NASA records. Others rest on Qur’anic counting conventions. The reader can then judge the cumulative pattern without being misled.

sections.heading: Why 54:2 matters
sections.text: The second verse is usually read as the reaction of the Meccan pagans to a seventh-century miracle. But the verse itself is more general. It says that whenever they see a sign, they turn away and call it continuing or old magic. In Qur’anic usage, “magic” is not always a literal admission that something supernatural happened. It often functions as an accusation of deception, manipulation, or rhetorical spellbinding. That matters for the Apollo reading. The claim is not that astronauts or NASA officials saw a miracle and literally said, “This is magic.” The claim is that a later audience can see the numerical pattern and dismiss it as manipulation, coincidence, or clever numerology. The rhetoric of “magic” fits the rejection of a sign, not necessarily a literal magical event.

sections.heading: Why 54:3 matters
sections.text: The third verse adds the polemical edge. The people reject, follow conjecture, and cling to what has already settled in their minds. In the traditional reading, this describes the Meccans who rejected Muḥammad. In a Qur’an-only reading, it can also describe later believers who prefer inherited hadith mythology over the Qur’an’s own logic. This does not mean every traditionalist is dishonest. It means the inherited interpretation should not be allowed to erase the verse’s own wording. The Qur’an says the moon split. Hadith turns that into a public miracle performed by Muḥammad. Those are not identical claims.

sections.heading: The theological problem with a seventh-century lunar spectacle
sections.text: The literal miracle reading faces three problems. First, the Qur’an does not identify Muḥammad as the agent of the split. It states the event without narrating a prophetic performance. Second, the Qur’an repeatedly refuses the demand that Muḥammad produce physical signs on request. The Prophet is a warner, and the Book is the sign that is recited to them. Third, the physical claim is enormous. If the moon visibly split into two parts and rejoined, the event should not have been a private local spectacle. A celestial rupture of that scale would be globally visible under the right sky conditions and would be expected to leave either extraordinary observational memory or physical evidence. Modern claims that NASA photographs show a scar of the split have been refuted; the famous Rima Ariadaeus image is a lunar rille or fault-like feature, not evidence that the Moon once divided and reassembled.

sections.heading: What this article is, and what it is not
sections.text: The argument should therefore be framed as a Qur’anic-prophetic reading, not as a crude proof-text meme. A meme can throw numbers on a screen. A serious article must say which numbers are exact, which are rounded, which depend on counting conventions, and which are interpretive.

sections.heading: Sources consulted
sections.text: NASA, Apollo 11 Record of Lunar Events. Gives lunar landing at 20:17:43 GMT on 20 July 1969, lunar module liftoff from the lunar surface at 17:54:00 GMT on 21 July 1969, ground elapsed time 124:22:00, and a lunar surface stay of 21:36:17. Lunar and Planetary Institute, Apollo 11 Lunar Samples. Reports that Apollo 11 returned 21.6 kilograms of lunar material, including rocks, regolith, and core tubes. NASA SP-4029 / Apollo by the Numbers. Gives the more precise lunar liftoff ignition time as mission elapsed time 124:22:00.79, corresponding to 17:54:00 GMT on 21 July 1969. QuranTalk Blog, “Splitting of the Moon.” Presents the Submitter-style Apollo 11 interpretation of Qur’an 54:1 and links the verse to the lunar module’s departure, lunar samples, and the 1389 AH / 1969 CE correspondence. Submitters Perspective, “Splitting of the Moon: Quranic Prophecy.” Earlier presentation of the same numerical argument, including the 21 July 1969 departure, 1389 verse count, and 19-based calculations. al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, no. 4864; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, nos. 2800b–2803. Canonical hadith versions of the traditional moon-splitting miracle-story through Ibn Masʿūd, Anas, and Ibn ʿAbbās. AFP Fact Check, “Social media posts falsely claim the Moon ‘was once split in two.’” Summarizes NASA’s response to the Rima Ariadaeus image and notes that the lunar rille is not evidence that the Moon was split and reassembled.

The people reject, follow conjecture, and cling to what has already settled in their minds. In the traditional reading, this describes the Meccans who rejected Muḥammad. In a Qur’an-only reading, it can also describe later believers who prefer inherited hadith mythology over the Qur’an’s own logic. This does not mean every traditionalist is dishonest. It means the inherited interpretation should not be allowed to erase the verse’s own wording. The Qur’an says the moon split. Hadith turns that into a public miracle performed by Muḥammad. Those are not identical claims. The theological problem with a seventh-century lunar spectacle The literal miracle reading faces three problems. First, the Qur’an does not identify Muḥammad as the agent of the split. It states the event without narrating a prophetic performance. Second, the Qur’an repeatedly refuses the demand that Muḥammad produce physical signs on request. The Prophet is a warner, and the Book is the sign that is recited to them. Third, the physical claim is enormous. If the moon visibly split into two parts and rejoined, the event should not have been a private local spectacle. A celestial rupture of that scale would be globally visible under the right sky conditions and would be expected to leave either extraordinary observational memory or physical evidence. Modern claims that NASA photographs show a scar of the split have been refuted; the famous Rima Ariadaeus image is a lunar rille or fault-like feature, not evidence that the Moon once divided and reassembled. What this article is, and what it is not The argument should therefore be framed as a Qur’anic-prophetic reading, not as a crude proof-text meme. A meme can throw numbers on a screen. A serious article must say which numbers are exact, which are rounded, which depend on counting conventions, and which are interpretive. Conclusion Sources consulted NASA, Apollo 11 Record of Lunar Events. Gives lunar landing at 20:17:43 GMT on 20 July 1969, lunar module liftoff from the lunar surface at 17:54:00 GMT on 21 July 1969, ground elapsed time 124:22:00, and a lunar surface stay of 21:36:17. Lunar and Planetary Institute, Apollo 11 Lunar Samples. Reports that Apollo 11 returned 21.6 kilograms of lunar material, including rocks, regolith, and core tubes. NASA SP-4029 / Apollo by the Numbers. Gives the more precise lunar liftoff ignition time as mission elapsed time 124:22:00.79, corresponding to 17:54:00 GMT on 21 July 1969. QuranTalk Blog, “Splitting of the Moon.” Presents the Submitter-style Apollo 11 interpretation of Qur’an 54:1 and links the verse to the lunar module’s departure, lunar samples, and the 1389 AH / 1969 CE correspondence. Submitters Perspective, “Splitting of the Moon: Quranic Prophecy.” Earlier presentation of the same numerical argument, including the 21 July 1969 departure, 1389 verse count, and 19-based calculations. al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, no. 4864; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, nos. 2800b–2803. Canonical hadith versions of the traditional moon-splitting miracle-story through Ibn Masʿūd, Anas, and Ibn ʿAbbās. AFP Fact Check, “Social media posts falsely claim the Moon ‘was once split in two.’” Summarizes NASA’s response to the Rima Ariadaeus image and notes that the lunar rille is not evidence that the Moon was split and reassembled.

title: The Hasanid Mahdi Hadith: The Name Formula and the Nafs al-Zakiyya Problem
description: An isnād-cum-matn analysis of the Ibn Masʿūd Mahdi report, showing how the formula ‘his name matches my name and his father’s name matches my father’s name’ points into the Hasanid–Abbasid struggle over Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya.

sections.heading: The Report and the Name Problem
sections.text: The report looks simple only when it is read as timeless eschatology. A man from the Prophet’s household will appear near the end of time. His name will match the Prophet’s name. His father’s name will match the Prophet’s father’s name. He will restore justice. In later Sunnī reception, this became one of the most familiar Mahdī proof-texts. The historical problem is that the report does not merely describe a future redeemer. It identifies him by a highly specific name formula. A bare “his name matches my name” points to any Muḥammad from the Prophet’s family. The fuller formula, “and his father’s name matches my father’s name,” narrows the referent to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. That was not an abstract possibility in the second/eighth century. It was the exact name of the most famous Ḥasanid messianic claimant of the early Abbasid period: Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan, known as al-Nafs al-Zakiyya. The question is therefore not whether later Sunnī books contain the report. They do. The question is when this formula became attached to a Prophetic isnād and why the report’s most charged wording points so neatly to a live political claimant who rebelled against al-Manṣūr in 145/762. This does not require the argument that every later transmitter in the books was lying. It also does not require a cartoon picture of ʿĀṣim as a villain. The evidence points to a more precise conclusion. The report becomes historically visible at ʿĀṣim’s circle. The clause that identifies Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh belongs to the partial common-link layer and is strongest in transmitters whose sectarian or political location already fits the Ḥasanid Mahdī environment.

sections.heading: What the Variant Map Shows
sections.text: The Ibn Masʿūd report survives in many books, but the spread is structurally misleading. The collector layer is wide. The report appears in Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Bazzār, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, and later Mahdī compilations. But the upper structure is narrow. The ordinary route is: > ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd → the Prophet The most stable early-looking wording is not the full later formula. It is the name-only form: This is the form found in the strongest-looking Sufyān routes. Al-Tirmidhī 2230, Aḥmad 3571, Aḥmad 3572, Aḥmad 3573, Aḥmad 4098, Aḥmad 4279, al-Bazzār’s Sufyān and al-Shaybānī routes, Ibn Ḥibbān 5954, and several Ṭabarānī routes preserve this simpler wording, or a close version of it. In this form, the report could support a general Ahl al-Bayt expectation without naming a single claimant. The father-name clause is different. It appears in selected PCL-level forms, especially through Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, Zāʾida, and ʿAmr b. Abī Qays. It is also bundled in Abū Dāwūd 4282, where Abū Dāwūd explicitly gathers several routes from ʿĀṣim and says their meanings are one, while also noting that Fiṭr adds the justice clause and that Sufyān’s wording lacks the father-name phrase. This is exactly the kind of place where a later harmonized matn can make a secondary clause look older than it is. | Wording family | Representative routes | What it suggests | |---|---|---| | Name-only core: “his name matches my name” | Sufyān al-Thawrī, Sufyān b. ʿUyayna, ʿUmar b. ʿUbayd, Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh, al-Shaybānī, ʿAbd al-Malik b. Abī Ghaniyya, Abū al-Aḥwaṣ asking ʿĀṣim directly | This is the recoverable base form of the ʿĀṣim report. It points to a Muḥammad from the Prophet’s house, but not yet to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. | | Father-name clause: “and his father’s name matches my father’s name” | Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, Zāʾida, ʿAmr b. Abī Qays, the composite Abū Dāwūd form, Ibn Ḥibbān 6824 | This is the politically exact form. It identifies a Muḥammad whose father is ʿAbdallāh. In the second/eighth century, that formula fits al-Nafs al-Zakiyya and later the Abbasid al-Mahdī. | | Justice-filling clause: “he fills the earth with justice” | Fiṭr, al-Aʿmash, Shuʿba, Sufyān b. ʿUyayna in some reports, ʿUthmān b. Shubruma, others | This looks like eschatological amplification. It converts a dynastic name notice into a full redeemer narrative. | | Expanded or anomalous forms | “from my community,” “his character matches my character,” black banners from the East | These are later ideological expansions, not evidence for a stable first/seventh-century Prophetic wording. | | Bypass attempts | Ṭabarānī 10208; al-Ḥākim 8434 | These are not independent early controls. One is a thin, name-only side-route. The other is judged fabricated and runs through a pro-ʿAlid/Rāfiḍī network. | The diagram below gives the structure behind the table.

sections.heading: ʿĀṣim Is the Recoverable Common Link
sections.text: ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd is famous as one of the transmitters of Qurʾānic recitation. The modern reader often meets him through the Ḥafṣ transmission of the Qurʾān. That can make a political hadith transmitted through him feel automatically secure. The rijāl material does not allow that simple move. Classical critics did not treat ʿĀṣim as an outright liar. They often respected him, especially in recitation. But the same material repeatedly distinguishes between his rank as a Qurʾān transmitter and his precision as a hadith transmitter. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal is reported to have said that ʿĀṣim was a righteous man, a reciter, and trustworthy, but that al-Aʿmash was more retentive in hadith. Yaʿqūb b. Sufyān says that in his hadith there was disturbance, while still calling him trustworthy. Ibn Saʿd calls him trustworthy but says he made many mistakes in hadith. That is exactly the profile one expects for a transmitter whose authority could carry material outward but whose solitary politically useful report should not be allowed to become early history by default. The point is not that ʿĀṣim must personally have invented every form of the report. The more careful claim is this: the report is not historically visible before his teaching circle, and the strongest formulation of the report changes below him. That makes ʿĀṣim the common-link layer for the base report and the partial common links below him the likely layer of editorial sharpening. This distinction matters because the father-name clause does not behave like an inherited stable phrase. It behaves like a political identifier added to a more general Ahl al-Bayt Mahdī expectation.

sections.heading: The Father-Name Clause Is the Fingerprint
sections.text: The phrase “his name matches my name” was useful but vague. Many Alids could be named Muḥammad. It created space for expectation without requiring one claimant. The phrase “and his father’s name matches my father’s name” closes that space. The Prophet’s name was Muḥammad. His father was ʿAbdallāh. A Mahdī whose name and father’s name match the Prophet’s is therefore Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. In the second/eighth-century political world, the obvious figure is Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan, al-Nafs al-Zakiyya. His father, ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan al-Maḥḍ, promoted him as the promised leader of the Prophet’s family. The historical reports about the al-Abwāʾ meeting make the connection explicit. After the murder of al-Walīd b. Yazīd in 126/744 and the turmoil that followed, Hāshimites gathered at al-Abwāʾ, between Mecca and Medina. In the Ḥasanid memory of the event, ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ called the family to pledge to his son: A second tradition names the future Abbasid rulers among the attendees. Ibrāhīm al-Imām, al-Saffāḥ, al-Manṣūr, Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī, ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ, and his sons Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm appear in the memory of the meeting. In that version, al-Manṣūr himself is made to say that people incline to no one more readily than this young man, meaning Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh, and the group pledges to him. These reports have to be read critically. Elad is right to treat the al-Abwāʾ cycle as a composite, post-revolt memory shaped by Ḥasanid anti-Abbasid polemic. But that caution helps the argument rather than weakening it. It shows that the memory of Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh as “the Mahdī” was part of the ideological struggle between the Ḥasanids and the Abbasids. The hadith formula does the same work in prophetic form. It turns a contested Hāshimid claim into foreknowledge.

sections.heading: The Hāshimid Blank: “al-Riḍā from the Family of Muḥammad”
sections.text: The larger political setting makes the report even clearer. The anti-Umayyad underground did not begin as a neatly separated Abbasid party on one side and a neatly separated Alid party on the other. It operated inside a broader Hāshimid revolutionary imagination. The slogan al-Riḍā min Āl Muḥammad, “the agreed-upon one from the family of Muḥammad,” was powerful precisely because it was vague. It allowed different factions to cooperate before the identity of the chosen leader was publicly fixed. That vagueness created a problem as soon as success became possible. Who, exactly, was al-Riḍā? The Ḥasanid answer was Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya. The Abbasid answer was different. Their claim drew on the alleged Abū Hāshim testament and the Khurāsānī daʿwa, then later on the black-banner apocalyptic language of the revolution. The Abbasids could claim the victorious army from the East. The Ḥasanids could claim the name formula. This is why the black-banner material matters. The report in al-Ḥākim 8434 is not merely a random weak parallel. It fuses the two revolutionary toolkits: black banners from the East and the Mahdī whose name and father’s name match the Prophet’s. That fusion is exactly what we should expect in a world where Hāshimid, ʿAlid, and Abbasid messianic symbols overlapped before being claimed by rival factions. The Abbasids then did something especially revealing. Al-Manṣūr’s own name was ʿAbdallāh. He named his heir Muḥammad and gave him the regnal title al-Mahdī. The Abbasid al-Mahdī was therefore also Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. The formula that fit al-Nafs al-Zakiyya could be co-opted by the dynasty that crushed him. This is not a coincidence to pass over quickly. It shows why the father-name report was so useful. It was a contested prophecy. The Ḥasanids could point to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan. The Abbasids could point to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. Muḥammad, al-Manṣūr’s son. The wording did not merely predict a future saint. It supplied a name-template usable in a succession struggle.

sections.heading: The Bypass Routes Do Not Rescue the Report
sections.text: A defender of the report might say that the ʿĀṣim common-link argument is too narrow because there are routes that seem to bypass him. Two routes matter most: the Ṭabarānī 10208 route through ʿAmr b. Murra and the al-Ḥākim 8434 route through Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and ʿAlqama. Neither route gives the report an early independent foundation. ### Ṭabarānī 10208: a weak side-route, not an early control Ṭabarānī 10208 runs: > Yūsuf b. Ḥawshab al-Shaybānī → Abū Yazīd al-Aʿwar → ʿAmr b. Murra → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Its wording is also not the dangerous wording. It says only: This route should not be rejected on chronological impossibility. The death dates do not make ʿAmr b. Murra hearing from Zirr impossible. The problem is more defensible: the route is thin, late in attestation, and does not carry the father-name clause. It may be an independent paraphrase of the name-only expectation, or it may be a side-route shaped by the ʿĀṣim tradition. Either way, it cannot establish the full Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh formula. ### al-Ḥākim 8434: the “bypass” that proves the context The al-Ḥākim 8434 route looks more dramatic because it bypasses Zirr and ʿĀṣim entirely. It runs through: > Ibn Abī Dārim → Ḥanān b. Sudayr → ʿAmr b. Qays → al-Ḥakam → Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī → ʿAlqama and ʿUbayda → Ibn Masʿūd Its matn combines the Mahdī name formula with black banners from the East. Al-Dhahabī’s judgement is blunt: “This is fabricated.” That should already prevent it from functioning as clean independent support. But the rijāl context makes it more important than a normal weak route. It is a documentary link to the very kind of partisan environment this thesis predicts. Al-Ḥākim’s own shaykh for the report, Ibn Abī Dārim, was a Kūfan Shīʿī/Rāfiḍī figure whom al-Dhahabī treats with suspicion. Al-Ḥākim himself is reported to have called him a Rāfiḍī and not trustworthy. Al-Dhahabī’s entry says that Ibn Abī Dārim composed material attacking some Companions and was not reliable in transmission. The same polemical profile is visible in the reports associated with him: the Fāṭima miscarriage accusation against ʿUmar and a sectarian tafsīr gloss making Pharaoh stand for ʿUmar. The bridge through Ḥanān b. Sudayr is just as revealing. Ḥanān belongs to a Kūfan Shīʿī Ṣayrafī family. Al-ʿUqaylī’s entry preserves material linking Ḥanān’s transmission environment to Sudayf al-Makkī, a poet and activist who attached himself to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya when he rose in Medina. The material says Sudayf inclined to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh, pledged to him, became one of his inner circle, attacked Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, exalted the Banū ʿAlī, and recited verses from Muḥammad’s own minbar calling him the Mahdī. In the same report-cycle, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is made to disown their material as having no foundation. That makes al-Ḥākim 8434 the opposite of what a defender needs. A true independent bypass would have to be earlier, cleaner, and less ideologically fitted. This one is later, judged fabricated, and runs straight through the pro-ʿAlid agitation network around the Ḥasanid Mahdī claim. Its black-banner language also belongs to the shared Hāshimid revolutionary apocalyptic vocabulary of the 120s–130s, later monopolized by the Abbasid Khurāsānī daʿwa.

sections.heading: Why Muḥammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya Fits the Hadith
sections.text: The historical fit is not limited to the name. Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya occupied the exact political role that the report creates. He was a Ḥasanid, from the Prophet’s family through ʿAlī and Fāṭima. His father was ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan al-Maḥḍ, a figure of extraordinary Alid pedigree because he was connected to both Ḥasanid and Ḥusaynid descent. The Ḥasanid claim did not present Muḥammad merely as a rebel. It presented him as the chosen one from the Prophet’s family. The al-Abwāʾ reports remember his father saying, “you know he is the Mahdī.” Under the Umayyads, the claim could remain within the broader anti-Umayyad Hāshimid movement. Under the Abbasids, it became a direct challenge. Al-Manṣūr hunted the Ḥasanids, imprisoned ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ and his relatives, forced the family into chains, and eventually crushed Muḥammad’s revolt in Medina in 145/762. Elad’s study emphasizes that this revolt was not a minor family quarrel. It was a politico-religious challenge to Abbasid legitimacy, supported by a wide range of non-Ṭālibī actors as well as Alid factions. The supporter map also matters for hadith criticism. The revolt attracted scholars, jurists, and transmitters. Mālik b. Anas is famously connected in the sources to legal reasoning that undercut coerced allegiance to the Abbasids. Sufyān al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa, Hishām b. ʿUrwa, and others appear in the broader support or sympathy lists with varying degrees of certainty. In Kūfa and Baṣra, the Zaydī and pro-ʿAlid networks around Muḥammad and his brother Ibrāhīm were especially important. That is precisely the kind of world where a Prophetic report naming a Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh from the Prophet’s family would have political value.

sections.heading: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and the Rival Alid Memory
sections.text: The Ḥasanid claim was not accepted by all Alids. The reports about Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq at al-Abwāʾ are important because they show a rival Alid response to the same claim. In these traditions, Jaʿfar refuses to pledge to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh and predicts Abbasid victory. Some versions have him point to al-Saffāḥ or al-Manṣūr; others have him foretell that Muḥammad and his brother Ibrāhīm will be killed. These reports are not neutral historical recordings either. Elad reads much of this material as Ḥusaynid/Imāmī memory, shaped after the failure of the Ḥasanid revolt, in order to justify Jaʿfar’s quietism and to distinguish the true Imāmī line from the activist Ḥasanid line. This is useful because it shows how crowded the field was. Different Alid groups fought over the meaning of the same events. The Ḥasanids had a Mahdī claim. The Ḥusaynid/Imāmī memory denied it. The Abbasids crushed it and later appropriated parts of it. The hadith formula belongs in that contested space. It is not floating above history. It is a scriptural weapon in a world where the identity of the rightful leader from the Prophet’s family was being fought over.

sections.heading: How the Matn Developed
sections.text: The report’s development can be summarized as a sequence of increasingly specific political meaning. A Name-only expectation A man from the Prophet’s household will rule; his name matches the Prophet’s name. This is broad and reusable. Muḥammad → B Father-name clause The father’s name also matches the Prophet’s father. This narrows the target to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh → C Justice redeemer layer The claimant is no longer only a dynastic figure. He fills the earth with justice after injustice. messianic expansion → D Black-banner fusion The name formula merges with eastern-banner apocalyptic, the shared revolutionary language later identified with the Abbasids. Khurāsān / East This sequence explains why the same hadith complex can serve more than one party. A general Ahl al-Bayt Muḥammad expectation could serve many. The father-name clause served the Ḥasanid Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. The black-banner form served the Abbasid revolutionary imagination, or at least the Hāshimid apocalyptic vocabulary that the Abbasids made dynastic. The later Abbasid title al-Mahdī then gave the dynasty its own Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh.

sections.heading: Objections
sections.text: ### “But Abū Dāwūd preserves the father-name clause.” He does, but Abū Dāwūd 4282 is a composite report. It brings together several PCLs from ʿĀṣim: ʿUmar b. ʿUbayd, Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh, Sufyān, Zāʾida, and Fiṭr. The collector explicitly says the wording is by meaning, and the report itself notes differences between the PCLs. Sufyān’s wording is the name-only “a man from my household whose name matches my name.” Fiṭr adds the justice clause. The composite form is not proof that every branch carried the father clause from the beginning. ### “But Ibn Ḥibbān 6824 has Sufyān with the father clause.” That report should be registered, but it should not control the whole family against the broader Sufyān pattern. The Sufyān material in al-Tirmidhī, Aḥmad, al-Bazzār, and Ṭabarānī is overwhelmingly name-only. A single later or harmonized Sufyān form with the father clause is better explained as contamination from the expanded wording than as the original form from which the name-only Sufyān family somehow descended. ### “But there are routes through other Companions.” There are broader Mahdī traditions from ʿAlī, Abū Saʿīd, Umm Salama, Abū Hurayra, and others. That does not solve the Ibn Masʿūd name-and-father-name report. The question here is not whether later Muslims circulated many Mahdī reports. The question is whether the specific formula name = my name, father = my father is early and independent. The most important parallel that carries the same identifier, the Qurra al-Muzanī route, runs through the discredited Baṣran family of Dāwūd b. al-Muḥabbar / al-Muḥabbar b. Qaḥdham, and al-Bazzār himself points away from it toward the better-known Abū Saʿīd line. That looks like a migrating formula, not an inherited Prophetic core. ### “But ʿAmr b. Murra could have heard from Zirr.” Yes. The chronology does not make that impossible. The rejection should not rest on a lifespan argument. It rests on attestation and content. Ṭabarānī 10208 is a lone late side-route with a thin lower chain, and it does not carry the father-name clause. Even if one accepts it as an independent name-only expectation, it does not prove the Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh formula. ### “But ʿĀṣim died before the 145 revolt.” That objection misunderstands the argument. The Ḥasanid Mahdī claim did not begin only when Muḥammad rose in 145. The al-Abwāʾ memory places the claim in the late Umayyad crisis after 126. ʿĀṣim died around 127/128, exactly on the edge of that world. The father-name clause also need not be ʿĀṣim’s original wording. The evidence suggests a base ʿĀṣim report that was sharpened at the PCL layer by transmitters active in the Muḥammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya window.

sections.heading: The Most Likely Reconstruction
sections.text: The most economical reconstruction is as follows. First, a Kūfan Ahl al-Bayt expectation circulated in ʿĀṣim’s circle: a man from the Prophet’s household, named like the Prophet, would rule. This was vague enough to belong to the wider Hāshimid revolutionary environment. Second, as the Ḥasanid claim of Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya sharpened, some transmitters expanded the formula by adding the father-name clause. This turned a general Muḥammad expectation into a Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh identifier. Third, the report absorbed justice-restoration language and, in a fabricated bypass route, black-banner language from the East. These expansions moved the report from a dynastic name notice into full apocalyptic propaganda. Fourth, after the Abbasid victory, the same formula became contestable. The Abbasids could crush the Ḥasanid Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh while naming their own heir Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh and calling him al-Mahdī. The formula survived because it could be reinterpreted after its first political target failed.

sections.heading: Source notes
sections.text: 1. For the main Ibn Masʿūd route through ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd, see Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, Musnad, nos. 3571–3573, 4098, 4279; Abū Dāwūd, Sunan, no. 4282; al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ, nos. 2230–2231; Ibn Ḥibbān, Ṣaḥīḥ, nos. 5954, 6824–6825; al-Bazzār, Musnad, nos. 1597–1599; al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-kabīr, Ibn Masʿūd entries nos. 10208–10230. 2. On the father-name clause through Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, Zāʾida, and ʿAmr b. Abī Qays, see Abū Dāwūd 4282; al-Ṭabarānī 10213, 10222, 10224; Ibn Ḥibbān 6824. The key control is that the strongest-looking Sufyān / Aḥmad / al-Tirmidhī name-only forms do not require the father-name clause. 3. For the lone non-ʿĀṣim side-route, see al-Ṭabarānī 10208: Yūsuf b. Ḥawshab → Abū Yazīd al-Aʿwar → ʿAmr b. Murra → Zirr → Ibn Masʿūd. Its wording is name-only: yuwāfiqu ismuhu ismī. 4. For the black-banner bypass judged fabricated, see al-Ḥākim, al-Mustadrak, no. 8434, with al-Dhahabī’s judgement: hādhā mawḍūʿ. Compare the rijāl notices on Ibn Abī Dārim in al-Dhahabī and al-Ḥākim, and the entry on Ḥanān b. Sudayr / Sudayf al-Makkī in al-ʿUqaylī, al-Ḍuʿafāʾ. 5. On ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd’s mixed rijāl profile, compare Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt; Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Jarḥ wa-l-taʿdīl; Yaʿqūb b. Sufyān, al-Maʿrifa wa-l-tārīkh; al-ʿUqaylī, al-Ḍuʿafāʾ; al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-kamāl; al-Dhahabī, Siyar aʿlām al-nubalāʾ. 6. On Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya, the al-Abwāʾ pledge, the role of ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ, the revolt of 145/762, and the supporter map, see Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī, Maqātil al-Ṭālibiyyīn; al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk; al-Balādhurī, Ansāb al-ashrāf; Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil; and Amikam Elad, The Rebellion of Muḥammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya in 145/762: Ṭālibīs and Early ʿAbbāsīs in Conflict (Leiden: Brill, 2016). 7. On the Ḥusaynid / Imāmī counter-memory of Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and the Ḥasanid claim, see Elad, Rebellion, Appendix 3, especially the sections on the struggle between Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan. 8. On the Abbasid daʿwa, the slogan al-Riḍā min Āl Muḥammad, and the ambiguity of the Hāshimid revolutionary claim, see Patricia Crone, “On the Meaning of the ʿAbbāsid Call to al-Riḍā,” in The Islamic World from Classical to Modern Times: Essays in Honor of Bernard Lewis (Princeton: Darwin Press, 1989), 95–111; Moshe Sharon, Black Banners from the East; and Elad, Rebellion, Introduction. 9. On black-banner apocalyptic and its Abbasid / anti-Abbasid uses, see David Cook, Studies in Muslim Apocalyptic (Princeton: Darwin Press, 2002), especially the discussions of historical apocalypses, the black banners, and al-Nafs al-Zakiyya as an apocalyptic sign. { .mahdiFlow { margin: 2.2rem 0; fullText: The Report and the Name Problem The report looks simple only when it is read as timeless eschatology. A man from the Prophet’s household will appear near the end of time. His name will match the Prophet’s name. His father’s name will match the Prophet’s father’s name. He will restore justice. In later Sunnī reception, this became one of the most familiar Mahdī proof-texts. The historical problem is that the report does not merely describe a future redeemer. It identifies him by a highly specific name formula. A bare “his name matches my name” points to any Muḥammad from the Prophet’s family. The fuller formula, “and his father’s name matches my father’s name,” narrows the referent to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. That was not an abstract possibility in the second/eighth century. It was the exact name of the most famous Ḥasanid messianic claimant of the early Abbasid period: Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan, known as al-Nafs al-Zakiyya. The question is therefore not whether later Sunnī books contain the report. They do. The question is when this formula became attached to a Prophetic isnād and why the report’s most charged wording points so neatly to a live political claimant who rebelled against al-Manṣūr in 145/762. This does not require the argument that every later transmitter in the books was lying. It also does not require a cartoon picture of ʿĀṣim as a villain. The evidence points to a more precise conclusion. The report becomes historically visible at ʿĀṣim’s circle. The clause that identifies Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh belongs to the partial common-link layer and is strongest in transmitters whose sectarian or political location already fits the Ḥasanid Mahdī environment. What the Variant Map Shows The Ibn Masʿūd report survives in many books, but the spread is structurally misleading. The collector layer is wide. The report appears in Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Bazzār, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, and later Mahdī compilations. But the upper structure is narrow. The ordinary route is: ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd → the Prophet The most stable early-looking wording is not the full later formula. It is the name-only form: This is the form found in the strongest-looking Sufyān routes. Al-Tirmidhī 2230, Aḥmad 3571, Aḥmad 3572, Aḥmad 3573, Aḥmad 4098, Aḥmad 4279, al-Bazzār’s Sufyān and al-Shaybānī routes, Ibn Ḥibbān 5954, and several Ṭabarānī routes preserve this simpler wording, or a close version of it. In this form, the report could support a general Ahl al-Bayt expectation without naming a single claimant. The father-name clause is different. It appears in selected PCL-level forms, especially through Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, Zāʾida, and ʿAmr b. Abī Qays. It is also bundled in Abū Dāwūd 4282, where Abū Dāwūd explicitly gathers several routes from ʿĀṣim and says their meanings are one, while also noting that Fiṭr adds the justice clause and that Sufyān’s wording lacks the father-name phrase. This is exactly the kind of place where a later harmonized matn can make a secondary clause look older than it is. | Wording family | Representative routes | What it suggests | |---|---|---| | Name-only core: “his name matches my name” | Sufyān al-Thawrī, Sufyān b. ʿUyayna, ʿUmar b. ʿUbayd, Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh, al-Shaybānī, ʿAbd al-Malik b. Abī Ghaniyya, Abū al-Aḥwaṣ asking ʿĀṣim directly | This is the recoverable base form of the ʿĀṣim report. It points to a Muḥammad from the Prophet’s house, but not yet to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. | | Father-name clause: “and his father’s name matches my father’s name” | Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, Zāʾida, ʿAmr b. Abī Qays, the composite Abū Dāwūd form, Ibn Ḥibbān 6824 | This is the politically exact form. It identifies a Muḥammad whose father is ʿAbdallāh. In the second/eighth century, that formula fits al-Nafs al-Zakiyya and later the Abbasid al-Mahdī. | | Justice-filling clause: “he fills the earth with justice” | Fiṭr, al-Aʿmash, Shuʿba, Sufyān b. ʿUyayna in some reports, ʿUthmān b. Shubruma, others | This looks like eschatological amplification. It converts a dynastic name notice into a full redeemer narrative. | | Expanded or anomalous forms | “from my community,” “his character matches my character,” black banners from the East | These are later ideological expansions, not evidence for a stable first/seventh-century Prophetic wording. | | Bypass attempts | Ṭabarānī 10208; al-Ḥākim 8434 | These are not independent early controls. One is a thin, name-only side-route. The other is judged fabricated and runs through a pro-ʿAlid/Rāfiḍī network. | The diagram below gives the structure behind the table. ʿĀṣim Is the Recoverable Common Link ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd is famous as one of the transmitters of Qurʾānic recitation. The modern reader often meets him through the Ḥafṣ transmission of the Qurʾān. That can make a political hadith transmitted through him feel automatically secure. The rijāl material does not allow that simple move. Classical critics did not treat ʿĀṣim as an outright liar. They often respected him, especially in recitation. But the same material repeatedly distinguishes between his rank as a Qurʾān transmitter and his precision as a hadith transmitter. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal is reported to have said that ʿĀṣim was a righteous man, a reciter, and trustworthy, but that al-Aʿmash was more retentive in hadith. Yaʿqūb b. Sufyān says that in his hadith there was disturbance, while still calling him trustworthy. Ibn Saʿd calls him trustworthy but says he made many mistakes in hadith. That is exactly the profile one expects for a transmitter whose authority could carry material outward but whose solitary politically useful report should not be allowed to become early history by default. The point is not that ʿĀṣim must personally have invented every form of the report. The more careful claim is this: the report is not historically visible before his teaching circle, and the strongest formulation of the report changes below him. That makes ʿĀṣim the common-link layer for the base report and the partial common links below him the likely layer of editorial sharpening. This distinction matters because the father-name clause does not behave like an inherited stable phrase. It behaves like a political identifier added to a more general Ahl al-Bayt Mahdī expectation. The Father-Name Clause Is the Fingerprint The phrase “his name matches my name” was useful but vague. Many Alids could be named Muḥammad. It created space for expectation without requiring one claimant. The phrase “and his father’s name matches my father’s name” closes that space. The Prophet’s name was Muḥammad. His father was ʿAbdallāh. A Mahdī whose name and father’s name match the Prophet’s is therefore Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. In the second/eighth-century political world, the obvious figure is Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan, al-Nafs al-Zakiyya. His father, ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan al-Maḥḍ, promoted him as the promised leader of the Prophet’s family. The historical reports about the al-Abwāʾ meeting make the connection explicit. After the murder of al-Walīd b. Yazīd in 126/744 and the turmoil that followed, Hāshimites gathered at al-Abwāʾ, between Mecca and Medina. In the Ḥasanid memory of the event, ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ called the family to pledge to his son: A second tradition names the future Abbasid rulers among the attendees. Ibrāhīm al-Imām, al-Saffāḥ, al-Manṣūr, Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī, ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ, and his sons Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm appear in the memory of the meeting. In that version, al-Manṣūr himself is made to say that people incline to no one more readily than this young man, meaning Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh, and the group pledges to him. These reports have to be read critically. Elad is right to treat the al-Abwāʾ cycle as a composite, post-revolt memory shaped by Ḥasanid anti-Abbasid polemic. But that caution helps the argument rather than weakening it. It shows that the memory of Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh as “the Mahdī” was part of the ideological struggle between the Ḥasanids and the Abbasids. The hadith formula does the same work in prophetic form. It turns a contested Hāshimid claim into foreknowledge. The Hāshimid Blank: “al-Riḍā from the Family of Muḥammad” The larger political setting makes the report even clearer. The anti-Umayyad underground did not begin as a neatly separated Abbasid party on one side and a neatly separated Alid party on the other. It operated inside a broader Hāshimid revolutionary imagination. The slogan al-Riḍā min Āl Muḥammad, “the agreed-upon one from the family of Muḥammad,” was powerful precisely because it was vague. It allowed different factions to cooperate before the identity of the chosen leader was publicly fixed. That vagueness created a problem as soon as success became possible. Who, exactly, was al-Riḍā? The Ḥasanid answer was Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya. The Abbasid answer was different. Their claim drew on the alleged Abū Hāshim testament and the Khurāsānī daʿwa, then later on the black-banner apocalyptic language of the revolution. The Abbasids could claim the victorious army from the East. The Ḥasanids could claim the name formula. This is why the black-banner material matters. The report in al-Ḥākim 8434 is not merely a random weak parallel. It fuses the two revolutionary toolkits: black banners from the East and the Mahdī whose name and father’s name match the Prophet’s. That fusion is exactly what we should expect in a world where Hāshimid, ʿAlid, and Abbasid messianic symbols overlapped before being claimed by rival factions. The Abbasids then did something especially revealing. Al-Manṣūr’s own name was ʿAbdallāh. He named his heir Muḥammad and gave him the regnal title al-Mahdī. The Abbasid al-Mahdī was therefore also Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. The formula that fit al-Nafs al-Zakiyya could be co-opted by the dynasty that crushed him. This is not a coincidence to pass over quickly. It shows why the father-name report was so useful. It was a contested prophecy. The Ḥasanids could point to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan. The Abbasids could point to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. Muḥammad, al-Manṣūr’s son. The wording did not merely predict a future saint. It supplied a name-template usable in a succession struggle. The Bypass Routes Do Not Rescue the Report A defender of the report might say that the ʿĀṣim common-link argument is too narrow because there are routes that seem to bypass him. Two routes matter most: the Ṭabarānī 10208 route through ʿAmr b. Murra and the al-Ḥākim 8434 route through Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and ʿAlqama. Neither route gives the report an early independent foundation. Ṭabarānī 10208: a weak side-route, not an early control Ṭabarānī 10208 runs: Yūsuf b. Ḥawshab al-Shaybānī → Abū Yazīd al-Aʿwar → ʿAmr b. Murra → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Its wording is also not the dangerous wording. It says only: This route should not be rejected on chronological impossibility. The death dates do not make ʿAmr b. Murra hearing from Zirr impossible. The problem is more defensible: the route is thin, late in attestation, and does not carry the father-name clause. It may be an independent paraphrase of the name-only expectation, or it may be a side-route shaped by the ʿĀṣim tradition. Either way, it cannot establish the full Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh formula. al-Ḥākim 8434: the “bypass” that proves the context The al-Ḥākim 8434 route looks more dramatic because it bypasses Zirr and ʿĀṣim entirely. It runs through: Ibn Abī Dārim → Ḥanān b. Sudayr → ʿAmr b. Qays → al-Ḥakam → Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī → ʿAlqama and ʿUbayda → Ibn Masʿūd Its matn combines the Mahdī name formula with black banners from the East. Al-Dhahabī’s judgement is blunt: “This is fabricated.” That should already prevent it from functioning as clean independent support. But the rijāl context makes it more important than a normal weak route. It is a documentary link to the very kind of partisan environment this thesis predicts. Al-Ḥākim’s own shaykh for the report, Ibn Abī Dārim, was a Kūfan Shīʿī/Rāfiḍī figure whom al-Dhahabī treats with suspicion. Al-Ḥākim himself is reported to have called him a Rāfiḍī and not trustworthy. Al-Dhahabī’s entry says that Ibn Abī Dārim composed material attacking some Companions and was not reliable in transmission. The same polemical profile is visible in the reports associated with him: the Fāṭima miscarriage accusation against ʿUmar and a sectarian tafsīr gloss making Pharaoh stand for ʿUmar. The bridge through Ḥanān b. Sudayr is just as revealing. Ḥanān belongs to a Kūfan Shīʿī Ṣayrafī family. Al-ʿUqaylī’s entry preserves material linking Ḥanān’s transmission environment to Sudayf al-Makkī, a poet and activist who attached himself to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya when he rose in Medina. The material says Sudayf inclined to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh, pledged to him, became one of his inner circle, attacked Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, exalted the Banū ʿAlī, and recited verses from Muḥammad’s own minbar calling him the Mahdī. In the same report-cycle, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is made to disown their material as having no foundation. That makes al-Ḥākim 8434 the opposite of what a defender needs. A true independent bypass would have to be earlier, cleaner, and less ideologically fitted. This one is later, judged fabricated, and runs straight through the pro-ʿAlid agitation network around the Ḥasanid Mahdī claim. Its black-banner language also belongs to the shared Hāshimid revolutionary apocalyptic vocabulary of the 120s–130s, later monopolized by the Abbasid Khurāsānī daʿwa. Why Muḥammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya Fits the Hadith The historical fit is not limited to the name. Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya occupied the exact political role that the report creates. He was a Ḥasanid, from the Prophet’s family through ʿAlī and Fāṭima. His father was ʿAbdallāh b. al-Ḥasan al-Maḥḍ, a figure of extraordinary Alid pedigree because he was connected to both Ḥasanid and Ḥusaynid descent. The Ḥasanid claim did not present Muḥammad merely as a rebel. It presented him as the chosen one from the Prophet’s family. The al-Abwāʾ reports remember his father saying, “you know he is the Mahdī.” Under the Umayyads, the claim could remain within the broader anti-Umayyad Hāshimid movement. Under the Abbasids, it became a direct challenge. Al-Manṣūr hunted the Ḥasanids, imprisoned ʿAbdallāh al-Maḥḍ and his relatives, forced the family into chains, and eventually crushed Muḥammad’s revolt in Medina in 145/762. Elad’s study emphasizes that this revolt was not a minor family quarrel. It was a politico-religious challenge to Abbasid legitimacy, supported by a wide range of non-Ṭālibī actors as well as Alid factions. The supporter map also matters for hadith criticism. The revolt attracted scholars, jurists, and transmitters. Mālik b. Anas is famously connected in the sources to legal reasoning that undercut coerced allegiance to the Abbasids. Sufyān al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa, Hishām b. ʿUrwa, and others appear in the broader support or sympathy lists with varying degrees of certainty. In Kūfa and Baṣra, the Zaydī and pro-ʿAlid networks around Muḥammad and his brother Ibrāhīm were especially important. That is precisely the kind of world where a Prophetic report naming a Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh from the Prophet’s family would have political value. Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and the Rival Alid Memory The Ḥasanid claim was not accepted by all Alids. The reports about Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq at al-Abwāʾ are important because they show a rival Alid response to the same claim. In these traditions, Jaʿfar refuses to pledge to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh and predicts Abbasid victory. Some versions have him point to al-Saffāḥ or al-Manṣūr; others have him foretell that Muḥammad and his brother Ibrāhīm will be killed. These reports are not neutral historical recordings either. Elad reads much of this material as Ḥusaynid/Imāmī memory, shaped after the failure of the Ḥasanid revolt, in order to justify Jaʿfar’s quietism and to distinguish the true Imāmī line from the activist Ḥasanid line. This is useful because it shows how crowded the field was. Different Alid groups fought over the meaning of the same events. The Ḥasanids had a Mahdī claim. The Ḥusaynid/Imāmī memory denied it. The Abbasids crushed it and later appropriated parts of it. The hadith formula belongs in that contested space. It is not floating above history. It is a scriptural weapon in a world where the identity of the rightful leader from the Prophet’s family was being fought over. How the Matn Developed The report’s development can be summarized as a sequence of increasingly specific political meaning. A Name-only expectation A man from the Prophet’s household will rule; his name matches the Prophet’s name. This is broad and reusable. Muḥammad → B Father-name clause The father’s name also matches the Prophet’s father. This narrows the target to Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh → C Justice redeemer layer The claimant is no longer only a dynastic figure. He fills the earth with justice after injustice. messianic expansion → D Black-banner fusion The name formula merges with eastern-banner apocalyptic, the shared revolutionary language later identified with the Abbasids. Khurāsān / East This sequence explains why the same hadith complex can serve more than one party. A general Ahl al-Bayt Muḥammad expectation could serve many. The father-name clause served the Ḥasanid Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. The black-banner form served the Abbasid revolutionary imagination, or at least the Hāshimid apocalyptic vocabulary that the Abbasids made dynastic. The later Abbasid title al-Mahdī then gave the dynasty its own Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh. Objections “But Abū Dāwūd preserves the father-name clause.” He does, but Abū Dāwūd 4282 is a composite report. It brings together several PCLs from ʿĀṣim: ʿUmar b. ʿUbayd, Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh, Sufyān, Zāʾida, and Fiṭr. The collector explicitly says the wording is by meaning, and the report itself notes differences between the PCLs. Sufyān’s wording is the name-only “a man from my household whose name matches my name.” Fiṭr adds the justice clause. The composite form is not proof that every branch carried the father clause from the beginning. “But Ibn Ḥibbān 6824 has Sufyān with the father clause.” That report should be registered, but it should not control the whole family against the broader Sufyān pattern. The Sufyān material in al-Tirmidhī, Aḥmad, al-Bazzār, and Ṭabarānī is overwhelmingly name-only. A single later or harmonized Sufyān form with the father clause is better explained as contamination from the expanded wording than as the original form from which the name-only Sufyān family somehow descended. “But there are routes through other Companions.” There are broader Mahdī traditions from ʿAlī, Abū Saʿīd, Umm Salama, Abū Hurayra, and others. That does not solve the Ibn Masʿūd name-and-father-name report. The question here is not whether later Muslims circulated many Mahdī reports. The question is whether the specific formula name = my name, father = my father is early and independent. The most important parallel that carries the same identifier, the Qurra al-Muzanī route, runs through the discredited Baṣran family of Dāwūd b. al-Muḥabbar / al-Muḥabbar b. Qaḥdham, and al-Bazzār himself points away from it toward the better-known Abū Saʿīd line. That looks like a migrating formula, not an inherited Prophetic core. “But ʿAmr b. Murra could have heard from Zirr.” Yes. The chronology does not make that impossible. The rejection should not rest on a lifespan argument. It rests on attestation and content. Ṭabarānī 10208 is a lone late side-route with a thin lower chain, and it does not carry the father-name clause. Even if one accepts it as an independent name-only expectation, it does not prove the Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh formula. “But ʿĀṣim died before the 145 revolt.” That objection misunderstands the argument. The Ḥasanid Mahdī claim did not begin only when Muḥammad rose in 145. The al-Abwāʾ memory places the claim in the late Umayyad crisis after 126. ʿĀṣim died around 127/128, exactly on the edge of that world. The father-name clause also need not be ʿĀṣim’s original wording. The evidence suggests a base ʿĀṣim report that was sharpened at the PCL layer by transmitters active in the Muḥammad al-Nafs al-Zakiyya window. The Most Likely Reconstruction The most economical reconstruction is as follows. First, a Kūfan Ahl al-Bayt expectation circulated in ʿĀṣim’s circle: a man from the Prophet’s household, named like the Prophet, would rule. This was vague enough to belong to the wider Hāshimid revolutionary environment. Second, as the Ḥasanid claim of Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh al-Nafs al-Zakiyya sharpened, some transmitters expanded the formula by adding the father-name clause. This turned a general Muḥammad expectation into a Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh identifier. Third, the report absorbed justice-restoration language and, in a fabricated bypass route, black-banner language from the East. These expansions moved the report from a dynastic name notice into full apocalyptic propaganda. Fourth, after the Abbasid victory, the same formula became contestable. The Abbasids could crush the Ḥasanid Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh while naming their own heir Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh and calling him al-Mahdī. title: The Kaysanite Mahdi Hadith: Abu al-Tufayl and the Ibn al-Hanafiyya Problem
description: An isnād-cum-matn analysis of the Ali Mahdi reports, arguing that the Abu al-Tufayl route fits the earliest Kaysanite use of Mahdi language for Muhammad b. al-Hanafiyya.

sections.heading: The Report
sections.text: The ʿAlī Mahdī reports are usually read backward from later Sunnī doctrine. A reader already knows the later Mahdī and therefore assumes that the report is simply about a future end-time redeemer from the Prophet’s household. That is not how the report looks when it is placed in its earliest political setting. The wording is strikingly broad. It does not say “from the descendants of Fāṭima.” It does not name al-Ḥasan or al-Ḥusayn. It does not give the familiar later name formula, “his name matches my name and his father’s name matches my father’s name.” It says only that a man from us, or from my family, will arise and fill the world with justice after oppression. That is exactly the kind of wording that could support Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya, the third famous son of ʿAlī, whose followers made him a messianic figure after the trauma of Karbalāʾ and the revolt of al-Mukhtār in Kūfa. The article does not need to claim that every later collector knew the original polemic. Later Sunnī reception could preserve the report as a generic Mahdī text after its first political target had faded. The task is to explain why this particular wording, through this particular network, appears where it does.

sections.heading: Two ʿAlī Reports, One Kaysanite Problem
sections.text: The surviving material forms two related families. The first is the Abū al-Ṭufayl family, preserved in Abū Dāwūd and Aḥmad: > ʿAlī → Abū al-Ṭufayl → al-Qāsim b. Abī Bazzah → Fiṭr b. Khalīfa → later collectors Its main wording is the justice-filling report: if only one day remained, God would send a man from the Prophet’s family to fill the earth with justice. The second is the Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya family, preserved in Ibn Mājah and Aḥmad: > ʿAlī → Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya → Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya → Yāsīn al-ʿIjlī → later collectors Its wording is shorter and even more revealing: This second route does not pass through Abū al-Ṭufayl, but it names the political world that makes the first route intelligible. A report about the Mahdī from the Household is transmitted through the family of Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya itself. That does not prove the Abū al-Ṭufayl report by independent attestation. It shows that the same ʿAlid-Hanafid memory world preserved Mahdī material in more than one channel.

sections.heading: Why Abū al-Ṭufayl Matters
sections.text: Abū al-Ṭufayl ʿĀmir b. Wāthila is not just a name in a chain. He is one of the few Companion figures whose political profile matters directly for the report. He was remembered as the last surviving Companion to have seen the Prophet, a supporter of ʿAlī, and a participant in ʿAlid politics. The historical and biographical reports also remember him as connected with al-Mukhtār b. Abī ʿUbayd, the Kūfan rebel who built his movement around Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya. The point is not merely that Abū al-Ṭufayl “liked ʿAlī.” Many transmitters did. The sharper point is that the report’s wording is precisely the kind of wording needed by the Kaysanite cause. It allows the promised figure to be from ʿAlī’s house without restricting him to the Fāṭimid Ḥasanid or Ḥusaynid line. That is what makes Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya possible. Later Sunnī Mahdī doctrine often solved the problem by placing the Mahdī through Fāṭima, usually through Ḥasan or Ḥusayn. This report does not. It preserves an earlier, less specified Alid expectation. That lack of specification is not a weakness in the Kaysanite reading. It is the clue.

sections.heading: The Kaysanite Setting
sections.text: The Kaysanite movement grew out of the political and theological aftermath of Karbalāʾ. Al-Mukhtār’s revolt in Kūfa, 66–67 AH, claimed to avenge al-Ḥusayn’s blood and mobilized support in the name of Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya. Muḥammad himself may have remained cautious or ambiguous, but the movement surrounding his name was not cautious. It presented him as the rightful leader from the House of ʿAlī. After Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya died, some of his followers refused to treat his death as final. In later heresiographical memory, a Kaysanite strand claimed that he was hidden at Mount Raḍwā and would return. This is one of the earliest Islamic settings where Mahdī, hidden return, and the restoration of justice converge around a named Alid figure. That matters for the hadith because the report does not need to say “Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya” explicitly. It only needs to say enough to make him fit: 1 “A man from us” Broad enough for ʿAlī’s non-Fāṭimid son, Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya. 2 “Ahl al-Bayt” Household language gives sacred legitimacy without naming the Ḥasanid or Ḥusaynid line. 3 “Justice after oppression” The slogan fits a defeated pro-ʿAlid movement explaining Umayyad violence and waiting for reversal. 4 “Rectified in one night” The quiescent or ambiguous claimant can suddenly become the divinely prepared leader. This is why the report should not be treated as an isolated pious saying. It is a theological solution to a factional problem. The Kaysanite movement needed a way to turn Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya’s ambiguous public role into a divinely timed mission. “God will rectify him in one night” does exactly that.

sections.heading: The Matn Is Not Fāṭimid Enough for Later Sunnism
sections.text: A useful way to test the report is to compare what it does not say. It does not contain the later Sunnī clause found in Abū Dāwūd 4284, where the Mahdī is said to be from the descendants of Fāṭima. It does not contain the Ibn Masʿūd name formula, “his name matches my name.” It does not tie the Mahdī to al-Ḥasan. It does not tie him to al-Ḥusayn. It does not specify a father named ʿAbdallāh. It is open-textured. That openness makes sense before later Mahdī doctrine hardened. In the earliest Alid messianic environment, several claimants could be imagined. The report’s vagueness is therefore politically functional. It lets the hearer complete the referent from the factional setting. For a Kaysanite audience, the completion is obvious: the man from ʿAlī’s house who will bring justice is Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya.

sections.heading: Fiṭr b. Khalīfa: The Lower Proliferator
sections.text: Fiṭr b. Khalīfa is the key lower transmitter in the Abū al-Ṭufayl family. Classical critics do not present him as a simple liar. Some call him trustworthy or acceptable. But his sectarian profile is exactly what matters here. He is a Kūfan transmitter, repeatedly described with Shīʿī leanings, and in some reports more sharply as a khashabī or extreme Shīʿī. Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh is reported to have avoided him because of his bad doctrine. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal is reported to have regarded him as reliable in hadith while still noting his Shīʿism. This is the same pattern we meet in other politically useful reports. The problem is not that the lower transmitter is automatically worthless. The problem is that a politically ideal matn is carried by a politically fitted network. Fiṭr is the sort of transmitter who could preserve, polish, or promote an Alid Mahdī report without needing to invent the whole thing himself. The Abū al-Ṭufayl layer gives the motive. Fiṭr gives the later Kūfan channel.

sections.heading: The Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya Family Route
sections.text: The Ibn Mājah and Aḥmad route is often treated as a separate corroboration. It is better read as a collateral witness to the same ideological environment. The chain runs through Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya from his father, Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya, from ʿAlī. Its wording says that the Mahdī is from the Household and that God will rectify him in one night. The family line is the entire point. The Mahdī saying is being carried through the son of the very figure whose followers made him a Mahdī. This is not a neutral accident. If a tradition about the Mahdī from the Household travels through Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya’s own family, then the report’s first political resonance is hard to miss. Later hadith grading may ask whether the isnād is acceptable. Historical analysis asks why this family would preserve this wording and what it would have meant in the first century after Karbalāʾ.

sections.heading: “God Will Rectify Him in One Night”
sections.text: The phrase “God will rectify him in one night” is especially useful for the Kaysanite case. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya was not a straightforward revolutionary commander like al-Mukhtār. The sources often show him as cautious, pressured, claimed by others, or reluctant to endorse the full violence of the movement done in his name. That ambiguity created a theological problem. How can a quiet or hesitant figure be the promised leader? The hadith solves it. God does not need a long public revolutionary career. God can rectify, prepare, or set right the Mahdī in a single night. A man who has not yet acted like the redeemer can still become the redeemer when the divine moment arrives. That is why this wording fits Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya better than it fits a generic future saint. It explains delay. It explains ambiguity. It explains why the claimant can be present, known, and not yet openly acting.

sections.heading: From Kaysanite Mahdī to Abbasid Daʿwa
sections.text: The Kaysanite afterlife also explains why these ideas survived. The movement around Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya did not disappear after al-Mukhtār’s defeat. Later Hāshimite and Abbasid ideology drew on channels associated with Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya’s son, Abū Hāshim. The famous claim that Abū Hāshim transmitted the imamate or daʿwa to the Abbasid line gave the Abbasids a way to inherit a portion of the earlier Alid-Hanafid religious capital. So the trajectory is not: > A timeless prophecy appears, and only later people apply it politically. The better reconstruction is: > Alid messianic claims formed in the first/seventh century; some were attached to Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya; those claims survived through Kaysanite-Hāshimite channels; later Sunnī books preserved some of the reports after the original factional target had become less visible.

sections.heading: Could It Have Been Created Below Abū al-Ṭufayl?
sections.text: Yes, and the article should be honest about that. The extant collector layer does not show a large fan-out directly from Abū al-Ṭufayl. The Abū al-Ṭufayl report is mainly visible through al-Qāsim b. Abī Bazzah and Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, with a small variation through Ḥabīb b. Abī Thābit reported in Aḥmad. That means a strict common-link argument cannot simply say, “Abū al-Ṭufayl is proven to be the common link in the same way ʿĀṣim is for the Ibn Masʿūd report.” The more defensible claim is layered: 1. The report’s claimed Companion-level bottleneck is Abū al-Ṭufayl. 2. Abū al-Ṭufayl has the right political motive and setting. 3. The lower proliferation is through Kūfan Shīʿī-friendly channels. 4. A collateral family route through Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya’s own descendants preserves a compatible Mahdī claim. That layered case is stronger than saying “Fiṭr fabricated it” or “Ibrāhīm fabricated it.” It explains both the isnād and the political meaning. It also explains why the report could later be accepted in Sunnī compilations: the wording was broad enough to be detached from the Kaysanite referent.

sections.heading: Objections
sections.text: ### “Abū al-Ṭufayl is a Companion, so he cannot be criticized.” That is a theological rule inside later Sunnī hadith theory, not a historical method. The historical question is not whether a Companion is automatically upright in doctrine. The question is whether this specific report, with this specific wording, is more likely to preserve seventh-century Prophetic speech or first-century Alid factional memory. Abū al-Ṭufayl’s known pro-ʿAlid profile is directly relevant because the report functions as pro-ʿAlid messianic legitimation. ### “The report only says Ahl al-Bayt, not Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya.” That is exactly why it works. A factional report does not always name the claimant. It often supplies a description that the intended audience can complete. “From us,” “from my family,” and “fills the earth with justice” were enough for a Kaysanite audience whose messianic focus was already Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya. ### “The later Mahdī is usually Fāṭimid.” Yes, and that is part of the argument. Later Sunnī and Shīʿī Mahdī traditions often move toward more specific Fāṭimid, Ḥasanid, Ḥusaynid, or name-formula identifiers. The Abū al-Ṭufayl report is earlier-looking precisely because it lacks those later restrictions. Its vagueness fits the period before the doctrine was standardized. ### “Ibn Mājah 4085 is a separate report.” It is. It should not be collapsed into the Abū al-Ṭufayl chain. But it is still important because it is a Mahdī report carried through Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya’s family. That makes it a contextual witness. It shows that this family and its circles were an obvious home for Mahdī language. ### “Fiṭr was considered reliable by some critics.” That is true. The argument does not require declaring Fiṭr a liar. His value lies in his location. A trustworthy or semi-trustworthy transmitter can still carry a partisan report. Rijāl reliability and historical origin are not the same question.

sections.heading: The Best Reconstruction
sections.text: The most economical reconstruction is this. A broad Alid Mahdī expectation formed in the aftermath of Karbalāʾ and the Mukhtārite revolt. In that setting, Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya could be presented as the promised figure from ʿAlī’s house who would restore justice. Abū al-Ṭufayl, remembered as a pro-ʿAlid Companion and connected to al-Mukhtār’s movement, is the ideal Companion-level voice for that claim. The report was then transmitted through al-Qāsim b. Abī Bazzah and especially Fiṭr b. Khalīfa, a Kūfan Shīʿī-leaning transmitter, before entering later Sunnī compilations. The family route through Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya confirms the same ideological environment from another angle. It does not prove the Abū al-Ṭufayl route independently, but it shows that Mahdī language was preserved precisely where the Kaysanite reading would predict: in the circles of Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya’s own family.

sections.heading: Sources consulted
sections.text: 1. Abū al-Ṭufayl justice-filling family. Abū Dāwūd, Sunan, no. 4283; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, Musnad, no. 773 and related ʿAlī reports; compare the variant note in Aḥmad where the report is also heard through Ḥabīb b. Abī Thābit from Abū al-Ṭufayl. 2. Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya family route. Ibn Mājah, Sunan, no. 4085; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, Musnad, no. 645: Yāsīn al-ʿIjlī from Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya from his father from ʿAlī. 3. Abū al-Ṭufayl’s rijāl and political profile. Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-kubrā; al-Dhahabī, Siyar aʿlām al-nubalāʾ; Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-tahdhīb; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-nihāya, biography of Abū al-Ṭufayl, where he is remembered as a partisan of ʿAlī and connected with al-Mukhtār. 4. Fiṭr b. Khalīfa. al-Dhahabī, Siyar aʿlām al-nubalāʾ; al-ʿUqaylī, al-Ḍuʿafāʾ; Ibn ʿAdī, al-Kāmil; Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-tahdhīb and Taqrīb al-tahdhīb. The key notices are that he was treated as usable by some critics while also being marked as Shīʿī, even sharply as khashabī in some reports. 5. al-Mukhtār, Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya, and Kaysanite ideology. al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk; al-Balādhurī, Ansāb al-ashrāf; Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī, Maqātil al-Ṭālibiyyīn; al-Nawbakhtī, Firaq al-Shīʿa; al-Ashʿarī, Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn; al-Shahrastānī, al-Milal wa-l-niḥal. 6.
