title: The Green Arabia Hadith: Suhayl, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and the Umayyad Reclamation World
description: A revised isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that the land of the Arabs will return to meadows and rivers: Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ as the common link, Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān al-Zayyāt as the more plausible motive-layer, and the late Umayyad world of land reclamation behind the image.

sections.heading: The claim
sections.text: The modern miracle claim usually begins with a climate headline. Arabia was once greener in the distant past, parts of it are greener today after rain, and the report says the land of the Arabs will “return” to meadows and rivers. The claim then treats the sentence as a scientifically precise prediction of modern climate change. That framing skips the older historical problem. The report is not a free-floating climate statement. It is a small eschatological clause embedded in changing bundles about wealth, zakāt, safe travel, killing, and the signs of the Hour. Its transmission does not spread from many independent Companions. It converges on one family line: Abū Hurayra → Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān → Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ. The point is not merely that Suhayl appears in the chain. The point is that every recoverable line containing the distinctive “meadows and rivers” clause runs through Suhayl, and the earliest technical notice we have, from al-Bazzār, already says so. That is more accurate than the older version of this blog. The old argument treated Suhayl as if the entire case depended on proving that he personally fabricated the report. The stronger argument is subtler. In isnād-cum-matn analysis, the common link is the point from which the report becomes visible and organized. He is not automatically the inventor. Here the matn, the family biography, and the historical setting make Abū Ṣāliḥ’s world the more plausible place to locate the kernel.

sections.heading: The report in its best-known form
sections.text: Aḥmad preserves a near-identical form through the same Qutayba–Yaʿqūb route, but with the added clause that killing will become widespread: Another Aḥmad version changes the surrounding material. The greening clause comes first, then safe travel between Iraq and Mecca, then harj: Ibn Ḥibbān has a shorter form with only harj and greening: Al-Ḥākim preserves the bare clause through Sufyān al-Thawrī, but his form contains an important hesitation: Sufyān’s hesitation matters. It does not destroy the report by itself, but it does show that the attribution was not as effortless as later apologetic citation makes it sound. The transmitter himself pauses over whether he knows it as a raised Prophetic statement.

sections.heading: The isnād: not a wide prophetic memory, but a Suhayl bundle
sections.text: The diagram corrects two common mistakes. The first mistake is the apologetic one: treating the existence of multiple later citations as if they were independent prophetic witnesses. They are not. Muslim, Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, al-Bazzār, and Abū ʿAwāna preserve different recensions, but the distinctive clause does not escape the line Suhayl → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra. The second mistake is the crude skeptical one: treating this as if there were no real transmission bundle at all. There is a bundle. After Suhayl, we have several students in different regional settings: Yaʿqūb al-Qārī in the Medinan line, Ismāʿīl b. Zakariyyā and Sufyān al-Thawrī in Kufan lines, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār in the Basran line. The problem is not that the whole thing is a single late citation. The problem is that the bundle begins only at Suhayl. That distinction is important. The correct conclusion is not “one weak liar invented it.” The correct conclusion is that the report becomes visible as a structured tradition in Suhayl’s lifetime, while the content and family context point one generation earlier.

sections.heading: al-Bazzār already noticed the bottleneck
sections.text: The most important early critical note comes from al-Bazzār. After transmitting the fullest form through ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār from Suhayl, he says: This is the key to the whole case. al-Bazzār is not saying that every surrounding theme is unique to Suhayl. The motifs of overflowing wealth, refused zakāt, harj, and secure travel have other lives in the hadith corpus. What is distinctive here is the way those motifs are joined to the clause that the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers. That clause is the family’s contribution. The apologetic argument often points to Muslim or al-Ḥākim and stops there. But al-Bazzār’s note shows that the bottleneck was visible to early hadith critics themselves. This is not a modern hostile invention.

sections.heading: Suhayl is the disseminator, not necessarily the author
sections.text: Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ was not an unknown nobody. He was a known Medinan transmitter, and several authorities accepted him. That has to be stated clearly because the older blog’s rijāl section leaned too hard on selective negative judgments. At the same time, he was not above criticism. Ibn Ḥajar summarizes him as truthful, but says his memory changed late. Critics also report that his Iraqi transmission was affected by forgetfulness. Abū Ḥātim’s formula is especially useful: his ḥadīth may be written, but is not used as proof. This is not a total rejection. It is a warning against building a miracle claim on a unique Suhayl-family clause. The route profile matches that warning. The “Green Arabia” clause does not come through Mālik b. Anas, even though Mālik transmits from Suhayl elsewhere. It comes through later non-Medinan lines: Kufan, Basran, and routes tied to Suhayl’s wider post-Medina circulation. That is precisely the layer where the report becomes movable as an eschatological unit.

sections.heading: Why Abū Ṣāliḥ matters more than Suhayl
sections.text: The real improvement in the argument is to move the motive one generation upstream. Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt, Suhayl’s father, is the figure whose profile most closely fits the report. He was a major transmitter from Abū Hurayra, and the chain Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra was one of the most useful ways to give Medinan authority to a report. But his biography adds details that make the “meadows and rivers” clause unusually intelligible. First, he was called al-Sammān, the ghee-seller, and al-Zayyāt, the oil-seller. Ibn Abī Ḥātim says he used to bring ghee and oil from Medina to Kufa. These are not random products. Ghee presupposes pastoral abundance. Oil presupposes agricultural and irrigated production. The report’s central imagery is precisely the world of pasture and irrigated land. Second, he moved along the Medina-Kufa corridor. That matters because the Umayyad and early Marwānid period was an age of estates, canals, land grants, and reclamation projects across Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the Hijaz. A transmitter who regularly moved between Medina and Kufa did not need a modern satellite image to imagine “Arab land” becoming productive. He lived in the commercial orbit of that transformation. Third, he was remembered as an ʿUthmānī. al-Mizzī reports that when ʿUthmān was mentioned, Abū Ṣāliḥ wept until his beard trembled. Some reports also place him among those who witnessed the siege of ʿUthmān’s house. This does not prove that he was a Marwānid propagandist. It does mean that his political temperament was not anti-Umayyad in the way a Kūfan anti-Marwānid rebel’s would be. A providential reading of agrarian abundance under the Umayyad order fits his world better than it fits a neutral Bedouin memory from the Prophet’s lifetime. The report therefore makes sense as an al-Sammān household tradition. Abū Ṣāliḥ supplies the Abū Hurayra authority and the commercial-ideological setting. Suhayl supplies the later hadith bundle.

sections.heading: The matn is not about hidden paleoclimate
sections.text: Modern apologetics tends to read the phrase “returns to meadows and rivers” through prehistoric climate studies. But the pre-modern reception points in another direction. The commentators did not need to invoke a lost green Arabia tens of thousands of years in the past. They read the report as a sign of settlement, cultivation, and irrigation. Al-Qurṭubī’s explanation is especially useful. He says the Arabs would turn away from their old habit of seeking rain-pastures and moving for war and raids, and would instead occupy themselves with planting the land, developing it, and channeling its waters. He even says this had already been seen in many of their lands and circumstances. That matters because it destroys the modern claim that the report is impressive only if interpreted as geological or paleoclimatic foresight. A major medieval commentator read it as social and agrarian transformation, not a scientific prediction about deep-time climate cycles. Ibn Kathīr also files the report among the signs of the Hour as a sign of abundance. In the hadith families themselves, the greening clause sits beside wealth overflowing, zakāt becoming hard to distribute, and the earth producing treasures. The point is not meteorology. The point is ominous abundance.

sections.heading: The historical setting: reviving dead land
sections.text: The late Umayyad period had a legal and fiscal language for making land productive: iḥyāʾ al-mawāt, the reviving of dead land. In legal theory, someone who revived dead land could acquire it, and such land could be taxed more lightly. The imam could also grant land. In practice, this created both opportunity and grievance. Reclamation could reward loyal elites and increase revenue, while also concentrating land and putting pressure on cultivators. This historical setting gives the report a motive. The phrase “the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers” is not just a climate image. It is a religiously charged version of a real social process: canals, reclaimed land, estates, produce, taxation, and the transformation of frontier or marginal land into productive property. That also explains why the report is ambivalent. It is framed as a sign of the Hour, so abundance is ominous. But the imagery itself is positive: pasture, water, fertility, wealth. It sacralizes an agrarian transformation while keeping it inside apocalyptic warning.

sections.heading: What does “the land of the Arabs” mean?
sections.text: A major weakness in the modern miracle reading is that it quietly assumes arḍ al-ʿarab means the modern Arabian Peninsula in a narrow geographical sense. That is not how the phrase always worked. Classical geographers could define the land or peninsula of the Arabs elastically. al-Aṣmaʿī’s definition, preserved by al-Bakrī, runs from the farthest south to the marches of Syria, while other boundary descriptions reach toward the Sawād of Iraq and the Baṭāʾiḥ. This matters because the documented agrarian transformations of the Umayyad period were not limited to the interior of today’s Saudi Arabia. They were especially visible in Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the frontier zones. So even if one takes the report literally, it does not have to mean “Riyadh becomes Switzerland.” In the world of early Arabic geography, “Arab land” could include the very regions where reclamation and irrigation were historically active. This is why the paper’s reconstruction is stronger than both modern apologetics and simplistic skepticism. It does not deny that landscapes changed. It asks whose world produced a prophecy in which Arab land became irrigated, pastoral, and productive.

sections.heading: Why the surrounding clauses look borrowed
sections.text: The Bazzār note matters because the greening clause does not float alone. It gets attached to other eschatological motifs. The overflowing wealth motif has wider attestation. So does the image of a man offering zakāt and finding no one to accept it. The harj motif, defined as killing, is also widely known. The safe travel between Iraq and Mecca motif belongs to a recognizable political-security imagination. These motifs could circulate independently and be joined to new local material. What the Suhayl bundle appears to have done is attach the distinctive agrarian image to familiar eschatological furniture. The report becomes more credible because it sounds like other end-times reports. But the distinctive line still points back to one family bundle. This is how retrospective prophecy often works. A new historical concern is framed with older recognized motifs so that it sounds like inherited sacred memory.

sections.heading: Why it is not enough to say “Muslim narrated it”
sections.text: The report is in Muslim, and that matters for later Sunni reception. But canonical placement is not a time machine. Muslim’s version is still a later collection-level witness to a report whose transmission history runs through Suhayl. al-Ḥākim’s grading also does not solve the problem, because his own cited route through Sufyān contains hesitation over the raised attribution. The issue is not whether the report can be made formally acceptable within later Sunni hadith grading. The issue is whether it is a clean miracle claim. It is not. A clean miracle claim would need an early, broad, independent transmission profile and a matn that cannot be better explained by the transmitter’s world. Here we have the opposite: a recoverable bottleneck, a family profile that fits the imagery, and a historical setting that explains the motive.

sections.heading: The revised verdict
sections.text: The older blog focused too much on whether Suhayl’s narrations are “weak.” That is not the best case. The best case is that the report is historically located. Suhayl is the common link and disseminator. Abū Ṣāliḥ is the probable origin-layer. The surrounding clauses are standard eschatological pieces. The distinctive greening clause fits the al-Sammān family’s commercial world and the late Umayyad reclamation order. Classical commentary reads the report through settlement and irrigation, not modern paleoclimate. The phrase “land of the Arabs” itself is geographically elastic enough to include the very regions undergoing transformation.

The report in its best-known form Aḥmad preserves a near-identical form through the same Qutayba–Yaʿqūb route, but with the added clause that killing will become widespread: Another Aḥmad version changes the surrounding material. The greening clause comes first, then safe travel between Iraq and Mecca, then harj: Ibn Ḥibbān has a shorter form with only harj and greening: Al-Ḥākim preserves the bare clause through Sufyān al-Thawrī, but his form contains an important hesitation: Sufyān’s hesitation matters. It does not destroy the report by itself, but it does show that the attribution was not as effortless as later apologetic citation makes it sound. The transmitter himself pauses over whether he knows it as a raised Prophetic statement. The isnād: not a wide prophetic memory, but a Suhayl bundle The diagram corrects two common mistakes. The first mistake is the apologetic one: treating the existence of multiple later citations as if they were independent prophetic witnesses. They are not. Muslim, Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, al-Bazzār, and Abū ʿAwāna preserve different recensions, but the distinctive clause does not escape the line Suhayl → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra. The second mistake is the crude skeptical one: treating this as if there were no real transmission bundle at all. There is a bundle. After Suhayl, we have several students in different regional settings: Yaʿqūb al-Qārī in the Medinan line, Ismāʿīl b. Zakariyyā and Sufyān al-Thawrī in Kufan lines, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār in the Basran line. The problem is not that the whole thing is a single late citation. The problem is that the bundle begins only at Suhayl. That distinction is important. The correct conclusion is not “one weak liar invented it.” The correct conclusion is that the report becomes visible as a structured tradition in Suhayl’s lifetime, while the content and family context point one generation earlier. al-Bazzār already noticed the bottleneck The most important early critical note comes from al-Bazzār. After transmitting the fullest form through ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār from Suhayl, he says: This is the key to the whole case. al-Bazzār is not saying that every surrounding theme is unique to Suhayl. The motifs of overflowing wealth, refused zakāt, harj, and secure travel have other lives in the hadith corpus. What is distinctive here is the way those motifs are joined to the clause that the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers. That clause is the family’s contribution. The apologetic argument often points to Muslim or al-Ḥākim and stops there. But al-Bazzār’s note shows that the bottleneck was visible to early hadith critics themselves. This is not a modern hostile invention. Suhayl is the disseminator, not necessarily the author Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ was not an unknown nobody. He was a known Medinan transmitter, and several authorities accepted him. That has to be stated clearly because the older blog’s rijāl section leaned too hard on selective negative judgments. At the same time, he was not above criticism. Ibn Ḥajar summarizes him as truthful, but says his memory changed late. Critics also report that his Iraqi transmission was affected by forgetfulness. Abū Ḥātim’s formula is especially useful: his ḥadīth may be written, but is not used as proof. This is not a total rejection. It is a warning against building a miracle claim on a unique Suhayl-family clause. The route profile matches that warning. The “Green Arabia” clause does not come through Mālik b. Anas, even though Mālik transmits from Suhayl elsewhere. It comes through later non-Medinan lines: Kufan, Basran, and routes tied to Suhayl’s wider post-Medina circulation. That is precisely the layer where the report becomes movable as an eschatological unit. Why Abū Ṣāliḥ matters more than Suhayl The real improvement in the argument is to move the motive one generation upstream. Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt, Suhayl’s father, is the figure whose profile most closely fits the report. He was a major transmitter from Abū Hurayra, and the chain Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra was one of the most useful ways to give Medinan authority to a report. But his biography adds details that make the “meadows and rivers” clause unusually intelligible. First, he was called al-Sammān, the ghee-seller, and al-Zayyāt, the oil-seller. Ibn Abī Ḥātim says he used to bring ghee and oil from Medina to Kufa. These are not random products. Ghee presupposes pastoral abundance. Oil presupposes agricultural and irrigated production. The report’s central imagery is precisely the world of pasture and irrigated land. Second, he moved along the Medina-Kufa corridor. That matters because the Umayyad and early Marwānid period was an age of estates, canals, land grants, and reclamation projects across Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the Hijaz. A transmitter who regularly moved between Medina and Kufa did not need a modern satellite image to imagine “Arab land” becoming productive. He lived in the commercial orbit of that transformation. Third, he was remembered as an ʿUthmānī. al-Mizzī reports that when ʿUthmān was mentioned, Abū Ṣāliḥ wept until his beard trembled. Some reports also place him among those who witnessed the siege of ʿUthmān’s house. This does not prove that he was a Marwānid propagandist. It does mean that his political temperament was not anti-Umayyad in the way a Kūfan anti-Marwānid rebel’s would be. A providential reading of agrarian abundance under the Umayyad order fits his world better than it fits a neutral Bedouin memory from the Prophet’s lifetime. The report therefore makes sense as an al-Sammān household tradition. Abū Ṣāliḥ supplies the Abū Hurayra authority and the commercial-ideological setting. Suhayl supplies the later hadith bundle. The matn is not about hidden paleoclimate Modern apologetics tends to read the phrase “returns to meadows and rivers” through prehistoric climate studies. But the pre-modern reception points in another direction. The commentators did not need to invoke a lost green Arabia tens of thousands of years in the past. They read the report as a sign of settlement, cultivation, and irrigation. Al-Qurṭubī’s explanation is especially useful. He says the Arabs would turn away from their old habit of seeking rain-pastures and moving for war and raids, and would instead occupy themselves with planting the land, developing it, and channeling its waters. He even says this had already been seen in many of their lands and circumstances. That matters because it destroys the modern claim that the report is impressive only if interpreted as geological or paleoclimatic foresight. A major medieval commentator read it as social and agrarian transformation, not a scientific prediction about deep-time climate cycles. Ibn Kathīr also files the report among the signs of the Hour as a sign of abundance. In the hadith families themselves, the greening clause sits beside wealth overflowing, zakāt becoming hard to distribute, and the earth producing treasures. The point is not meteorology. The point is ominous abundance. The historical setting: reviving dead land The late Umayyad period had a legal and fiscal language for making land productive: iḥyāʾ al-mawāt, the reviving of dead land. In legal theory, someone who revived dead land could acquire it, and such land could be taxed more lightly. The imam could also grant land. In practice, this created both opportunity and grievance. Reclamation could reward loyal elites and increase revenue, while also concentrating land and putting pressure on cultivators. This historical setting gives the report a motive. The phrase “the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers” is not just a climate image. It is a religiously charged version of a real social process: canals, reclaimed land, estates, produce, taxation, and the transformation of frontier or marginal land into productive property. That also explains why the report is ambivalent. It is framed as a sign of the Hour, so abundance is ominous. But the imagery itself is positive: pasture, water, fertility, wealth. It sacralizes an agrarian transformation while keeping it inside apocalyptic warning. What does “the land of the Arabs” mean? A major weakness in the modern miracle reading is that it quietly assumes arḍ al-ʿarab means the modern Arabian Peninsula in a narrow geographical sense. That is not how the phrase always worked. Classical geographers could define the land or peninsula of the Arabs elastically. al-Aṣmaʿī’s definition, preserved by al-Bakrī, runs from the farthest south to the marches of Syria, while other boundary descriptions reach toward the Sawād of Iraq and the Baṭāʾiḥ. This matters because the documented agrarian transformations of the Umayyad period were not limited to the interior of today’s Saudi Arabia. They were especially visible in Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the frontier zones. So even if one takes the report literally, it does not have to mean “Riyadh becomes Switzerland.” In the world of early Arabic geography, “Arab land” could include the very regions where reclamation and irrigation were historically active. This is why the paper’s reconstruction is stronger than both modern apologetics and simplistic skepticism. It does not deny that landscapes changed. It asks whose world produced a prophecy in which Arab land became irrigated, pastoral, and productive. Why the surrounding clauses look borrowed The Bazzār note matters because the greening clause does not float alone. It gets attached to other eschatological motifs. The overflowing wealth motif has wider attestation. So does the image of a man offering zakāt and finding no one to accept it. The harj motif, defined as killing, is also widely known. The safe travel between Iraq and Mecca motif belongs to a recognizable political-security imagination. These motifs could circulate independently and be joined to new local material. What the Suhayl bundle appears to have done is attach the distinctive agrarian image to familiar eschatological furniture. The report becomes more credible because it sounds like other end-times reports. But the distinctive line still points back to one family bundle. This is how retrospective prophecy often works. A new historical concern is framed with older recognized motifs so that it sounds like inherited sacred memory. Why it is not enough to say “Muslim narrated it” The report is in Muslim, and that matters for later Sunni reception. But canonical placement is not a time machine. Muslim’s version is still a later collection-level witness to a report whose transmission history runs through Suhayl. al-Ḥākim’s grading also does not solve the problem, because his own cited route through Sufyān contains hesitation over the raised attribution. The issue is not whether the report can be made formally acceptable within later Sunni hadith grading. The issue is whether it is a clean miracle claim. It is not. A clean miracle claim would need an early, broad, independent transmission profile and a matn that cannot be better explained by the transmitter’s world. Here we have the opposite: a recoverable bottleneck, a family profile that fits the imagery, and a historical setting that explains the motive. The revised verdict The older blog focused too much on whether Suhayl’s narrations are “weak.” That is not the best case. The best case is that the report is historically located. Suhayl is the common link and disseminator. Abū Ṣāliḥ is the probable origin-layer. The surrounding clauses are standard eschatological pieces. The distinctive greening clause fits the al-Sammān family’s commercial world and the late Umayyad reclamation order. Classical commentary reads the report through settlement and irrigation, not modern paleoclimate. The phrase “land of the Arabs” itself is geographically elastic enough to include the very regions undergoing transformation. Sources consulted 1. Core hadith variants. Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ in rijāl. al-Dhahabī, Mīzān al-iʿtidāl, entry on Suhayl b. title: The Killing of ʿUmar and the Afflictions: Ḥudhayfa, the Door, and Kufan Fitna Memory
description: A full isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that ʿUmar was the closed door before the sea-like afflictions: the Abū Wāʾil and Ribʿī transmission families, the al-Aʿmash problem, the broken-door motif, and the historical motive behind turning ʿUmar’s murder into prophecy.

sections.heading: The Killing of ʿUmar and the Afflictions
sections.text: The report is usually presented as a clean miracle prophecy. ʿUmar asks about future afflictions, Ḥudhayfa says there is a closed door between him and them, the door will be broken, and later Ḥudhayfa identifies the door as ʿUmar. Since ʿUmar was assassinated and the Muslim community later entered civil war, apologists treat the narration as a prediction that could only have come from revelation. That reading is too simple. The report is better understood as a Kūfan retrospective theology of the first civil war. It takes three things everyone already knew by the late first and early second century: ʿUmar was murdered, the political order after him became unstable, and the first civil war shattered the memory of communal unity. It then turns those known facts into a symbolic scene in which Ḥudhayfa, the famous Companion of secrets and afflictions, explains the whole future by means of a closed door.

sections.heading: The report in question
sections.text: The narrative has a memorable shape, but that is precisely the point. It is not merely a loose prediction of trouble. It is a staged interpretive scene. ʿUmar asks. Ḥudhayfa answers indirectly. The door is broken rather than opened. The audience is too afraid to ask the meaning. Masrūq finally asks. The hidden answer is ʿUmar. This dramatic structure is not incidental decoration. It is how the report turns remembered political history into a prophetic-seeming riddle.

sections.heading: What the report actually predicts
sections.text: The first mistake is to treat every sentence in the narration as a direct statement from the Prophet. In the report itself, the most secure Prophetic saying is the opening material about ordinary afflictions in a man’s family, wealth, child, and neighbor being expiated by acts of devotion. The “sea-like afflictions” are introduced as something ʿUmar asks about, and the door explanation is given by Ḥudhayfa in the later conversation. This matters because the apologetic version usually says, “The Prophet predicted the assassination of ʿUmar.” The report does not actually give a public scene in which the Prophet names ʿUmar, names his killer, gives the year, or describes the assassination. The decisive identification appears only at the end, through a later disclosure: the group asks Ḥudhayfa, and Masrūq is sent to ask him directly. The report is therefore built like a remembered explanation of history, not like a public prediction before the event. This is already enough to weaken the miracle claim. The report does not have to be read as a pre-644 CE prediction. It can be read as a post-644 CE, post-fitna explanation of why later Muslim history seemed to collapse after ʿUmar’s death.

sections.heading: The transmission map
sections.text: The old version of this article leaned too heavily on al-Aʿmash as if he alone were the common link and therefore the obvious fabricator. That needs correcting. Al-Aʿmash is a major proliferator of the most famous form, but he is not the only route through which the story circulates. The material also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil, through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil, and through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. That does not save the prophecy claim. It sharpens the problem. The report is not a broad public Companion memory. It is a Kūfan Ḥudhayfa dossier. Its recoverable early centers are Abū Wāʾil and Ribʿī, both Kūfan transmitters, and its major later spread is through Kūfan figures such as al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Jāmiʿ. The most important result is that the evidence does not point to a miraculous public prediction. It points to a set of Kūfan and Iraqi transmitters preserving, shaping, and expanding a Ḥudhayfa-centered explanation of post-ʿUmar civil strife.

sections.heading: The Abū Wāʾil family: the famous form
sections.text: The famous version runs through Abū Wāʾil, whose name is Shuqayq b. Salama. From him the report branches mainly through al-Aʿmash. Bukhārī repeats this family several times. Muslim also preserves it through Abū Muʿāwiya from al-Aʿmash. Ibn Ḥibbān gives essentially the same form through Musaddad → Yaḥyā → al-Aʿmash → Shuqayq. This is the family in which the report is most polished. It contains the full staged sequence: ʿUmar asks, Ḥudhayfa distinguishes personal fitna from sea-like fitna, Ḥudhayfa speaks of a closed door, ʿUmar asks if it will be broken or opened, and Masrūq later asks who the door was. The answer is ʿUmar. The presence of several routes inside this family does not make them independent witnesses to the original event. Bukhārī’s multiple citations are not five separate origins. They are repetitions and branches of a shared Abū Wāʾil-Kūfan report. The center of gravity remains the same.

sections.heading: The Jāmiʿ and ʿĀṣim routes: support, but still the same Kūfan world
sections.text: The report also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil in Bukhārī. This is useful because it prevents the analysis from being reduced to “al-Aʿmash alone made it up.” The story was larger than one man. But it is still the same Abū Wāʾil channel from Ḥudhayfa. Another supporting line goes through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil. Al-Tirmidhī’s route is especially interesting because Shuʿba reports from al-Aʿmash, Ḥammād, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala, all saying they heard Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa. That looks like a cluster of Kūfan students who knew a report attached to Abū Wāʾil. Al-Bazzār also preserves a strange route through ʿĀṣim from Zirr from Ḥudhayfa. But al-Bazzār himself flags the problem. He says that a group narrated the report from ʿĀṣim from Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa, and that he did not know anyone who narrated it from ʿĀṣim from Zirr except Muṭarrif. This means the Zirr route should not be treated as a clean independent Companion-transmitter path. It is probably a displacement or confusion within the wider ʿĀṣim material.

sections.heading: The Ribʿī family: a different matn complex
sections.text: The second major family runs through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. Muslim preserves it through Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq from Ribʿī. Aḥmad and al-Bazzār preserve similar material. This family is not just a duplicate of the Abū Wāʾil version. It includes the famous image of afflictions being presented to hearts like a mat, one strand after another, until hearts become either white and resistant or black and overturned. This matters because it shows that the “door” motif is embedded inside a larger Ḥudhayfa fitna complex. In the Ribʿī family, Ḥudhayfa says that he told ʿUmar there was a closed door between him and those afflictions, and that the door was a man who would be killed or die. This version explains the metaphor without needing the final Masrūq scene as strongly as the Abū Wāʾil form does. The Ribʿī family therefore looks like a parallel development, not a pristine independent confirmation. It has the same historical logic: ʿUmar’s removal marks the transition from controlled order to uncontrolled fitna. But it packages the idea inside a different sermon on hearts and moral testing.

sections.heading: The ʿAbd al-Razzāq report: early circulation without a full chain
sections.text: ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves a version through Maʿmar from Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī. It says that ʿUmar asked who would tell them about the afflictions, Ḥudhayfa answered, and the broken-door exchange followed. This is important because it is early and shows the story circulating beyond the exact al-Aʿmash line. But it also lacks the full Companion-to-Successor chain that would make it independent proof. Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī are not presented as hearing this scene from Ḥudhayfa. The report is a piece of early Basran-Iraqi fitna lore in Maʿmar’s material. Its value is not that it proves the prophecy. Its value is that it shows the “ʿUmar as door” story had become memorable and portable by the time these Iraqi transmitters were active. That is exactly what one would expect from a retrospective explanation of the first civil war. It becomes a compact moral formula: the door was ʿUmar; the door was broken; therefore the community never returned to its earlier unity.

sections.heading: The matn is built like retrospective history
sections.text: The matn has several layers. The first layer is a common moral teaching: a person faces trials through family, wealth, children, and neighbors, and acts of worship expiate these trials. This is general religious advice. It does not require knowledge of the future. The second layer is the “waves of the sea.” This is vague, but it is not meaningless. After the murder of ʿUthmān, the battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn, the rise of factional politics, and later Umayyad and anti-Umayyad violence, “fitna like the waves of the sea” was exactly the language one would use to describe the past. The third layer is the door. A door can be opened or broken. If opened, it might be closed again. If broken, the rupture is permanent. This distinction only becomes powerful after one already knows how ʿUmar died. He was not replaced by a normal administrative transition. He was murdered. The door was not opened; it was broken. The fourth layer is the later identification. The transmitters are afraid to ask Ḥudhayfa who the door is. Masrūq is sent. Ḥudhayfa answers: ʿUmar. That is a dramatic device. It makes the answer feel hidden, dangerous, and authoritative. It also makes the meaning appear to be discovered rather than invented.

sections.heading: Why ʿUmar?
sections.text: The motive becomes clearer once we ask what the report accomplishes. It does not merely predict that a person will die. Everyone dies. Nor does it merely predict that fitna will happen. The Qurʾān already says that believers will be tested, and early Muslims had no shortage of real political turmoil to interpret. The report does something more specific. It makes ʿUmar the barrier between the community and the age of civil strife. That is an extremely useful memory. It sanctifies ʿUmar’s rule as the last intact door of communal order. It also explains later chaos without having to say bluntly that the Companions failed. The fitna was not simply bad policy, factional ambition, or tribal conflict. It was the destiny of a broken door. The Qurʾān does not require a hidden prophecy to explain trials. It treats testing as a basic condition of faith. The hadith report adds something else: a political chronology. ʿUmar becomes the threshold. Before him, the door is closed. After him, the waves begin.

sections.heading: Why Ḥudhayfa?
sections.text: Ḥudhayfa is the perfect narrator for this kind of material. In Islamic memory he is not just another Companion. He is the Companion associated with secrets, hypocrisy, and future afflictions. A report placed through Ḥudhayfa can sound like privileged knowledge even when its historical setting is vague. He also fits the geography. The report’s recoverable transmission is heavily Kūfan, and Ḥudhayfa’s memory was important in Iraqi fitna discourse. The first civil war mattered intensely in Kūfa. ʿAlī’s capital, the battle of Ṣiffīn, the Khārijites, pro-ʿAlid and anti-ʿAlid currents, and later anti-Umayyad movements all made Iraq a natural place for traditions that explained how fitna began. A report through Ḥudhayfa lets later transmitters speak about civil war while avoiding direct factional accusation. Instead of saying “this party caused the disaster” or “that Companion caused the disaster,” the report says that the door was broken and the sea-like afflictions came. It turns political blame into sacred chronology.

sections.heading: The historical pressure behind the story
sections.text: The murder of ʿUmar was not a simple isolated event. Historical sources preserve the immediate shock and its aftermath. Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ places ʿUmar’s stabbing near the end of Dhū al-Ḥijja in 23 AH and says he lived several days after being stabbed. Al-Ṭabarī gives the same basic chronological memory. The aftermath was politically charged. Al-Balādhurī reports that ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar, in response to his father’s murder, killed al-Hurmuzān, Jufayna, and the daughter of Abū Luʾluʾa after accusing them of involvement. This became a dispute under ʿUthmān. That means the murder of ʿUmar already generated a moral and legal crisis before the later civil wars even began. Then came the ʿUthmān crisis. Historical reports describe complaints against ʿUthmān, the mobilization of provincial opposition, and eventually his killing. Whether one accepts every detail of later historiography or not, the larger memory is unmistakable: the post-ʿUmar order was remembered as the beginning of a chain of unresolved crises. This is why the report would be attractive in Kūfan circles. Kūfa was not a neutral archive. It was one of the main theaters of early Islamic political memory. A compact Ḥudhayfa report explaining why fitna became unstoppable would have been useful across multiple groups: quietists could use it to discourage participation in civil war; Sunnis could use it to elevate ʿUmar; and later transmitters could use it to narrate early chaos as fate rather than as the failure of their heroes.

sections.heading: The self-authenticating line
sections.text: One line deserves special attention: > “I narrated to him a report that was not from the errors.” This is not a neutral phrase. It functions like a built-in guarantee. The report knows that it is asking the audience to accept a hidden interpretation of history. So the narrative gives the interpretation a seal of certainty: Ḥudhayfa says he told ʿUmar a report free of mistakes. That line does not make the report stronger historically. It makes it more revealing literarily. It is exactly the kind of sentence that appears when a report is aware that its claim rests on private knowledge that cannot be checked. The audience is being told not only what happened, but how confidently it should believe what happened.

sections.heading: The “broken” door is the giveaway
sections.text: The door could have been opened. Instead, it is broken. The difference matters. An opened door can be shut again. A broken door cannot. The report therefore explains why later history did not return to the idealized age before the first civil war. This is ex eventu logic. Once the narrator knows that ʿUmar was assassinated, and once he knows that the subsequent period was remembered as irreversible political rupture, “broken” becomes the perfect word. It is not just a prediction of death. It is an interpretation of the assassination as the irreversible destruction of the communal barrier. Some variants sharpen the point even more by saying that the door would not be closed until the Day of Resurrection. That looks like later apocalyptic inflation. The more the community’s history appears permanently fractured, the more the report can stretch the broken door into an end-times condition.

sections.heading: The report is not weak in the simplistic way
sections.text: A careful critique should not pretend that the whole report collapses because every transmitter is unreliable. That is not true. Ibn Ḥajar describes Abū Wāʾil as trustworthy, Kūfan, and a mukhadram. He describes Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh as trustworthy, devout, and a mukhadram. He describes Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid and Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq as trustworthy. Even al-Aʿmash is described as trustworthy, a ḥāfiẓ, and a recitation expert, though he practiced tadlīs. The tadlīs point must be used carefully. In several core versions al-Aʿmash uses explicit hearing language from Shuqayq or Abū Wāʾil, so it is not enough to dismiss the report by saying “al-Aʿmash was a mudallis.” The stronger point is methodological: reliable transmitters can still preserve a retrospective political interpretation as if it were early sacred memory. ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala is a more mixed figure. Ibn Ḥajar calls him truthful but with mistakes, a proof in Qurʾānic recitation, and says his ḥadīth in the two Ṣaḥīḥs comes in supporting form. That fits the evidence here. His Abū Wāʾil route supports the existence of the story in Kūfan transmission, but the anomalous Zirr route in al-Bazzār shows how easily the report could shift within the Ḥudhayfa transmitter network.

sections.heading: How the report should be classified
sections.text: The report is not a simple one-man invention at al-Aʿmash’s level. That claim is too narrow. It is also not a clean miracle prophecy. The best classification is: 1. Base saying: a general Prophetic or early moral saying about ordinary trials in family, wealth, children, and neighbors. 2. Fitna expansion: Ḥudhayfa-centered Iraqi material about the sea-like afflictions. 3. Historical interpretation: ʿUmar is made the closed door between the community and those afflictions. 4. Narrative dramatization: Masrūq’s later question reveals the hidden meaning. 5. Canonical reception: Bukhārī and Muslim preserve the report as part of a larger Sunni memory of ʿUmar, fitna, and moral decline. The miracle claim depends on collapsing all five layers into one public Prophetic prediction. The report itself does not require that reading.

sections.heading: Why this narrative was useful
sections.text: The report was useful because it solved several problems at once. First, it elevated ʿUmar. He becomes the door that kept catastrophic fitna away. This is a powerful piece of Sunni memory. ʿUmar is not merely the second caliph. He is the barrier between order and chaos. Second, it explained why the community fell into civil war without directly blaming revered figures. The door was broken. Once that happened, the waves came. The metaphor reduces the need to assign political blame. Third, it served quietist purposes. If the fitna after ʿUmar is an irreversible sea, then the pious response is caution, withdrawal, and suspicion of political mobilization. That is why the report sits naturally among other fitan reports warning against civil conflict. Fourth, it gave Kūfan transmitters a way to make sense of their own inherited trauma. Kūfa was a city of civil-war memory. The report does not come from nowhere. It comes from the world that most needed a sacred explanation for why the early community fractured.

sections.heading: What a fulfillment argument misses
sections.text: A fulfillment argument says: ʿUmar died, fitna followed, therefore the Prophet knew the future. A historical-critical reading says: later Muslims knew ʿUmar died and fitna followed, so they told the story of ʿUmar as the broken door. The report is not impressive because it describes an unforeseeable detail. It is revealing because it captures how early Muslims turned trauma into theology. The report’s power is not precision. It does not name Abū Luʾluʾa. It does not name the date. It does not name the shūrā, ʿUthmān, the rebels, the battle of the Camel, Ṣiffīn, or the Umayyads. Its power is symbolic. ʿUmar’s death becomes a threshold. Everything after him becomes the sea.

fullText: The Killing of ʿUmar and the Afflictions The report is usually presented as a clean miracle prophecy. ʿUmar asks about future afflictions, Ḥudhayfa says there is a closed door between him and them, the door will be broken, and later Ḥudhayfa identifies the door as ʿUmar. Since ʿUmar was assassinated and the Muslim community later entered civil war, apologists treat the narration as a prediction that could only have come from revelation. That reading is too simple. The report is better understood as a Kūfan retrospective theology of the first civil war. It takes three things everyone already knew by the late first and early second century: ʿUmar was murdered, the political order after him became unstable, and the first civil war shattered the memory of communal unity. It then turns those known facts into a symbolic scene in which Ḥudhayfa, the famous Companion of secrets and afflictions, explains the whole future by means of a closed door. The report in question The narrative has a memorable shape, but that is precisely the point. It is not merely a loose prediction of trouble. It is a staged interpretive scene. ʿUmar asks. Ḥudhayfa answers indirectly. The door is broken rather than opened. The audience is too afraid to ask the meaning. Masrūq finally asks. The hidden answer is ʿUmar. This dramatic structure is not incidental decoration. It is how the report turns remembered political history into a prophetic-seeming riddle. What the report actually predicts The first mistake is to treat every sentence in the narration as a direct statement from the Prophet. In the report itself, the most secure Prophetic saying is the opening material about ordinary afflictions in a man’s family, wealth, child, and neighbor being expiated by acts of devotion. The “sea-like afflictions” are introduced as something ʿUmar asks about, and the door explanation is given by Ḥudhayfa in the later conversation. This matters because the apologetic version usually says, “The Prophet predicted the assassination of ʿUmar.” The report does not actually give a public scene in which the Prophet names ʿUmar, names his killer, gives the year, or describes the assassination. The decisive identification appears only at the end, through a later disclosure: the group asks Ḥudhayfa, and Masrūq is sent to ask him directly. The report is therefore built like a remembered explanation of history, not like a public prediction before the event. This is already enough to weaken the miracle claim. The report does not have to be read as a pre-644 CE prediction. It can be read as a post-644 CE, post-fitna explanation of why later Muslim history seemed to collapse after ʿUmar’s death. The transmission map The old version of this article leaned too heavily on al-Aʿmash as if he alone were the common link and therefore the obvious fabricator. That needs correcting. Al-Aʿmash is a major proliferator of the most famous form, but he is not the only route through which the story circulates. The material also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil, through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil, and through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. That does not save the prophecy claim. It sharpens the problem. The report is not a broad public Companion memory. It is a Kūfan Ḥudhayfa dossier. Its recoverable early centers are Abū Wāʾil and Ribʿī, both Kūfan transmitters, and its major later spread is through Kūfan figures such as al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Jāmiʿ. The most important result is that the evidence does not point to a miraculous public prediction. It points to a set of Kūfan and Iraqi transmitters preserving, shaping, and expanding a Ḥudhayfa-centered explanation of post-ʿUmar civil strife. The Abū Wāʾil family: the famous form The famous version runs through Abū Wāʾil, whose name is Shuqayq b. Salama. From him the report branches mainly through al-Aʿmash. Bukhārī repeats this family several times. Muslim also preserves it through Abū Muʿāwiya from al-Aʿmash. Ibn Ḥibbān gives essentially the same form through Musaddad → Yaḥyā → al-Aʿmash → Shuqayq. This is the family in which the report is most polished. It contains the full staged sequence: ʿUmar asks, Ḥudhayfa distinguishes personal fitna from sea-like fitna, Ḥudhayfa speaks of a closed door, ʿUmar asks if it will be broken or opened, and Masrūq later asks who the door was. The answer is ʿUmar. The presence of several routes inside this family does not make them independent witnesses to the original event. Bukhārī’s multiple citations are not five separate origins. They are repetitions and branches of a shared Abū Wāʾil-Kūfan report. The center of gravity remains the same. The Jāmiʿ and ʿĀṣim routes: support, but still the same Kūfan world The report also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil in Bukhārī. This is useful because it prevents the analysis from being reduced to “al-Aʿmash alone made it up.” The story was larger than one man. But it is still the same Abū Wāʾil channel from Ḥudhayfa. Another supporting line goes through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil. Al-Tirmidhī’s route is especially interesting because Shuʿba reports from al-Aʿmash, Ḥammād, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala, all saying they heard Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa. That looks like a cluster of Kūfan students who knew a report attached to Abū Wāʾil. Al-Bazzār also preserves a strange route through ʿĀṣim from Zirr from Ḥudhayfa. But al-Bazzār himself flags the problem. He says that a group narrated the report from ʿĀṣim from Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa, and that he did not know anyone who narrated it from ʿĀṣim from Zirr except Muṭarrif. This means the Zirr route should not be treated as a clean independent Companion-transmitter path. It is probably a displacement or confusion within the wider ʿĀṣim material. The Ribʿī family: a different matn complex The second major family runs through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. Muslim preserves it through Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq from Ribʿī. Aḥmad and al-Bazzār preserve similar material. This family is not just a duplicate of the Abū Wāʾil version. It includes the famous image of afflictions being presented to hearts like a mat, one strand after another, until hearts become either white and resistant or black and overturned. This matters because it shows that the “door” motif is embedded inside a larger Ḥudhayfa fitna complex. In the Ribʿī family, Ḥudhayfa says that he told ʿUmar there was a closed door between him and those afflictions, and that the door was a man who would be killed or die. This version explains the metaphor without needing the final Masrūq scene as strongly as the Abū Wāʾil form does. The Ribʿī family therefore looks like a parallel development, not a pristine independent confirmation. It has the same historical logic: ʿUmar’s removal marks the transition from controlled order to uncontrolled fitna. But it packages the idea inside a different sermon on hearts and moral testing. The ʿAbd al-Razzāq report: early circulation without a full chain ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves a version through Maʿmar from Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī. It says that ʿUmar asked who would tell them about the afflictions, Ḥudhayfa answered, and the broken-door exchange followed. This is important because it is early and shows the story circulating beyond the exact al-Aʿmash line. But it also lacks the full Companion-to-Successor chain that would make it independent proof. Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī are not presented as hearing this scene from Ḥudhayfa. The report is a piece of early Basran-Iraqi fitna lore in Maʿmar’s material. Its value is not that it proves the prophecy. Its value is that it shows the “ʿUmar as door” story had become memorable and portable by the time these Iraqi transmitters were active. That is exactly what one would expect from a retrospective explanation of the first civil war. It becomes a compact moral formula: the door was ʿUmar; the door was broken; therefore the community never returned to its earlier unity. The matn is built like retrospective history The matn has several layers. The first layer is a common moral teaching: a person faces trials through family, wealth, children, and neighbors, and acts of worship expiate these trials. This is general religious advice. It does not require knowledge of the future. The second layer is the “waves of the sea.” This is vague, but it is not meaningless. After the murder of ʿUthmān, the battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn, the rise of factional politics, and later Umayyad and anti-Umayyad violence, “fitna like the waves of the sea” was exactly the language one would use to describe the past. The third layer is the door. A door can be opened or broken. If opened, it might be closed again. If broken, the rupture is permanent. This distinction only becomes powerful after one already knows how ʿUmar died. He was not replaced by a normal administrative transition. He was murdered. The door was not opened; it was broken. The fourth layer is the later identification. The transmitters are afraid to ask Ḥudhayfa who the door is. Masrūq is sent. Ḥudhayfa answers: ʿUmar. That is a dramatic device. The Qurʾān already says that believers will be tested, and early Muslims had no shortage of real political turmoil to interpret. The report does something more specific. It makes ʿUmar the barrier between the community and the age of civil strife. That is an extremely useful memory. It sanctifies ʿUmar’s rule as the last intact door of communal order. It also explains later chaos without having to say bluntly that the Companions failed. The fitna was not simply bad policy, factional ambition, or tribal conflict. Ḥudhayfa is the perfect narrator for this kind of material. In Islamic memory he is not just another Companion. He is the Companion associated with secrets, hypocrisy, and future afflictions. A report through Ḥudhayfa lets later transmitters speak about civil war while avoiding direct factional accusation. Instead of saying “this party caused the disaster” or “that Companion caused the disaster,” the report says that the door was broken and the sea-like afflictions came. It turns political blame into sacred chronology. The historical pressure behind the story The murder of ʿUmar was not a simple isolated event. Historical sources preserve the immediate shock and its aftermath. Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ places ʿUmar’s stabbing near the end of Dhū al-Ḥijja in 23 AH and says he lived several days after being stabbed. Al-Ṭabarī gives the same basic chronological memory. The aftermath was politically charged. Al-Balādhurī reports that ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar, in response to his father’s murder, killed al-Hurmuzān, Jufayna, and the daughter of Abū Luʾluʾa after accusing them of involvement. This became a dispute under ʿUthmān. That means the murder of ʿUmar already generated a moral and legal crisis before the later civil wars even began. Then came the ʿUthmān crisis. Historical reports describe complaints against ʿUthmān, the mobilization of provincial opposition, and eventually his killing. Whether one accepts every detail of later historiography or not, the larger memory is unmistakable: the post-ʿUmar order was remembered as the beginning of a chain of unresolved crises. A compact Ḥudhayfa report explaining why fitna became unstoppable would have been useful across multiple groups: quietists could use it to discourage participation in civil war; Sunnis could use it to elevate ʿUmar; and later transmitters could use it to narrate early chaos as fate rather than as the failure of their heroes. The self-authenticating line One line deserves special attention: “I narrated to him a report that was not from the errors.” This is not a neutral phrase. It functions like a built-in guarantee. The report knows that it is asking the audience to accept a hidden interpretation of history. So the narrative gives the interpretation a seal of certainty: Ḥudhayfa says he told ʿUmar a report free of mistakes. That line does not make the report stronger historically. It makes it more revealing literarily. It is exactly the kind of sentence that appears when a report is aware that its claim rests on private knowledge that cannot be checked. title: The Dhū al-Khalaṣa Prophecy: Daws, Abū Hurayra, and the Shrine-Survival Problem
description: A full isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that the women of Daws will circle Dhū al-Khalaṣa before the Hour: the al-Zuhrī bottleneck, Maʿmar’s house-over-the-stone clue, the separate Jarīr destruction family, and the reason Daws and Abū Hurayra were selected.

sections.heading: The claim
sections.text: The apologetic claim is simple. A pre-Islamic idol called Dhū al-Khalaṣa was destroyed in the Prophet’s lifetime. Centuries later, the shrine allegedly reappeared in southern Arabia and was destroyed again in the modern period. Therefore, the report in which the Prophet predicts that the women of Daws will one day circle Dhū al-Khalaṣa is presented as a fulfilled prophecy. sections.heading: The report in question
sections.text: Muslim’s form has the same core, but adds a useful geographical gloss: The language is deliberately humiliating. It does not merely say that people will worship an idol. It says that the women of Daws will move their bodies around it. This is not neutral ethnography. It is tribal shame language placed into an end-times frame.

sections.heading: The isnād: one polished prophetic stem
sections.text: The branches after al-Zuhrī are not independent origins. Bukhārī has Shuʿayb from al-Zuhrī. Muslim and ʿAbd al-Razzāq have Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Al-Bazzār has ʿUqayl from al-Zuhrī. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim has Muḥammad b. Abī ʿAtīq from Ibn Shihāb. The spread begins after al-Zuhrī, not before him. That does not prove by itself that al-Zuhrī invented the report. It does mean that the famous prophetic form is recoverable to an al-Zuhrī-centered transmission environment, not to a public, multiply witnessed Prophetic statement.

sections.heading: The smoking gun: the house over the stone
sections.text: The most important version is the Maʿmar route because it preserves an aside that Bukhārī’s shorter form does not foreground. Ibn Ḥibbān preserves the same clue in an even sharper form: This is the line that explains the report’s motive. The old idol had supposedly been destroyed. Yet Maʿmar’s world still knew of a stone and a built house over it. That is not a clean fulfilled prophecy appearing out of nowhere centuries later. It is a living site-memory problem already visible in the transmission itself. The hadith answers that problem by turning the site into an apocalyptic sign. The old sanctuary is not simply a ruin. It is a future relapse waiting to happen.

sections.heading: The destruction report is separate
sections.text: The destruction story is often cited as if it supports the prophecy. It supports the existence and importance of the sanctuary, but it does not independently support the future prediction. It is a separate report family. Other versions say that Jarīr set out with cavalry from Aḥmas, demolished it, burned it, and killed those found around it. Muslim’s versions also call it the Yemeni Kaʿba and place it in the Khathʿam/Bajīla environment. sections.heading: Dhū al-Khalaṣa was not simply “the idol of Daws”
sections.text: This is where the apologetic reading becomes too flat. The prophecy version says Daws. But the broader historical memory does not restrict Dhū al-Khalaṣa to Daws. Ibn Hishām says that Dhū al-Khalaṣa belonged to Daws, Khathʿam, Bajīla, and those Arabs who lived in their lands at Tabāla. Al-Balādhurī describes it as a white stone at Tabāla and as an idol of Bajīla, Khathʿam, and Azd al-Sarāt. Ibn Ḥazm expands the associated groups even further, listing Bajīla, Khathʿam, al-Ḥārith b. Kaʿb, Jurm, Zubayd, al-Ghawth b. Murr, and Banū Hilāl b. ʿĀmir, and locating it between Mecca and Yemen. Ibn ʿAsākir preserves later legendary material in which the Arabs as a whole are said to have revered the site. Al-Hamdānī lists Dhū al-Khalaṣa among the sacred geographies of Arabia, alongside Mecca, Īliyāʾ, al-Lāt near Nakhlah, and the Kaʿba of Najrān. So why does the prophecy focus on Daws? It is not an outsider saying, “Those southern tribes will return to paganism.” It is an internal tribal witness saying, in effect, “My own people’s women will one day circle the old idol.” That is why the wording is so humiliating. It does not say “Daws will worship.” It says “the buttocks of the women of Daws will move around it.” The report makes the future relapse bodily, tribal, and shameful.

sections.heading: The Daws conversion template
sections.text: The selection of Daws also fits a pre-existing conversion story. Daws is remembered in the sīra and hadith material as a tribe whose guidance was difficult and required prophetic prayer. That memory gives the Dhū al-Khalaṣa prophecy a narrative arc. Daws was once resistant, then guided by prophetic mercy, and now the eschatological report imagines Daws relapsing back into the cultic world from which it had been saved. Whether one treats that conversion story as historical or literary, it shows that Daws already carried a recognizable symbolic role in early Islamic memory. It was not random.

sections.heading: What would push Saʿīd or al-Zuhrī to transmit such a report?
sections.text: The question of motive should not be flattened into one sentence: “al-Zuhrī fabricated it for the Umayyads.” That is too crude. The report’s motive becomes clearer when Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī are placed in their own worlds. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is not a clean candidate for simple Umayyad propaganda. Historical reports remember him refusing the Umayyad demand to pledge allegiance to al-Walīd and Sulaymān while ʿAbd al-Malik was still alive. He was beaten, dressed in rough garments, paraded, and imprisoned for that refusal. That memory matters. If the report entered at Saʿīd’s layer, it is better explained as Medinan moral-apocalyptic commentary than as a court-sponsored anti-Yemeni slogan. Saʿīd’s world had witnessed the collapse of the old order into civil war, coercive bayʿa politics, hereditary succession, and the transformation of religion into state control. In such an atmosphere, a report about Arabia eventually reverting to the religion of its fathers makes sense. It is a warning about post-Prophetic decline. Al-Zuhrī’s position is different. He is the perfect figure for the report’s polished circulation because he sits between Saʿīd’s Medinan authority and Umayyad-era writing and diffusion. Ibn Saʿd and al-Balādhurī preserve the famous report in which al-Zuhrī says that scholars disliked writing knowledge until the rulers compelled them, after which they thought it wrong to prevent Muslims from it. They also preserve the memory that after al-Walīd b. Yazīd was killed, written materials from al-Zuhrī’s knowledge were found in such quantity that they were carried on pack animals. Al-Zuhrī is also remembered as having sat with Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib for years. That makes al-Zuhrī the natural common-link for a report like this. He could attach a southern shrine-memory to Saʿīd, Saʿīd to Abū Hurayra, and Abū Hurayra to Daws. sections.heading: The “Yemeni Kaʿba” angle
sections.text: The phrase “Yemeni Kaʿba” is not just a geographical curiosity. It matters because it places Dhū al-Khalaṣa inside a sacred-political hierarchy. In the Islamic order, Mecca is the sanctuary. The Kaʿba is the center. A rival or quasi-rival sanctuary remembered as the Yemeni Kaʿba is not merely a local idol; it is a rival sacred memory. A report predicting the shameful return of people to this Yemeni sanctuary implicitly subordinates it to the Islamic Meccan order. It says: the true Kaʿba remains the center of worship, while the “Yemeni Kaʿba” becomes a sign of end-times degeneration. This is why the report’s southern geography, Dawsi framing, and Abū Hurayra attribution work so well together. The story is not simply “idols will return.” It is: a famous Dawsi authority predicts that his own tribal world will regress to a southern pagan sanctuary remembered as a rival Kaʿba.

sections.heading: The collateral variants: a wider return-to-idols motif
sections.text: The exact Daws report is al-Zuhrī-shaped, but the motif is wider. Other reports imagine the end of time as a return to ancestral cults after Islam has declined. Muslim preserves a report from ʿĀʾisha in which the Prophet says that night and day will not pass away until al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā are worshiped. When ʿĀʾisha objects that she thought the Qurʾānic promise had ended such worship, the response is that God will send a good wind to take the believers, and those who remain will return to the religion of their fathers. Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād preserves a report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr: This is not the same report. It is not even phrased as a Prophetic hadith here. But it shows how Dhū al-Khalaṣa could function inside a wider Syrian apocalyptic imagination: Arabia returns to paganism, Syria falls to Rome, and the final age begins. Nuʿaym also preserves a form in which, after Jesus and after a wind takes the believers, people return to the religion of their fathers. Then Abū Hurayra’s line appears almost as a vivid comment: “As if I can see the buttocks of the women of Daws...” That form is valuable because it suggests that the Daws phrase could circulate as an illustrative apocalyptic image inside a broader return-to-idols framework. There is also a striking variant in al-Ḥākim’s Mustadrak. In a report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr, a man is asked his tribe and says he is from Banū ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. The reply then says: This is extremely important. It shows that the formula “women of [tribe] around Dhū al-Khalaṣa” could be adapted. In Abū Hurayra’s version the tribe is Daws because Abū Hurayra is Dawsi. In the ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr variant, the target can become Banū ʿĀmir in response to a tribal exchange. That does not prove the Abū Hurayra version was copied from the Banū ʿĀmir version. It proves something more general: the report belongs to a flexible apocalyptic shame motif, not a single cleanly preserved public prophecy.

sections.heading: The matn development
sections.text: The development looks like this: | Layer | Evidence | Function | |---|---|---| | Shrine memory | Dhū al-Khalaṣa as a white stone at Tabāla, linked to Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others | Establishes a real southern sacred site | | Destruction memory | Jarīr destroys the house called the Yemeni Kaʿba | Explains Islamic triumph over the old cult | | Survival problem | Reports that it remained, or that a house stood over the stone “today” | Creates the need for explanation | | Dawsi framing | Abū Hurayra is Dawsi, and Daws has a conversion-story template | Makes the prophecy an internal tribal warning | | Apocalyptic upgrade | The women of Daws return to Dhū al-Khalaṣa before the Hour | Converts site survival into prophecy | | Later fulfillment claim | Modern stories of a revived shrine | Misread the report as a miracle instead of recognizing the earlier site afterlife |

sections.heading: The rijāl question
sections.text: Sunni rijāl literature does not give a simple “weak transmitter” solution here. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is one of the most prestigious Medinan authorities. Al-Zuhrī is central to early Sunni transmission. Abū Hurayra is one of the most frequently used Companion authorities. That is precisely why the report is effective. The critique is not: > “The chain contains an obviously rejected liar.” The critique is: > “The exact prophetic form has a narrow al-Zuhrī stem, the matn selects Daws for a reason, and the Maʿmar version preserves the contemporary shrine-survival clue that explains why the prophecy was useful.” This is an isnād-cum-matn argument, not a one-line rijāl dismissal.

sections.heading: Why the modern fulfillment claim fails
sections.text: The modern fulfillment claim usually says: Dhū al-Khalaṣa returned, people worshiped around it, and it was destroyed again. But the Maʿmar note already says there was a built house over the stone in his own period or in the memory available to him. That means the old cultic site had a visible afterlife long before the modern event. So the modern episode cannot function as a clean miracle. It is part of a longer pattern of shrine memory, local sacred geography, and recurrent attempts to interpret or suppress the site. The correct question is not: > “How could the Prophet know this shrine would return?” The correct question is: > “Why did a second/eighth-century transmission environment already know of a house over the old stone, and why did it preserve a prophecy saying people would one day return to it?” Once that question is asked, the report becomes intelligible without miracle.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The Dhū al-Khalaṣa report is not a straightforward fulfilled prophecy. The exact prophetic wording is narrow and al-Zuhrī-centered. The destruction report is separate. The site is not consistently Dawsi in the historical memory. The old sanctuary is described as belonging to a wider southern tribal landscape: Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others. It is remembered as a white stone at Tabāla and as the Yemeni Kaʿba. The most important clue is Maʿmar’s note: there was already a built house over the stone. That makes the motive visible. The prophecy was not produced because the shrine unexpectedly reappeared centuries later. It was produced because the shrine, stone, or sacred memory had not disappeared cleanly in the first place. Daws and Abū Hurayra were selected because they made the report rhetorically stronger. Abū Hurayra was Dawsi, so the report becomes an internal tribal confession. A famous Muslim authority from Daws is made to predict that his own tribal world will return to an old pagan sanctuary. That is far more powerful than a generic warning that Arabs will worship idols again.

The matn development The development looks like this: | Layer | Evidence | Function | |---|---|---| | Shrine memory | Dhū al-Khalaṣa as a white stone at Tabāla, linked to Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others | Establishes a real southern sacred site | | Destruction memory | Jarīr destroys the house called the Yemeni Kaʿba | Explains Islamic triumph over the old cult | | Survival problem | Reports that it remained, or that a house stood over the stone “today” | Creates the need for explanation | | Dawsi framing | Abū Hurayra is Dawsi, and Daws has a conversion-story template | Makes the prophecy an internal tribal warning | | Apocalyptic upgrade | The women of Daws return to Dhū al-Khalaṣa before the Hour | Converts site survival into prophecy | | Later fulfillment claim | Modern stories of a revived shrine | Misread the report as a miracle instead of recognizing the earlier site afterlife | The rijāl question Sunni rijāl literature does not give a simple “weak transmitter” solution here. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is one of the most prestigious Medinan authorities. Al-Zuhrī is central to early Sunni transmission. Abū Hurayra is one of the most frequently used Companion authorities. That is precisely why the report is effective. The critique is not: “The chain contains an obviously rejected liar.” The critique is: “The exact prophetic form has a narrow al-Zuhrī stem, the matn selects Daws for a reason, and the Maʿmar version preserves the contemporary shrine-survival clue that explains why the prophecy was useful.” This is an isnād-cum-matn argument, not a one-line rijāl dismissal. Why the modern fulfillment claim fails The modern fulfillment claim usually says: Dhū al-Khalaṣa returned, people worshiped around it, and it was destroyed again. But the Maʿmar note already says there was a built house over the stone in his own period or in the memory available to him. That means the old cultic site had a visible afterlife long before the modern event. So the modern episode cannot function as a clean miracle. It is part of a longer pattern of shrine memory, local sacred geography, and recurrent attempts to interpret or suppress the site. The correct question is not: “How could the Prophet know this shrine would return?” The correct question is: “Why did a second/eighth-century transmission environment already know of a house over the old stone, and why did it preserve a prophecy saying people would one day return to it?” Once that question is asked, the report becomes intelligible without miracle. Conclusion The Dhū al-Khalaṣa report is not a straightforward fulfilled prophecy. The exact prophetic wording is narrow and al-Zuhrī-centered. The destruction report is separate. The site is not consistently Dawsi in the historical memory. The old sanctuary is described as belonging to a wider southern tribal landscape: Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others. It is remembered as a white stone at Tabāla and as the Yemeni Kaʿba. The most important clue is Maʿmar’s note: there was already a built house over the stone. That makes the motive visible. The prophecy was not produced because the shrine unexpectedly reappeared centuries later. It was produced because the shrine, stone, or sacred memory had not disappeared cleanly in the first place. Daws and Abū Hurayra were selected because they made the report rhetorically stronger. Abū Hurayra was Dawsi, so the report becomes an internal tribal confession. A famous Muslim authority from Daws is made to predict that his own tribal world will return to an old pagan sanctuary. That is far more powerful than a generic warning that Arabs will worship idols again. Sources consulted 1.
