title: Quran 22:15: Suicide or Salvation?
description: A close reading of Quran 22:15, the contested words sabab and sama, the classical strangulation reading, and the case for reading the verse as a call to sever dependence on anything besides God.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Translation Forensics · Quran 22:15 Did God tell a man to hang himself? That is how many readers first encounter Quran 22:15 in English. The verse is often rendered as a sarcastic command to tie a rope to the ceiling, strangle oneself, and see whether that removes one’s rage. The problem is not that the verse is simple and translators have ignored it. The problem is that a chain of interpretive choices has been turned into the verse itself. The Arabic can be read another way. The contested words are not obscure: sabab , sama , li-yaqtaʿ , kayd , and the pronoun in yanṣuruhu . Each one was discussed in the classical tradition. The question is whether the suicide reading is the only reading the language allows, and whether it is the reading that best fits the Quran’s own usage.

sections.heading: The Verse in One Sentence
sections.text: A literal word-for-word rendering can sound strange: The dispute begins because several words can be narrowed in more than one direction. If sabab is narrowed to “rope,” sama is narrowed to “ceiling,” and li-yaqtaʿ is supplied with “his breath” or “himself,” the verse becomes a hanging scene. If sabab is read as “means” or “connection,” sama as heaven, and li-yaqtaʿ as severing dependence, the verse becomes a challenge to the person who thinks God will not support him: turn upward to God and cut off the false attachments that feed your rage. Common strangulation reading Rope → ceiling → hang himself This reading depends on narrowing sabab to a rope, glossing sama as the ceiling of a house, and supplying the object of “cut” as the man’s breath, body, or connection to the ground. Quran-consistent reading Means → heaven → sever dependence This reading keeps the wider Quranic sense of sabab as a means or connection, keeps sama as heaven, and reads “cut” as severing the false dependencies that do not remove distress.

sections.heading: Word-by-Word Map
sections.text: مَن whoever كَانَ يَظُنُّ thinks / assumes أَن لَّن يَنصُرَهُ اللَّهُ that God will not help him فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ in this world and the Hereafter فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ let him extend a means / connection إِلَى السَّمَاءِ toward the sky / heaven ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ then let him cut / sever فَلْيَنظُرْ then let him look هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ whether his plan removes مَا يَغِيظُ what enrages or distresses him

sections.heading: Why the Suicide Reading Creates a Problem
sections.text: The Quran does not allow an interpretation to be judged in isolation from the rest of the Quran. It asks the reader to notice internal consistency: A reading of 22:15 that turns the verse into a literal command to hang oneself has to be measured against verses where the Quran says God does not command indecency and where self-killing is forbidden. This does not mean every violent or sarcastic image in the Quran must be softened. It means we should be careful before turning a rhetorical challenge into a divine instruction. The verse can mock the futility of the doubter’s rage without telling a human being to commit suicide.

sections.heading: How the Strangulation Reading Entered Tafsir
sections.text: The strangulation reading is not a modern accident. It appears in classical tafsir and was inherited by many English translators. The strongest versions of that reading gloss sabab as a rope, sama as the ceiling of the house, and “cut” as strangling oneself. Tafsir al-Jalalayn Ceiling and strangulation Al-Jalalayn explains the “sky” as the ceiling of the house, the sabab as a rope tied to that ceiling and to the neck, and “cut” as choking oneself by cutting off connection to the ground. Ibn Kathir The inherited report Ibn Kathir transmits the familiar explanation through early authorities: the man stretches a rope to the ceiling of his house and strangles himself with it. Al-Fayruzabadi The same narrowing The verse is again explained as a man tying a rope to the ceiling and hanging himself because of rage over God’s support or over his own provision.

sections.heading: Popular English Translations
sections.text: Many English translations simply reproduce the strangulation reading. The result is that a reader encounters the tafsir as though it were the direct meaning of the verse. Dr. Mustafa Khattab “Let them stretch out a rope to the ceiling and strangle themselves.” Saheeh International “Let him extend a rope to the ceiling, then cut off [his breath].” Hilali & Khan “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and let him strangle himself.” M. Pickthall “Let him stretch a rope up to the roof ... and let him hang himself.” A. Yusuf Ali “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and cut himself off.” The same pattern keeps appearing: ceiling, hanging, strangling, cutting off breath. Those words are not all in the verse. They are a tradition of explanation that translators have allowed into the translation.

sections.heading: What the Classical Sources Also Preserve
sections.text: The strangulation reading became dominant, but the classical sources preserve more than one interpretive tool. Once those tools are collected, the verse does not have to be read as a divine command to self-harm. ### The Pronoun Was Disputed The common reading assumes that the pronoun in yanṣuruhu means “God will not help Muhammad.” But exegetes also record another reading: the pronoun can return to man , the “whoever” at the beginning of the verse. On that reading, the verse addresses the person who thinks God will not help or provide for him in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Razi on 22:15 أَنَّ الْهَاءَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ، رَاجِعٌ إِلَى مَنْ فِي أَوَّلِ الْآيَةِ ... فَكَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: مَنْ كَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَرْزُقَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ “The pronoun in ‘God will not help him’ returns to ‘whoever’ at the start of the verse … as if it said: whoever thinks that God will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter.” Al-Qurtubi records the same option, and al-Tabari preserves the explanation that “support” here means provision, with yanṣuruhu read in the sense of yarzuquhu . That reading changes the emotional scene. The verse is no longer about a man enraged by the Prophet’s victory. It can be read as a person who thinks God will not support him and is told to redirect his dependence upward. ### Sabab Means a Means or Connection The word sabab can mean a rope, but “rope” is not the only sense and not always the central sense. Al-Qurtubi defines it broadly: Al-Qurtubi السَّبَبُ مَا يُتَوَصَّلُ بِهِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ “A sabab is that by which one reaches a thing.” That is why “means,” “connection,” or “way” is often the better starting point. A rope is one kind of sabab , but not every sabab is a noose. ### The Quran Uses Sabab as a Way or Means The Quran’s own usage matters. In Surat Ghafir, Pharaoh tells Haman to build a tower so that he may reach the means to the heavens: Here the phrase asbab al-samawat cannot mean nooses to ceilings. It means ways, means, or routes of ascent toward the heavens. That makes it relevant to 22:15, where sabab and sama appear together. The Quran also uses the same root with cutting language: In 2:166, the asbab are cut off, meaning relationships, ties, or dependencies are severed. That is a stronger Quranic parallel for 22:15 than the idea of cutting off one’s breath. The Quran itself shows that sabab can be something relational that is severed. 22:15 bi-sababin ... thumma li-yaqtaʿ extend a means, then cut 2:166 wa-taqaṭṭaʿat bihim al-asbab the ties / means between them are cut off ### Sama Is Not Automatically a Ceiling The word in the verse is al-sama . Translating it as “the ceiling of his house” is a tafsir gloss. Commentators justify that gloss by saying that Arabs may call anything above a person sama . But the literal sense remains sky or heaven, and the real-sky reading is preserved in the exegetical tradition. Al-Qurtubi reports Ibn Zayd’s reading that it means the known sky. Al-Razi lists the real sky as an interpretive option. Ibn Ashur also reports the same broader possibility. So the reading “toward heaven” is not a modern rescue attempt. It is one of the possibilities already visible in the tradition. ### Even the Strangulation Reading Is Rhetorical Even when classical exegetes adopt the strangulation reading, they do not treat the verse as practical religious instruction. They treat it as a rhetorical challenge, a way of showing that the doubter’s rage cannot overturn God’s decree. Al-Razi states the logic of that kind of interpretation: Al-Razi كُلُّ مَا كَانَ الْمَذْكُورُ أَبْعَدَ مِنَ الْإِمْكَانِ كَانَ أَوْلَى بِأَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْمُرَادَ “The more impossible the mentioned act is, the more fitting it is as the intended figurative sense.” That means the worst English rendering is not merely “rope” or “ceiling.” It is the impression that the verse is a literal command to commit suicide. Even within the strangulation reading, the verse is a rhetorical taunt about futility, not a devotional instruction.

sections.heading: The Reading That Makes the Most Sense
sections.text: Rashad Khalifa’s translation is unusual because it does not import the ceiling/noose scenario into the verse. He reads the verse through reliance on God: This reading does not require pretending the classical strangulation interpretation never existed. It does something more useful. It notices that the key words have broader Quranic meanings and that the verse can be read as guidance for the person who doubts God’s support. 1 He thinks God will not support him. 2 He is told to extend his means toward heaven. 3 He cuts the false dependencies beneath him. 4 He sees whether that plan removes what troubles him. The reading is not just more comforting. Comfort by itself is not evidence. It is stronger because it makes better use of the Quran’s own language. Sabab is a means or connection. Asbab can be cut off as ties and dependencies. Sama can remain heaven without being reduced to a ceiling. The pronoun can refer to the doubter himself. The whole sentence can function as a challenge to misplaced dependence rather than a command to self-destruction.

sections.heading: What the Verse Is Saying
sections.text: The verse is addressing a person who thinks God will not support him. It challenges him to test the logic of his own dependence. If he thinks support will not come from God, let him direct his means upward and cut the false attachments that keep him trapped in rage or despair. Then let him see whether that plan removes what is troubling him. This reading turns the verse back into Quranic guidance. The person is not told to end his life. He is told to stop imagining that his frustration can defeat God’s decree or that his support must come from somewhere other than God.

sections.heading: A More Coherent Translation
sections.text: A fuller explanatory translation would be: The shorter version stays closer to the Arabic. The fuller version explains the interpretation. What should not be done is to make “ceiling,” “noose,” “breath,” or “strangle himself” sound like words the verse itself required.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Quran 22:15 has often been read through a hanging scene: rope, ceiling, neck, strangulation. That reading is old, but age does not make every supplied detail part of the verse. The verse says sabab , not noose. It says sama , not ceiling. It says “cut,” without saying “cut off his breath.” It asks whether the person’s kayd , his plan or effort, will remove what enrages him. The Quran gives us better controls than inherited habit. It uses sabab for means, ways, and connections. It uses cutting of asbab for severed ties. It refuses the idea that God commands indecency or self-destruction. Read inside that larger pattern, 22:15 is not a divine command to suicide. fullText: Translation Forensics · Quran 22:15 Did God tell a man to hang himself? That is how many readers first encounter Quran 22:15 in English. The verse is often rendered as a sarcastic command to tie a rope to the ceiling, strangle oneself, and see whether that removes one’s rage. The problem is not that the verse is simple and translators have ignored it. The problem is that a chain of interpretive choices has been turned into the verse itself. The Arabic can be read another way. The contested words are not obscure: sabab , sama , li-yaqtaʿ , kayd , and the pronoun in yanṣuruhu . Each one was discussed in the classical tradition. The question is whether the suicide reading is the only reading the language allows, and whether it is the reading that best fits the Quran’s own usage. The Verse in One Sentence A literal word-for-word rendering can sound strange: The dispute begins because several words can be narrowed in more than one direction. If sabab is narrowed to “rope,” sama is narrowed to “ceiling,” and li-yaqtaʿ is supplied with “his breath” or “himself,” the verse becomes a hanging scene. If sabab is read as “means” or “connection,” sama as heaven, and li-yaqtaʿ as severing dependence, the verse becomes a challenge to the person who thinks God will not support him: turn upward to God and cut off the false attachments that feed your rage. Common strangulation reading Rope → ceiling → hang himself This reading depends on narrowing sabab to a rope, glossing sama as the ceiling of a house, and supplying the object of “cut” as the man’s breath, body, or connection to the ground. Quran-consistent reading Means → heaven → sever dependence This reading keeps the wider Quranic sense of sabab as a means or connection, keeps sama as heaven, and reads “cut” as severing the false dependencies that do not remove distress. Word-by-Word Map مَن whoever كَانَ يَظُنُّ thinks / assumes أَن لَّن يَنصُرَهُ اللَّهُ that God will not help him فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ in this world and the Hereafter فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ let him extend a means / connection إِلَى السَّمَاءِ toward the sky / heaven ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ then let him cut / sever فَلْيَنظُرْ then let him look هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ whether his plan removes مَا يَغِيظُ what enrages or distresses him Why the Suicide Reading Creates a Problem The Quran does not allow an interpretation to be judged in isolation from the rest of the Quran. It asks the reader to notice internal consistency: A reading of 22:15 that turns the verse into a literal command to hang oneself has to be measured against verses where the Quran says God does not command indecency and where self-killing is forbidden. This does not mean every violent or sarcastic image in the Quran must be softened. It means we should be careful before turning a rhetorical challenge into a divine instruction. The verse can mock the futility of the doubter’s rage without telling a human being to commit suicide. How the Strangulation Reading Entered Tafsir The strangulation reading is not a modern accident. It appears in classical tafsir and was inherited by many English translators. The strongest versions of that reading gloss sabab as a rope, sama as the ceiling of the house, and “cut” as strangling oneself. Tafsir al-Jalalayn Ceiling and strangulation Al-Jalalayn explains the “sky” as the ceiling of the house, the sabab as a rope tied to that ceiling and to the neck, and “cut” as choking oneself by cutting off connection to the ground. Ibn Kathir The inherited report Ibn Kathir transmits the familiar explanation through early authorities: the man stretches a rope to the ceiling of his house and strangles himself with it. Al-Fayruzabadi The same narrowing The verse is again explained as a man tying a rope to the ceiling and hanging himself because of rage over God’s support or over his own provision. Popular English Translations Many English translations simply reproduce the strangulation reading. The result is that a reader encounters the tafsir as though it were the direct meaning of the verse. Dr. Mustafa Khattab “Let them stretch out a rope to the ceiling and strangle themselves.” Saheeh International “Let him extend a rope to the ceiling, then cut off [his breath].” Hilali & Khan “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and let him strangle himself.” M. Pickthall “Let him stretch a rope up to the roof ... and let him hang himself.” A. Yusuf Ali “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and cut himself off.” The same pattern keeps appearing: ceiling, hanging, strangling, cutting off breath. Those words are not all in the verse. They are a tradition of explanation that translators have allowed into the translation. What the Classical Sources Also Preserve The strangulation reading became dominant, but the classical sources preserve more than one interpretive tool. Once those tools are collected, the verse does not have to be read as a divine command to self-harm. The Pronoun Was Disputed The common reading assumes that the pronoun in yanṣuruhu means “God will not help Muhammad.” But exegetes also record another reading: the pronoun can return to man , the “whoever” at the beginning of the verse. On that reading, the verse addresses the person who thinks God will not help or provide for him in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Razi on 22:15 أَنَّ الْهَاءَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ، رَاجِعٌ إِلَى مَنْ فِي أَوَّلِ الْآيَةِ ... فَكَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: مَنْ كَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَرْزُقَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ “The pronoun in ‘God will not help him’ returns to ‘whoever’ at the start of the verse … as if it said: whoever thinks that God will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter.” Al-Qurtubi records the same option, and al-Tabari preserves the explanation that “support” here means provision, with yanṣuruhu read in the sense of yarzuquhu . That reading changes the emotional scene. The verse is no longer about a man enraged by the Prophet’s victory. It can be read as a person who thinks God will not support him and is told to redirect his dependence upward. Sabab Means a Means or Connection The word sabab can mean a rope, but “rope” is not the only sense and not always the central sense. Al-Qurtubi defines it broadly: Al-Qurtubi السَّبَبُ مَا يُتَوَصَّلُ بِهِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ “A sabab is that by which one reaches a thing.” That is why “means,” “connection,” or “way” is often the better starting point. A rope is one kind of sabab , but not every sabab is a noose. The Quran Uses Sabab as a Way or Means The Quran’s own usage matters. In Surat Ghafir, Pharaoh tells Haman to build a tower so that he may reach the means to the heavens: Here the phrase asbab al-samawat cannot mean nooses to ceilings. It means ways, means, or routes of ascent toward the heavens. That makes it relevant to 22:15, where sabab and sama appear together. The Quran also uses the same root with cutting language: In 2:166, the asbab are cut off, meaning relationships, ties, or dependencies are severed. That is a stronger Quranic parallel for 22:15 than the idea of cutting off one’s breath. The Quran itself shows that sabab can be something relational that is severed. 22:15 bi-sababin ... thumma li-yaqtaʿ extend a means, then cut 2:166 wa-taqaṭṭaʿat bihim al-asbab the ties / means between them are cut off Sama Is Not Automatically a Ceiling The word in the verse is al-sama . Translating it as “the ceiling of his house” is a tafsir gloss. Commentators justify that gloss by saying that Arabs may call anything above a person sama . But the literal sense remains sky or heaven, and the real-sky reading is preserved in the exegetical tradition. Al-Qurtubi reports Ibn Zayd’s reading that it means the known sky. Al-Razi lists the real sky as an interpretive option. Ibn Ashur also reports the same broader possibility. So the reading “toward heaven” is not a modern rescue attempt. It is one of the possibilities already visible in the tradition. Even the Strangulation Reading Is Rhetorical Even when classical exegetes adopt the strangulation reading, they do not treat the verse as practical religious instruction. They treat it as a rhetorical challenge, a way of showing that the doubter’s rage cannot overturn God’s decree. Al-Razi states the logic of that kind of interpretation: Al-Razi كُلُّ مَا كَانَ الْمَذْكُورُ أَبْعَدَ مِنَ الْإِمْكَانِ كَانَ أَوْلَى بِأَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْمُرَادَ “The more impossible the mentioned act is, the more fitting it is as the intended figurative sense.” That means the worst English rendering is not merely “rope” or “ceiling.” It is the impression that the verse is a literal command to commit suicide. Even within the strangulation reading, the verse is a rhetorical taunt about futility, not a devotional instruction. The Reading That Makes the Most Sense Rashad Khalifa’s translation is unusual because it does not import the ceiling/noose scenario into the verse. He reads the verse through reliance on God: This reading does not require pretending the classical strangulation interpretation never existed. It does something more useful. It notices that the key words have broader Quranic meanings and that the verse can be read as guidance for the person who doubts God’s support. 1 He thinks God will not support him. 2 He is told to extend his means toward heaven. 3 He cuts the false dependencies beneath him. 4 He sees whether that plan removes what troubles him. The reading is not just more comforting. Comfort by itself is not evidence. It is stronger because it makes better use of the Quran’s own language. Sabab is a means or connection. Asbab can be cut off as ties and dependencies. Sama can remain heaven without being reduced to a ceiling. The pronoun can refer to the doubter himself. The whole sentence can function as a challenge to misplaced dependence rather than a command to self-destruction. What the Verse Is Saying The verse is addressing a person who thinks God will not support him. It challenges him to test the logic of his own dependence. If he thinks support will not come from God, let him direct his means upward and cut the false attachments that keep him trapped in rage or despair. Then let him see whether that plan removes what is troubling him. This reading turns the verse back into Quranic guidance. The person is not told to end his life. He is told to stop imagining that his frustration can defeat God’s decree or that his support must come from somewhere other than God. A More Coherent Translation A fuller explanatory translation would be: The shorter version stays closer to the Arabic. The fuller version explains the interpretation. What should not be done is to make “ceiling,” “noose,” “breath,” or “strangle himself” sound like words the verse itself required. Conclusion Quran 22:15 has often been read through a hanging scene: rope, ceiling, neck, strangulation. That reading is old, but age does not make every supplied detail part of the verse. The verse says sabab , not noose. It says sama , not ceiling. It says “cut,” without saying “cut off his breath.” It asks whether the person’s kayd , his plan or effort, will remove what enrages him. The Quran gives us better controls than inherited habit. It uses sabab for means, ways, and connections. It uses cutting of asbab for severed ties. It refuses the idea that God commands indecency or self-destruction. Read inside that larger pattern, 22:15 is not a divine command to suicide. It is a challenge to the person who doubts God’s support: turn upward, cut false reliance, and see whether rage survives when dependence is placed where it belongs. { .article-opening { margin: 0 0 2.6rem; title: The Traditional Distortion of 4:3 - Polygamy
description: A close reading of Quran 4:3 in its orphan-justice context, the traditional four-wife limit, the reports of the Prophet

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Quran 4:3 · Marriage · Orphan Justice The verse begins with orphans. Later law often begins with men. Quran 4:3 is usually introduced as “the polygamy verse.” That label already shifts the reader’s attention. The verse does not open with male desire, household expansion, or a general right to multiple wives. It opens with fear of injustice toward orphans. The traditional reading then creates a second problem. It treats 4:3 as a clear Quranic limit of four wives, while hadith and sira reports portray the Prophet with nine wives at the same time. The usual solution is to create a prophetic exception. But that solution has to be tested against the Quran's own language about the Prophet following revelation, not standing above it.

sections.heading: The Shape of the Verse
sections.text: The verse has a clear internal movement: Condition If you fear injustice toward orphans The opening concern is not sexual access or male privilege. It is fear of failing the vulnerable. Permission Then marry two, three, or four The permission appears inside a social problem, not as a detached marital ideal. Restriction If you fear injustice, then one The verse ends by pushing the reader back toward reduced harm, not expanded desire. That structure matters. If the fear of injustice is removed from the verse, the whole moral logic changes. The verse becomes a permission slip. Inside its own wording, however, the permission is surrounded by caution.

sections.heading: The Early Tafsir Did Not Forget the Orphans
sections.text: The earliest exegetical record does not read 4:3 as a free-floating celebration of polygamy. It repeatedly connects the verse to orphan property, orphan girls, and fear of injustice. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Urwa asks Aisha about the verse. Her answer places the verse in the setting of an orphan girl under the care of a guardian who shares her property. Her wealth and beauty tempt the guardian to marry her without giving her the dowry she would receive from someone else.

sections.heading: Is “Two, Three, or Four” a Hard Limit?
sections.text: Traditional law treats the verse as establishing a maximum of four wives. It also uses reports in which men who entered Islam with more than four wives were told to keep four and separate from the rest. The report of Ghaylan b. Salama is the most famous example: he accepted Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet reportedly commanded him to choose four of them.

sections.heading: The Hadith Problem: Nine Wives
sections.text: Sahih al-Bukhari preserves the report from Anas that the Prophet would go around to all his wives in one night and that he had nine wives.

sections.heading: The Actual Dilemma
sections.text: Option 1 4:3 is a hard Quranic cap of four. Then hadith reports of nine simultaneous wives require a clear Quranic exception. The burden is on the tradition to show that exception rather than assume it. Option 2 4:3 is not a cap by grammar alone. Then the familiar four-wife rule depends heavily on juristic tradition and reports like Ghaylan, not on an obvious standalone reading of the verse. Option 3 4:3 is conditional and justice-centered. This reading does not begin with male entitlement. It begins with vulnerability, fairness, and fear of harm. The third option is the one most faithful to the verse's moral movement. It does not need to solve every later legal question at once. It simply refuses to let later law detach the verse from its own opening condition.

sections.heading: Justice Is Not a Decorative Clause
sections.text: The verse does not merely say, “marry two, three, or four.” It says that if you fear you will not be just, then one. Then later in the same surah, the Quran says that people will not be able to be fully just between wives, even if they desire to do so. Traditional law often distinguishes between material justice and emotional justice. A jurist may say that 4:3 requires fair maintenance, time, and outward treatment, while 4:129 says perfect emotional equality is impossible. That distinction is coherent as a legal harmonization. But it should not erase the force of the warning. The Quran itself places plural marriage under the shadow of injustice. The verse does not encourage expansion. It warns against harm. Every movement in the verse narrows the permission when justice is feared: from plural marriage to one, and from male initiative to accountability before God. That is why the common presentation of polygamy as a standing male right is a distortion of emphasis even before one reaches the legal details.

sections.heading: How the Distortion Happens
sections.text: The distortion has three steps. 1 Detach the phrase from the condition “Two, three, or four” is lifted out of the orphan-justice frame and treated as a general male allowance. 2 Minimize the justice warning The verse's own movement toward one wife is treated as a technical footnote rather than the ethical center of the passage. 3 Use hadith to manage contradiction Reports of the Prophet's nine wives are preserved, then handled by an assumed exception that many readers never test against the Quran. This is why the popular discourse is so often backwards. The Quranic passage is cautious and conditional. The later discourse becomes expansive and defensive.

sections.heading: What the Verse Actually Gives
sections.text: Quran 4:3 gives a limited permission in a setting of vulnerability. It is not an ideal. It is not a command. It is not a male status symbol. It is not a tool for humiliating a first wife or collecting women. The verse says that if justice is feared, reduce. It does not say that if desire increases, expand.

sections.heading: Final Reading
sections.text: The rendering leaves the verse's tension intact. It does not pretend that the verse has no plural-marriage permission. It also does not let the permission swallow the condition.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Quran 4:3 begins with fear of injustice toward orphans and ends with the instruction to marry one if justice is feared. The verse is cautious from beginning to end. Early tafsir preserved that concern, even while jurists developed the four-wife ceiling. The hadith tradition then introduced another pressure by portraying the Prophet with nine wives, forcing later scholars to create an exception. A Quran-centered reading does not have to follow that path. It can keep the verse where it begins: with justice, vulnerability, and restraint. If the condition is absent, the verse is being misused. If justice is feared, the verse points to one. And if later reports or legal customs turn this warning into a broad entitlement, then the problem is not with the Quranic text. The problem is with the tradition that moved the center of the verse from the orphan to the man.

fullText: Quran 4:3 · Marriage · Orphan Justice The verse begins with orphans. Later law often begins with men. Quran 4:3 is usually introduced as “the polygamy verse.” That label already shifts the reader’s attention. The verse does not open with male desire, household expansion, or a general right to multiple wives. It opens with fear of injustice toward orphans. The traditional reading then creates a second problem. It treats 4:3 as a clear Quranic limit of four wives, while hadith and sira reports portray the Prophet with nine wives at the same time. The usual solution is to create a prophetic exception. But that solution has to be tested against the Quran's own language about the Prophet following revelation, not standing above it. The Shape of the Verse The verse has a clear internal movement: Condition If you fear injustice toward orphans The opening concern is not sexual access or male privilege. It is fear of failing the vulnerable. Permission Then marry two, three, or four The permission appears inside a social problem, not as a detached marital ideal. Restriction If you fear injustice, then one The verse ends by pushing the reader back toward reduced harm, not expanded desire. That structure matters. If the fear of injustice is removed from the verse, the whole moral logic changes. The verse becomes a permission slip. Inside its own wording, however, the permission is surrounded by caution. The Early Tafsir Did Not Forget the Orphans The earliest exegetical record does not read 4:3 as a free-floating celebration of polygamy. It repeatedly connects the verse to orphan property, orphan girls, and fear of injustice. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Urwa asks Aisha about the verse. Her answer places the verse in the setting of an orphan girl under the care of a guardian who shares her property. Her wealth and beauty tempt the guardian to marry her without giving her the dowry she would receive from someone else. Al-Tabari preserves several explanations. Some connect the verse to men taking orphan property to fund numerous marriages. Others say that just as people feared injustice with orphans, they should also fear injustice toward women. Qatada says men in the pre-Islamic period would marry ten or fewer women, and that God permitted four and reduced them to four. Al-Tabari's preferred explanation is that the verse warns against injustice in women just as the previous verse warned against injustice in orphan wealth. Aisha The verse addresses a guardian tempted to marry an orphan girl under his care without giving her a fair dowry. Ikrima / Ibn Abbas strand Some reports connect the verse to men taking orphan wealth while marrying many women. Qatada / al-Tabari The verse moves from fear of injustice toward orphans to fear of injustice toward women, limiting pre-Islamic excess. These are not identical interpretations. That is important. The early record itself shows that the verse was being explained through a cluster of justice concerns: orphan girls, orphan wealth, excessive wives, and unequal treatment of women. None of those readings makes the verse a simple general entitlement. Is “Two, Three, or Four” a Hard Limit? Traditional law treats the verse as establishing a maximum of four wives. It also uses reports in which men who entered Islam with more than four wives were told to keep four and separate from the rest. The report of Ghaylan b. Salama is the most famous example: he accepted Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet reportedly commanded him to choose four of them. There is a real debate here. The phrase mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ is distributive: twos, threes, and fours. The same pattern appears in 35:1 for the wings of angels. That parallel matters because 35:1 immediately says that God adds to creation what He wills. So the phrase itself is not always a mathematical ceiling by its own grammar. In 4:3, the traditional ceiling comes from the verse's legal reading, the justice condition, and the hadith reports used by jurists. It is not simply the grammar alone. Quran 4:3 mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ Plural marriage appears inside a warning about justice and orphans. Quran 35:1 mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ The same numerical form describes angelic wings, then adds that God increases creation as He wills. This creates a problem for simplistic traditional claims. If four is a Quranic ceiling, then the later reports about the Prophet's nine wives need a Quranic explanation. If four is not a ceiling by grammar alone, then traditionalists should stop pretending that 4:3 is a simple proof-text for their later legal package. The Hadith Problem: Nine Wives Sahih al-Bukhari preserves the report from Anas that the Prophet would go around to all his wives in one night and that he had nine wives. This is where the tension becomes unavoidable. The same tradition that reads 4:3 as a four-wife limit also preserves reports in which the Prophet has nine wives. Traditional law answers by saying the Prophet had special rules. The Quran does give the Prophet some specific marriage rulings in 33:50. But 33:52 then says: Whatever one does with these verses, they do not allow a lazy answer. The Quran does not present the Prophet as an independent legislator who may simply override God's boundaries. The traditional solution therefore has to do more than say, “The Prophet is an exception.” It has to show that the exception is clear in the Quran itself, and that the reports about nine simultaneous wives match the Quran's own sequence and restrictions. The Actual Dilemma Option 1 4:3 is a hard Quranic cap of four. Then hadith reports of nine simultaneous wives require a clear Quranic exception. The burden is on the tradition to show that exception rather than assume it. Option 2 4:3 is not a cap by grammar alone. Then the familiar four-wife rule depends heavily on juristic tradition and reports like Ghaylan, not on an obvious standalone reading of the verse. Option 3 4:3 is conditional and justice-centered. This reading does not begin with male entitlement. It begins with vulnerability, fairness, and fear of harm. The third option is the one most faithful to the verse's moral movement. It does not need to solve every later legal question at once. It simply refuses to let later law detach the verse from its own opening condition. Justice Is Not a Decorative Clause The verse does not merely say, “marry two, three, or four.” It says that if you fear you will not be just, then one. Then later in the same surah, the Quran says that people will not be able to be fully just between wives, even if they desire to do so. Traditional law often distinguishes between material justice and emotional justice. A jurist may say that 4:3 requires fair maintenance, time, and outward treatment, while 4:129 says perfect emotional equality is impossible. That distinction is coherent as a legal harmonization. But it should not erase the force of the warning. The Quran itself places plural marriage under the shadow of injustice. The verse does not encourage expansion. It warns against harm. Every movement in the verse narrows the permission when justice is feared: from plural marriage to one, and from male initiative to accountability before God. That is why the common presentation of polygamy as a standing male right is a distortion of emphasis even before one reaches the legal details. How the Distortion Happens The distortion has three steps. 1 Detach the phrase from the condition “Two, three, or four” is lifted out of the orphan-justice frame and treated as a general male allowance. 2 Minimize the justice warning The verse's own movement toward one wife is treated as a technical footnote rather than the ethical center of the passage. 3 Use hadith to manage contradiction Reports of the Prophet's nine wives are preserved, then handled by an assumed exception that many readers never test against the Quran. This is why the popular discourse is so often backwards. The Quranic passage is cautious and conditional. The later discourse becomes expansive and defensive. What the Verse Actually Gives Quran 4:3 gives a limited permission in a setting of vulnerability. It is not an ideal. It is not a command. It is not a male status symbol. It is not a tool for humiliating a first wife or collecting women. The verse says that if justice is feared, reduce. It does not say that if desire increases, expand. Final Reading The rendering leaves the verse's tension intact. It does not pretend that the verse has no plural-marriage permission. It also does not let the permission swallow the condition. Early tafsir preserved that concern, even while jurists developed the four-wife ceiling. The hadith tradition then introduced another pressure by portraying the Prophet with nine wives, forcing later scholars to create an exception. A Quran-centered reading does not have to follow that path. It can keep the verse where it begins: with justice, vulnerability, and restraint. If the condition is absent, the verse is being misused. If justice is feared, the verse points to one. And if later reports or legal customs turn this warning into a broad entitlement, then the problem is not with the Quranic text. title: Gabriel’s Six Hundred Wings and Qur’an 53:10
description: A critical look at the hadith claim that Gabriel had six hundred wings, its dependence on one Kūfan exegetical route through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī, and the Qur’anic problem around 53:10 and 35:1.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.text: The Qur’an describes angels as messengers with wings, but it does not say that Gabriel has six hundred wings. That number comes from hadith. The report is usually presented as if it were a broad, independent description of Gabriel’s created form. But when the isnāds are mapped, the picture is much narrower. The main “six hundred wings” reports pass through one Kūfan exegetical route: Ibn Masʿūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī. After al-Shaybānī, the report fans out through several later transmitters and enters Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī. That later spread can make the report look wider than it is. But above the spread, the tradition is compact. This matters because the report is not just giving a detail about angels. It is explaining Qur’an 53:9–10. The hadith tells us that Ibn Masʿūd understood the passage as a reference to Muhammad seeing Gabriel. The problem is that this explanation pushes the verse away from its simpler Qur’anic grammar.

sections.heading: The Verse Being Explained
sections.text: The verse says that He revealed to His servant what He revealed. The natural reading is that God is the revealer and Muhammad is the servant. The hadith explanation shifts the focus. It reads the surrounding scene as Muhammad seeing Gabriel in his true form, and then adds that Gabriel had six hundred wings. The issue is not only the number of wings. The issue is the exegetical move. The report turns a verse about revelation from God to His servant into a report about Gabriel’s appearance. The wording is simple, but its function is large. It is not a free-floating angelology report. It is a tafsīr report. Zirr is asked about Qur’an 53, and he answers by transmitting Ibn Masʿūd’s statement about Gabriel. That is why the chain and the context matter.

sections.heading: The Isnād Map
sections.text: The diagram below replaces the older raw image with a cleaner route map. The important point is not how many boxes appear at the bottom. The important point is where all the lines meet. Every listed route comes down through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī. For a lay reader, this means the report has a bottleneck. A bottleneck is the point in a transmission map where many later roads collapse into one earlier road. Here, the later collectors preserve several routes, but they are not independent at the level that matters. They all return to the same Kūfan exegetical strand. That does not automatically prove the report is invented. But it prevents an exaggerated claim. One cannot simply say, “Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī all have it, therefore it is broadly established.” The real question is where the report becomes recoverable before the collectors. The answer is al-Shaybānī from Zirr from Ibn Masʿūd. This table shows why the report should be discussed as one exegetical family, not as a broad multi-origin tradition. The collector-facing routes differ. The upper route does not.

sections.heading: The Matn Problem
sections.text: The matn is short. But the interpretive problem is large. Notice the structure. The report begins with a question about a Qur’anic verse. It ends with a claim about Gabriel’s wings. That means the report is doing tafsīr work. It is telling the reader how to understand the vision scene in Sūrat al-Najm. The problem is that Qur’an 53:10 reads as God revealing to His servant. The servant is Muhammad. The revealer is God. The hadith explanation places Gabriel at the center and makes the point of the verse the Prophet’s vision of Gabriel. That is not the most natural reading of the verse itself. This does not mean a reader must deny that Gabriel appears elsewhere in Sūrat al-Najm. The point is narrower. The hadith report is not merely preserving a neutral historical memory. It is intervening in the meaning of a verse. It supplies an exegetical explanation and then builds angelology on top of that explanation.

sections.heading: Qur’an 35:1 and the Wings of Angels
sections.text: Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as messengers with wings: two, three, and four. The same verse also says that God increases in creation what He wills. That last clause matters because it is often used as the traditional answer to the objection. A defender can say, “The verse mentions two, three, and four, but then says God increases in creation, so six hundred is possible.” That response is possible, but it does not remove the critical problem. The Qur’an itself does not say Gabriel has six hundred wings. The hadith supplies that number through one exegetical chain. The question is not whether God could create an angel with more wings. The question is whether this specific report has strong enough textual and transmission evidence to impose six hundred wings onto Gabriel and then use that as the explanation of Sūrat al-Najm. The better argument is therefore precise. Qur’an 35:1 does not directly teach six hundred wings. Qur’an 53:10 does not naturally require Gabriel as the subject of “His servant.” The six-hundred-wings claim comes from a narrow hadith-tafsīr strand, not from the Qur’an itself.

sections.heading: Why the Bottleneck Matters
sections.text: Hadith reports can look stronger than they are when later branches are counted as if each branch were an independent origin. Here, the report appears in Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī, but the major routes converge through al-Shaybānī. That means the collector spread is real, but the early spread is limited. The key question is not, “How many books contain this?” The key question is, “Where does the report become recoverable?” For this family, the answer is: Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd. That makes al-Shaybānī the visible bottleneck of the preserved family. Zirr is also central because he is the one being asked about the verse. Ibn Masʿūd is the Companion authority used to anchor the explanation. But the later literary spread does not create multiple independent Companion-level witnesses.

sections.heading: The Report as Exegesis, Not Independent Angelology
sections.text: The most important correction is conceptual. The report is often treated as if it were mainly about the physical form of Gabriel. But the report itself begins as an explanation of Sūrat al-Najm. The question is about Qur’anic wording. The answer is a hadith explanation. That changes how the report should be evaluated. If it were an independent report from multiple Companions saying, “The Prophet saw Gabriel with six hundred wings,” the issue would be one thing. But the recoverable family is specifically Ibn Masʿūd’s interpretation transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī. The number belongs to that exegetical tradition. It is also important that the Qur’an does not need the six-hundred-wings report to make sense. Qur’an 53:10 can be read as God revealing to His servant. Qur’an 35:1 already gives a restrained description of angels as winged messengers. The hadith adds a dramatic number and then attaches it to a disputed reading of the vision passage.

sections.heading: What the Diagram Shows
sections.text: The diagram does not show that every individual in the chain was unreliable. That is not the point. It shows that the report is structurally narrow. The chain does not branch at Ibn Masʿūd into multiple students. It does not branch at Zirr into many independent transmitters. It branches below al-Shaybānī. That means the “six hundred wings” tradition is not a broad early memory. It is a compact Kūfan tafsīr report that later became widely cited because major compilers preserved its branches. The same pattern appears in many hadith studies. A report can have many later witnesses but still depend on one earlier bottleneck. Once that bottleneck is identified, the report has to be argued from that bottleneck, not from the number of later books.

sections.heading: Final Verdict
sections.text: The “Gabriel had six hundred wings” report is best understood as a narrow exegetical hadith family, not as Qur’anic angelology. Its main preserved routes all converge through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī from Zirr b. Ḥubaysh from Ibn Masʿūd. The later branches into Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī show that the report circulated well below al-Shaybānī, but they do not create independent early origins above him. The Qur’anic issue is also important. Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as having wings in twos, threes, and fours, while also saying God increases in creation what He wills. That means the verse should not be used in a simplistic way, as if it mechanically forbids all increase. But it also does not teach six hundred wings. The six-hundred number is supplied by hadith, not by the Qur’an. Qur’an 53:10 is even more central. The verse naturally reads as God revealing to His servant. The hadith turns the passage into a statement about Muhammad seeing Gabriel and then adds the six-hundred-wings detail. That is an exegetical move, and the isnād map shows that the move is preserved through one compact Kūfan route. So the strongest conclusion is careful but clear: the Qur’an does not require the six-hundred-wings doctrine, and the hadith evidence for it depends on a narrow tafsīr bottleneck. The report is not a broad independent memory of Gabriel’s form. It is Ibn Masʿūd’s Qur’an-exegesis tradition as transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī.

Qur’an 35:1 already gives a restrained description of angels as winged messengers. The hadith adds a dramatic number and then attaches it to a disputed reading of the vision passage. What the Diagram Shows The diagram does not show that every individual in the chain was unreliable. That is not the point. It shows that the report is structurally narrow. The chain does not branch at Ibn Masʿūd into multiple students. It does not branch at Zirr into many independent transmitters. It branches below al-Shaybānī. That means the “six hundred wings” tradition is not a broad early memory. It is a compact Kūfan tafsīr report that later became widely cited because major compilers preserved its branches. The same pattern appears in many hadith studies. A report can have many later witnesses but still depend on one earlier bottleneck. Once that bottleneck is identified, the report has to be argued from that bottleneck, not from the number of later books. Final Verdict The “Gabriel had six hundred wings” report is best understood as a narrow exegetical hadith family, not as Qur’anic angelology. Its main preserved routes all converge through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī from Zirr b. Ḥubaysh from Ibn Masʿūd. The later branches into Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī show that the report circulated well below al-Shaybānī, but they do not create independent early origins above him. The Qur’anic issue is also important. Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as having wings in twos, threes, and fours, while also saying God increases in creation what He wills. That means the verse should not be used in a simplistic way, as if it mechanically forbids all increase. But it also does not teach six hundred wings. The six-hundred number is supplied by hadith, not by the Qur’an. Qur’an 53:10 is even more central. The verse naturally reads as God revealing to His servant. The hadith turns the passage into a statement about Muhammad seeing Gabriel and then adds the six-hundred-wings detail. That is an exegetical move, and the isnād map shows that the move is preserved through one compact Kūfan route. So the strongest conclusion is careful but clear: the Qur’an does not require the six-hundred-wings doctrine, and the hadith evidence for it depends on a narrow tafsīr bottleneck. The report is not a broad independent memory of Gabriel’s form. It is Ibn Masʿūd’s Qur’an-exegesis tradition as transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī. title: The Sunni-Quranic Abrogation Dilemma
description: A source-based critique of Quranic abrogation in Sunni legal theory, showing how the doctrine creates an unstable index of supposedly inactive verses and conflicts with the Quran

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Quranic Epistemology · Abrogation · Sunni Legal Theory The problem is not merely that scholars disagreed. The problem is that the doctrine gives them permission to retire revelation. The Sunni doctrine of Quranic abrogation says that some Quranic rulings were replaced by later rulings. In its narrowest form, it means that a later revealed command cancels an earlier command when both cannot be practiced together. In its wider historical use, however, it became a way to explain away verses that sat uneasily with later law, later warfare theory, or inherited legal assumptions. That is where the dilemma begins. If a verse from God can remain in the mushaf while its ruling is treated as no longer operative, then ordinary believers need a reliable way to know which verses still bind them. The classical tradition never produced a universally agreed Quranic index of abrogated verses. It produced lists, counter-lists, reductions, reclassifications, and debates over whether many alleged cases were abrogation at all.

sections.heading: The Quranic Baseline
sections.text: The Quran repeatedly describes God's words as complete, true, just, and not subject to alteration. Any doctrine that says a verse is present in recitation but no longer operative has to be measured against that baseline. These verses do not disappear because later scholars developed a technical category called naskh. A Muslim can try to argue that abrogation is not "changing God's words" because God Himself replaces one ruling with another. But then the evidence must be clear. It cannot rest on later discomfort, broad contradiction claims, or an inherited habit of declaring difficult verses mansukh. Quranic claim God's words are complete and unalterable. The text presents itself as guidance, not as a book whose operative parts must later be sorted by conflicting scholarly lists. Sunni naskh claim Some verses remain recited but no longer rule. That claim requires an external method for identifying inactive verses with certainty. The dilemma The method is disputed. The classical tradition preserves disagreement over which verses are abrogated and even over what should count as abrogation.

sections.heading: The Verses Usually Used for Abrogation
sections.text: The two verses most often invoked are 2:106 and 16:101. These verses mention replacing or causing an aya to be forgotten. The traditional argument reads aya here as a Quranic verse. That reading is possible, but it is not the only possible reading of the word. In the Quran, aya can mean a sign, proof, miracle, or revealed communication. The context of 16:101 also includes the accusation that Muhammad is fabricating, which means the verse is defending God's authority over revelation rather than giving later jurists a blank license to cancel difficult verses. The safer reading is this: if God replaces one aya with another, that is God's action. It does not follow that later scholars may take every apparent tension, every historical sequence, or every legal inconvenience and declare one Quranic passage inactive.

sections.heading: Al-Suyuti Tried to Narrow the Chaos
sections.text: Al-Suyuti did not invent the abrogation problem. He inherited a field already swollen with claims. In al-Itqan fi Ulum al-Quran , he reports that people had greatly multiplied the number of alleged abrogated verses, then he gives a reduced list. He says the refined list has twenty cases and puts it into verse so it can be remembered.

sections.heading: Ibn al-Jawzi Shows the Same Problem from Another Angle
sections.text: Ibn al-Jawzi wrote a full work on the abrogating and abrogated verses, Nawasikh al-Quran . The book does not present a simple, universally agreed list. It discusses a large field of alleged abrogation cases. In the printed arrangement available online, the section on verses claimed to be abrogated introduces a discussion of 247 issues across 62 surahs.

sections.heading: The Categories Make the Dilemma Worse
sections.text: The doctrine did not stop at ordinary legal replacement. Classical manuals discuss several kinds of abrogation, including: Type Meaning Why it creates pressure Ruling abrogated, recitation remains The verse is still in the Quran, but its legal force is gone. The reader encounters God's words but is told not to apply the apparent ruling. Recitation abrogated, ruling remains The words are no longer recited as Quran, but the law supposedly remains. A binding law is attached to wording no longer present in the mushaf. Both recitation and ruling abrogated The words and ruling are both said to have been removed. The doctrine depends almost entirely on reports outside the present Quranic text. Al-Suyuti preserves these categories and gives examples, including the famous report attributed to Aisha about ten known sucklings being abrogated by five known sucklings, while some people still recited the latter after the Prophet's death.

sections.heading: The Table Problem
sections.text: The difficulty becomes visible when later scholars and editors build tables of alleged abrogated verses. In one table attached to Ibn al-Jawzi's work, a verse such as 2:109 is listed with scholars who claimed abrogation and scholars who denied it. The same table identifies al-Nahhas among those who claimed abrogation while listing Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Suyuti, and others among those who denied it.

sections.heading: The Epistemological Crisis
sections.text: A doctrine about divine guidance should not make divine guidance harder to identify. If God intended some verses to remain in the Quran while their rulings no longer apply, then the believer needs more than scholarly confidence. He needs certainty. The classical tradition often answers by saying that only qualified scholars can know these matters. But that answer shifts the problem. The scholars themselves disagreed. Some expanded the list. Others reduced it. Some called cases abrogation. Others called the same cases specification, restriction, explanation, or time-limited command. Option 1 Accept broad abrogation The Quran becomes dependent on later scholarly lists to know which commands still operate. Option 2 Accept narrow abrogation Most classical claims collapse, and many famous examples have to be reclassified. Option 3 Reject intra-Quranic cancellation The Quran remains internally binding, while apparent tensions must be solved by context, scope, and careful reading. The third option fits the Quranic self-description best. It does not require pretending that scholars never noticed tension. It simply refuses to let later inherited tension cancel God's words.

sections.heading: What Naskh Often Does in Practice
sections.text: In practice, many abrogation claims do not solve contradictions. They avoid interpretation. A verse about patience is treated as cancelled by a verse about fighting. A verse about forgiveness is treated as cancelled by a verse about combat. A verse about bequest is treated as cancelled by inheritance law. A verse about private consultation is treated as cancelled after one incident. Sometimes this is defended through chronology. Sometimes it is defended by legal need. Sometimes the proof is much weaker than the claim. The Quran gives a different reading discipline: If the Quran contains no contradiction, the first task is reconciliation, not cancellation. A contradiction should not be manufactured by ignoring conditions, context, audience, genre, and scope. If falsehood does not come to it from before it or behind it, the burden is on the person who claims that one Quranic statement has legally neutralized another. That burden is rarely met with the kind of certainty the doctrine requires.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The doctrine of abrogation was supposed to protect the coherence of revelation. In practice, it often made the Quran dependent on later scholarly sorting. Al-Suyuti had to reduce inflated lists. Ibn al-Jawzi had to discuss and sift through large numbers of alleged cases. Classical authorities warned that abrogation cannot rest on loose opinion. Yet the doctrine continued to be used as a way to retire verses from active force. A book that calls itself complete and unalterable should not require believers to wonder which of God's words are no longer operative. Apparent tension should be handled through context, qualification, and careful interpretation. It should not be handled by building a second book beside the Quran, one that tells the reader which parts of the first book no longer count.
