It is possible to be considerably more specific than that. Levitical priestly duty splits into two tiers. The narrower tier is the Kohathite and Amramite-specific transport duty described in Numbers 4, and the broader tier covers the Aaronic functions of teaching, blessing, purity adjudication, atonement, guarding sacred space, and judging disputes. Teaching and the Judgment of Purity Deuteronomy 33:10 and Leviticus 10:11 assign the priesthood the specific duty to “teach Your laws to Jacob and Your instructions to Israel,” The Blessing Formula Numbers 6:22-27 sets out the priestly benediction, the specific words God commands Aaron and his sons to pronounce over the people. The instruction is explicit about who is authorized to perform it. Leviticus 9:22 then shows Aaron actually carrying this out, immediately after his ordination as high priest, in the same physical posture the text keeps returning to. Luke’s ascension scene reproduces that exact gesture, hands raised over the people, and assigns it to Jesus rather than to a priest of Aaron’s line. Hands raised in blessing Aaron “lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them” (Leviticus 9:22) Jesus, “lifting up his hands, blessed them” (Luke 24:50) Who is authorized to bless “Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus shall you bless” (Numbers 6:22-23) Jesus pronounces the blessing himself, without a priestly intermediary There is a separate, smaller pattern worth noting alongside this one, though it is not itself drawn from Aaronic law. At the feeding of the 5,000 and again at the Last Supper, Mark records Jesus performing the identical four-step action of taking bread, blessing it, breaking it, and giving it out. That four-verb sequence is not a priestly formula from Numbers or Leviticus. It is the ordinary Jewish table blessing, the berakah any head of a household would recite over bread at an everyday meal, with no restriction to Aaron's line at all. What is notable is not its priestly origin, since it has none, but its exact repetition. Mark uses the same four verbs, in the same order, for both the feeding miracle and the supper, tying the two scenes together as a matched pair rather than two unrelated meals. Read alongside the hands-raised blessing gesture above, the two patterns point in the same general direction without being the same kind of evidence: one shows Jesus occupying a role Aaronic law reserves for the priesthood, and the other shows Mark deliberately linking two meals through a shared, ordinary liturgical action. --- The Davidic Motivation Davidic messianism was the dominant, pre-existing expectation—Aaronic wasn’t. By the Second Temple period, the scriptural apparatus for a coming Davidic ruler was enormous and already fixed in the popular imagination. The Rhetorical Advantage of David If you’re a Gospel writer trying to persuade an audience—Jewish or God-fearing Gentile—that this specific man is the promised deliverer, “son of David” is the category with instant recognition and a citation apparatus ten times deeper than anything Aaronic material offers. Matthew’s whole formula-quotation structure (“this was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet…”) is only viable because the Davidic prophetic corpus is that rich. You couldn’t build the same rhetorical machine out of Aaronic material, since there isn’t enough of it, and what exists doesn’t point as cleanly at an individual coming figure. A Title Fixed Before the Gospels Were Written The title “Messiah” itself was already Davidic-coded before any Gospel was written. Paul—writing in the 50s CE, decades before Mark—already passes on a received tradition that Jesus is descended from David, embedded in what looks like a pre-Pauline confessional formula. Writing to a Post-Temple Audience Matthew is almost certainly writing after 70 CE, to a community watching the entire cultic infrastructure—altar, sacrifice, functioning priesthood—cease to exist. A messianic claim rooted in Davidic kingship needs no operative Temple to remain meaningful; “kingdom” language ports over easily into something spiritual/eschatological. A messianic claim rooted in priestly office is much harder to sustain rhetorically once there’s no altar left to serve at. The Davidic framing is simply more durable messaging for the audience these texts are being written for. The actual Aaronic institution was the antagonist, not a plausible identity to claim. By Jesus’s lifetime the high priesthood was Rome-appointed, Sadducee-controlled, and, per the Passion narratives themselves, the institution that orchestrates his death (Annas, Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin’s priestly faction). Claiming Jesus continues or fulfills that specific line would be self-defeating in a text whose climax depicts that same line condemning him. Melchizedek as a Way Around the Broken Line This is likely a real part of why Hebrews goes a different direction entirely rather than doubling down on Aaronic descent. It roots Jesus’s priesthood in Melchizedek, a figure from before Levi even existed (Genesis 14, older than Sinai, outside the tribal system altogether). The psalm that destabilizes the Davidic label in Mark's earliest Gospel is the same psalm that, four verses on, grounds a priesthood older than Levi. Hebrews is not reaching outside scripture for a workaround; it is following the same text to a different verse. This lets the author claim priestly authority for Jesus while owing nothing to, and carrying no contamination from, the corrupted Hasmonean-then-Herodian-then-Roman-appointed high priesthood the same broader tradition treats as illegitimate. Melchizedek isn’t necessarily a rejection of priestly Christology; it was simply a way to get priestly Christology without touching the compromised institutional line. A Rabbinic Parallel to the Same Two Verses Hebrews is not the only tradition that fastens onto this psalm to settle a question about priesthood. The Babylonian Talmud, discussing why the priesthood belongs to Abraham's line rather than to Melchizedek himself, cites the same two verses in the same order, Psalm 110:1 and then Psalm 110:4, to make its own, unrelated argument. Two very different traditions, writing centuries apart and for entirely different purposes, both stop at the same pair of verses when a text needs to explain why the priesthood in question does not run through the ordinary Aaronic line. The Talmud is not a source for Hebrews; the Babylonian Talmud was redacted centuries after the New Testament and cannot be read backward as its influence. What the parallel shows instead is that the two verses in Psalm 110 were, independently, recognized in both traditions as the place to go when a priesthood needed grounding outside the hereditary system. It also puts on display exactly how flexible the Hebrew of verse 4 is: the Talmud renders the same phrase as "a king of righteousness," the Gender-Sensitive JPS renders it "a rightful king by My decree," and the reading Hebrews depends on takes it as the proper name Melchizedek. All three are legitimate readings of מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק; which one a text prefers depends entirely on what argument it is trying to make with it. The Political Danger of a Davidic Claim A straightforwardly Davidic royal claim was politically live and dangerous. Rome executed Jesus under a titulus reading “King of the Jews,” reading the claim as insurrectionary regardless of how the Gospels wanted to spiritualize it. But rhetorically, casting Jesus as the fulfillment of the nationalist hope while redefining its politics (“my kingdom is not from this world”) let the writers inherit the emotional and scriptural power of Davidic hope while defusing its revolutionary content. That’s a very different kind of narrative labor than an Aaronic claim would require, since nobody needed to defuse a priestly claim politically, because it was never going to read as a threat to Rome the way “son of David” did. Davidic identity was the load-bearing confessional premise the whole movement needed—recognizable, prophetically over-determined, politically useful once reframed, and durable past 70 CE. Aaronic material had none of those institutional pressures pushing it forward, which is exactly why it shows up unforced, structurally, and without argument. Nobody needed it to do apologetic work, so nobody made it into a claim. --- Conclusion The previous piece established that Jesus’s Davidic credentials rest on a genealogy through a man who was not his biological father, that Elizabeth and Mary were both connected to Aaron’s line, and that Second Temple Judaism had a real category for a priestly messiah standing alongside a Davidic king. This piece adds on to the argument with positive support toward the Aaronic claim. Amram was never simply the name of one man a thousand years removed from Mary; it was already functioning as a clan name inside the Torah’s own priestly source, the same way “sons of Aaron” functions throughout Exodus and Leviticus, and by the Second Temple period it carried its own weight as a name associated with priestly election. The priesthood that Amram’s line was supposed to steward had, by Jesus’s own lifetime, been bought, deposed, and reassigned so many times over two centuries that a significant part of the religious community considered it illegitimate—which is the actual context the temple cleansing and its language of zeal belong to. And once the Gospels are read for specifically priestly detail rather than general moral tone, the pattern runs far deeper than the temple cleansing alone. It reaches into the blood theology of the Last Supper, the reversed contagion of the healing narratives, the blessing formula repeated at two separate meals, the priestly judgment language Jesus repeatedly uses when he pronounces people clean, and the priestly ceremony of water baptism conducted by one of Levitic descent. Taken as a whole, the case for Jesus as Messiah ben Aaron looks considerably stronger once it rests on more than temperament and teaching style—once it rests on the actual mechanics of a broken priesthood, a name that meant more than a single father, and a set of textual details in the Gospels that line up with Aaronic law far too specifically to be accidental. title: The Wisdom of Solomon and the End of Jesus
description: A close reading of Q 3:54–55, Q 4:157–159, and Q 5:117 against the Wisdom of Solomon

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Sean Anthony has proposed that the Qur'an's account of the end of Jesus's earthly mission is best read against late ancient Jewish polemics against, and parody of, the life of Jesus of Nazareth.

sections.heading: The Qur'anic Criteria
sections.text: Q 3:54–55 supplies the earlier of the Qur'an's two accounts of the end of Jesus's mission, in compressed form: the Israelites plot against Jesus, God plots in response and plots best of all, and God then tells Jesus that He will take him, raise him to Himself, and purify him from the disbelievers. Q 4:156–159 supplies the second account, embedded in an extended polemic against the People of Scripture in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Here the Qur'an cites the hostile claim directly, denies both the killing and the crucifixion, states that the matter was made to appear otherwise to the opponents, that those who differed over it were in doubt with no real knowledge, and concludes that God raised Jesus to Himself. Q 5:117 supplies a third, retrospective fragment in Jesus's own voice: as long as he remained among his people he was a witness over them, and once God took him, God alone remained watchful over them. Read together, these three passages yield five criteria a Jewish-scriptural analogue to the Qur'an's account should satisfy.

sections.heading: Control Texts: Other Candidates for the Righteous-Sufferer Analogue
sections.text: Four other texts belong to the same broad current of Second Temple and post-Temple Jewish literature and have each been proposed as background to the Gospel Passion or related qur'anic material: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, the court tales of Daniel 3 and 6, and the martyrdom narratives of 2 and 4 Maccabees. Running each against the five criteria shows why none is a rival candidate to Wisdom of Solomon. Isaiah 53 satisfies the shameful-death and misperception criteria more clearly than any other candidate. The servant is "cut off from the land of the living" and given "his grave... with the wicked" (Isa 53:8–9), and the community's initial judgment — "we accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted" (Isa 53:4) — is corrected within the poem itself. But Isaiah 53 supplies no equivalent to the first and second criteria: no named hostile agents are shown plotting against the servant, and his status as God's son is never at issue. Isaiah 53 has no sonship language at all.

sections.heading: The Wisdom of Solomon as Jewish-Scriptural Analogue
sections.text: The Wisdom of Solomon is a work of Alexandrian diaspora Judaism, composed in literary Greek and voiced through the persona of Solomon, most often dated to the late first century BCE or early first century CE.

sections.heading: Wisdom 2 and the Gospel Passion Narrative
sections.text: The correspondence between Wisdom and the Qur'an's Jesus material gains a further layer once Wisdom 2's place in the New Testament's own Passion tradition is taken into account. Matthew's account of the mockery at the cross has long been read as drawing directly on Wisdom 2's scene of the wicked testing a self-proclaimed son of God. This reproduces the logic, and much of the vocabulary, of Wisdom 2:18. Douglas Moo's study of the Old Testament and deuterocanonical background of the Gospel Passion narratives treats the Matthean taunt as dependent on Wisdom 2 alongside Psalm 22, and commentators on Matthew have long placed the two texts side by side for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: Wisdom 3, 5, and the Motifs Absent from the Toledot Yeshu
sections.text: Anthony's own comparison supplies a further test of this argument. He scores nine motifs shared by the Toledot Yeshu, Q 3:54–55, and Q 4:156–159, and three of the qur'anic motifs take a minus sign under Toledot Yeshu: God's cleansing of Jesus from his disbelieving opponents, the exaltation of Jesus's followers over the disbelieving Israelites, and Jesus's role as an eschatological witness against his own community.

sections.heading: The Wisdom of Solomon in the Palestinian-Syriac Scriptural Contact Zone
sections.text: A comparison of this kind depends on Wisdom of Solomon having a plausible route into the Qur'an's late antique environment. The book's transmission history supplies one. Wisdom of Solomon began as a Greek Jewish composition from Hellenistic Alexandria, written in a monotheistic, Exodus-centered idiom for a Greek-reading Jewish community for whom the Septuagint already functioned as scripture.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 satisfies, in a single continuous unit, all five criteria drawn from the Qur'an's own account of Jesus's end. The wicked plot against the righteous man. They test whether his claim to be God's son is genuine by condemning him to insult, torture, and a shameful death. They believe, once he is gone, that they have destroyed him. The text answers them from outside their own perspective, placing the righteous man's soul in God's hand and describing his removal as protection rather than defeat. Q 3:54–55, Q 4:157–159, and Q 5:117 move through the same sequence: hostile plotting, a claim of killing and crucifixion, the exposure of that claim as conjecture rather than knowledge, and God's own taking and raising of Jesus. The Toledot Yeshu supplies a hostile narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel directly, scene by scene, and it is this narrative, or something like it, that the Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 appear to be citing. Wisdom of Solomon supplies the older interpretive grammar that had already shaped how a scene of that kind could be told and understood, since it is Wisdom 2's mockery of a righteous son of God that stands behind Matthew's own account of the taunting at the cross. What the Qur'an adds to this inherited grammar is its own account of what Jesus was in the first place. Wisdom lets its righteous man call God his father and claim sonship as his own boast; the Qur'an gives Jesus none of that language, having the wicked in the text say only that they killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God. The wicked in Wisdom are wrong to think a righteous son of God can be destroyed by a shameful death. The Qur'an's opponents are wrong for the same reason and for a further one — even if a death had occurred, it would have marked the end of a servant's mission rather than the defeat of a divine son.

fullText: Sean Anthony has proposed that the Qur'an's account of the end of Jesus's earthly mission is best read against late ancient Jewish polemics against, and parody of, the life of Jesus of Nazareth. This piece extends Anthony's reorientation of the discussion toward Jewish sources by turning to a different kind of text: the Wisdom of Solomon, a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom book composed centuries before Muḥammad's mission and read as scripture by both Jewish and Christian communities of the late antique Near East. Wisdom 2–5 supplies a scriptural grammar in which the elements of the qur'anic dispute over Jesus's end already appear together, in sequence, applied to an unnamed righteous man rather than to a fictionalized biography of Jesus. The Qur'anic Criteria Q 3:54–55 supplies the earlier of the Qur'an's two accounts of the end of Jesus's mission, in compressed form: the Israelites plot against Jesus, God plots in response and plots best of all, and God then tells Jesus that He will take him, raise him to Himself, and purify him from the disbelievers. Q 4:156–159 supplies the second account, embedded in an extended polemic against the People of Scripture in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Here the Qur'an cites the hostile claim directly, denies both the killing and the crucifixion, states that the matter was made to appear otherwise to the opponents, that those who differed over it were in doubt with no real knowledge, and concludes that God raised Jesus to Himself. Q 5:117 supplies a third, retrospective fragment in Jesus's own voice: as long as he remained among his people he was a witness over them, and once God took him, God alone remained watchful over them. Read together, these three passages yield five criteria a Jewish-scriptural analogue to the Qur'an's account should satisfy. 1. Hostile Plotting against the Righteous Figure Q 3:54 opens with the plot itself — "they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters." The verse gives no content to the Israelites' scheme and lets the divine response define its shape. A relevant analogue needs a righteous figure opposed by hostile agents whose violence or intrigue becomes the occasion for a divine reversal rather than a defeat. 2. The Testing of Divine Sonship or Protection His opponents elsewhere dismiss Jesus's signs as sorcery: which is to say they contest the divine source of his authority rather than merely his person. Anthony reads these two verses as the Qur'an's rebuttal of a specific accusation preserved in the Toledot Yeshu, where Jesus's miracles are explained away as learned sorcery. 3. Condemnation to a Shameful Death The addition of crucifixion beyond mere killing matters. Crucifixion in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East was a punishment built for public humiliation as much as for death, and the opponents' claim asserts mastery over Jesus's body and reputation together. A relevant analogue needs the wicked to condemn the righteous figure specifically to a shameful, public death. 4. Hostile Misperception Mistaken for Knowledge Q 4:157 moves from shubbiha lahum ("it was made to appear so to them") to shakk ("doubt"), ʿilm ("knowledge"), ẓann ("conjecture"), and yaqīn ("certainty"), stripping the opponents' claim of the status of knowledge and reducing it to conjecture. A relevant analogue needs observers who take an appearance for certainty and are shown, within the text itself, to have mistaken the one for the other. 5. Divine Taking and Preservation beyond Hostile Reach Q 3:55 gives the fuller triad of taking, raising, and purification, and Q 5:117 supplies Jesus's own retrospective description of the moment God took him. Q 39:42 anchors the sense of the verb tawaffī used throughout this material, naming God's taking of souls both at death and during sleep and leaving the precise mode of the taking to context rather than to the verb itself. Control Texts: Other Candidates for the Righteous-Sufferer Analogue Four other texts belong to the same broad current of Second Temple and post-Temple Jewish literature and have each been proposed as background to the Gospel Passion or related qur'anic material: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, the court tales of Daniel 3 and 6, and the martyrdom narratives of 2 and 4 Maccabees. Running each against the five criteria shows why none is a rival candidate to Wisdom of Solomon. Isaiah 53 satisfies the shameful-death and misperception criteria more clearly than any other candidate. The servant is "cut off from the land of the living" and given "his grave... with the wicked" (Isa 53:8–9), and the community's initial judgment — "we accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted" (Isa 53:4) — is corrected within the poem itself. But Isaiah 53 supplies no equivalent to the first and second criteria: no named hostile agents are shown plotting against the servant, and his status as God's son is never at issue. Isaiah 53 has no sonship language at all. Psalm 22 comes closer than Isaiah 53 to the sonship-testing criterion, since the psalmist's tormentors mock him in terms that anticipate both Wisdom 2 and the Gospel taunt at the cross: "He committed his cause to the Lord, let him deliver him, let him rescue him, for he delights in him" (Ps 22:8) — the same logic that organizes Wisdom 2:18 and Matthew 27:43, a connection well established in Passion-narrative scholarship. Daniel 3 and 6 supply the hostile-plot criterion as directly as any text considered here, and something like the sonship-testing criterion, since the officials' scheme doubles as a test of whether the protagonists' God can and will save them (Dan 3:15, 6:20). 2 and 4 Maccabees supply the hostile-plot and shameful-death criteria as fully as Wisdom does. Antiochus's persecution is a sustained hostile plot, and the martyrs voice a hope for bodily resurrection — "the King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life" (2 Macc 7:9) — gesturing toward the fifth criterion. Isaiah 53 No No Yes Yes Partial Psalm 22 Yes Partial Partial No No Daniel 3 / 6 Yes Partial No No No 2 & 4 Maccabees Yes No Yes No Partial Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes No single control text satisfies more than three of the five criteria, and none combines the sonship test with corrected misperception — the pairing structurally closest to the Qur'an's own rhetorical move in Q 4:157, where the opponents' claim is dismantled by stripping their certainty of the status of knowledge. Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 is the only text that supplies all five elements together, in the same sequence, applied to the same figure, within a single continuous unit. The Wisdom of Solomon as Jewish-Scriptural Analogue The Wisdom of Solomon is a work of Alexandrian diaspora Judaism, composed in literary Greek and voiced through the persona of Solomon, most often dated to the late first century BCE or early first century CE. Wisdom 2: The Wicked Plot and Test the Righteous Man Wisdom 2 opens with the reasoning of the ungodly: life is short, death final, the soul no more than breath that disperses. From this anthropology the wicked derive an ethic of predation. Their hostility settles on one figure in particular — a righteous man who exposes their conduct as sin against the law, calls himself a child of God, and boasts that God is his father. They move from proposition to action, deciding to examine his patience with insult and torture and to condemn him to a shameful death, reasoning that his own claim of divine protection will be tested by whether that protection actually arrives (Wis 2:19–20). The sequence answers the first three criteria at once. The wicked plot, as the Israelites plot against Jesus in Q 3:54. Their test targets the righteous man's claim to be God's son, not simply his life — the same way the sorcery charge in Q 5:110 and Q 61:6 targets Jesus's claim to divine backing rather than simply his safety. Their chosen instrument is a shameful death, exactly the qualifier the Qur'an adds in Q 4:157 by naming crucifixion alongside killing. Sonship Reworded: The Wicked's Boast in the Qur'an Wisdom's wicked do not attack an anonymous holy man. They quote him: he "professes to have knowledge of God, and calls himself a child of the Lord" (Wis 2:13), and "boasts that God is his father" (Wis 2:16). The wicked's own summary of his claim supplies the theology they intend to test — sonship of God, stated as directly as Hellenistic Greek allows. The Qur'an's opponents make the same structural move in Q 4:157 — they too are quoted boasting about a man they claim to have killed — but the content of the boast has changed. They do not say "we killed the son of God." They say "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God." The title that would answer to Wisdom's "child of the Lord" is absent. Two other titles stand in its place: son of Mary, and messenger of God. This is not an isolated turn of phrase. Q 4:171 makes the identical substitution outside any hostile speech, addressing the People of Scripture directly. The formula the Qur'an places in the mouths of Jesus's killers is the same formula the Qur'an uses for its own confession of Jesus. Self-description quoted by the hostile party "Calls himself a child of the Lord" (2:13); "boasts that God is his father" (2:16) "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God" What is being tested Literal divine sonship Prophetic office and human parentage Function of the substitution — Retains the accusatory shape of the boast while correcting its theology This kind of move — folding a doctrinal correction into a reported claim rather than refuting it afterward — is a documented feature of how the Qur'an handles material drawn from Jewish and Christian tradition. Much of the Qur'an's engagement with biblical narrative proceeds by subtext: it assumes the audience already knows a prior text, then reshapes that text's details to make a theological point rather than arguing with it directly, as Gabriel Reynolds has shown. Wisdom 3: Apparent Death and the Reversal of Perception Wisdom 3 opens by placing the fate of the righteous beyond the reach of the wicked's test. The chapter states its opposition between perception and reality as plainly as any text in Second Temple literature could state it — the foolish read a departure as a death and a death as a destruction, and the text corrects them from outside their own perspective, in the same gesture by which Q 4:157 moves from denying the hostile act to denying that the opponents possessed any knowledge of what they claimed to have witnessed. "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them" (3:1) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine possession overrules hostile interpretation "In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died" (3:2) "They did not kill him... but it was made to appear so to them" (4:157) Hostile or foolish observers mistake appearance for fact "Their departure was thought to be an affliction, and their going from us to be their destruction" (3:2–3) "We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary" (4:157) Apparent defeat is misread as real defeat "But they are at peace" (3:3) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine reality reverses the public reading of events Karina Hogan's study of what she calls the "ambiguity of death" in Wisdom, building on Michael Kolarcik's earlier analysis of the book's literary structure, shows this reversal is deliberate rather than incidental. Wisdom exploits the same vocabulary of death for two audiences at once: for the wicked, physical death confirms their belief in annihilation; for the righteous, the identical event marks the end of suffering and the beginning of nearness to God. Wisdom 4: The Righteous Man Taken from among Sinners Wisdom 4 turns from apparent death to the logic of removal: the one who pleases God is loved by Him and taken away while still living among sinners. The people who witness this fail to understand it, unaware that grace and mercy belong to God's elect and that He watches over His holy ones (Wis 4:14–15). This passage corresponds most closely to Q 3:55. The one who pleases God is loved by him (4:10) "I am taking you" Divine favor defines the figure from the outset Taken while still living among sinners, "lest wickedness change his understanding" (4:10–11) "And raising you to Myself" A verb of taking marks the removal The removal is protective, not punitive (4:11) "And purifying you from those who disbelieve" The removal separates the righteous figure from the hostile community Onlookers "see and do not understand" (4:14) Opponents have "no knowledge... only conjecture" (4:157) Onlookers witness the event without grasping it Grace and mercy belong to God's elect (4:15) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine favor, not hostile action, defines the outcome Hostile plotting The wicked lie in wait for the righteous man Wis 2:12 Testing of divine sonship They test whether God will deliver him as His son Wis 2:17–18 Shameful death They condemn him to a shameful death Wis 2:20 Misperception as false knowledge The foolish think he has died and mistake his departure for destruction Wis 3:2–3 Divine taking and preservation His soul is in God's hand; he is taken from among sinners Wis 3:1; 4:10–14 Wisdom 2 and the Gospel Passion Narrative The correspondence between Wisdom and the Qur'an's Jesus material gains a further layer once Wisdom 2's place in the New Testament's own Passion tradition is taken into account. Matthew's account of the mockery at the cross has long been read as drawing directly on Wisdom 2's scene of the wicked testing a self-proclaimed son of God. This reproduces the logic, and much of the vocabulary, of Wisdom 2:18. Douglas Moo's study of the Old Testament and deuterocanonical background of the Gospel Passion narratives treats the Matthean taunt as dependent on Wisdom 2 alongside Psalm 22, and commentators on Matthew have long placed the two texts side by side for exactly this reason. This connection changes what a comparison between the Qur'an and Wisdom of Solomon can claim. The Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 boast that they killed and crucified Jesus in circumstances that, on the Gospel's own telling, were narrated in the language Wisdom 2 had already supplied for the mockery of a righteous man tested as God's son. Anthony's Toledot Yeshu material gives the Qur'an's audience a Jewish counter-narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel's account of Jesus's death and resurrection. Wisdom 3, 5, and the Motifs Absent from the Toledot Yeshu Anthony's own comparison supplies a further test of this argument. He scores nine motifs shared by the Toledot Yeshu, Q 3:54–55, and Q 4:156–159, and three of the qur'anic motifs take a minus sign under Toledot Yeshu: God's cleansing of Jesus from his disbelieving opponents, the exaltation of Jesus's followers over the disbelieving Israelites, and Jesus's role as an eschatological witness against his own community. God cleanses Jesus of his disbelieving opponents (Q 3:55) Absent The righteous man is taken away while still living among sinners, "lest wickedness change his understanding" (Wis 4:10–11) Followers of Jesus are exalted over the disbelieving Israelites (Q 3:55) Absent "They will govern nations and rule over peoples, and the Lord will reign over them forever" (Wis 3:8) Jesus is an eschatological witness against his ummah (Q 4:159; Q 5:117) Absent The righteous man stands before those who once condemned him, who confess, "we fools! We accounted his life madness" (Wis 5:1–5) Wisdom 3:8 answers the second gap only in a qualified sense — the verse belongs to the poem's shift from the singular righteous man of chapter 2 to the collective "righteous" of chapters 3 through 5, so its promise exalts the righteous as a class rather than naming a teacher's own followers. The third gap calls for Wisdom 5:1–8, which completes the confrontation staged in chapter 2. The wicked, who had condemned the righteous man to a shameful death, now stand before him at the reckoning. Q 4:159 states that "not one of the People of Scripture will fail to believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he shall bear witness against them," and Q 5:117 has Jesus describe his own role among his people in the same terms — a witness present while he remained among them and absent once God took him. Wisdom 5 stages this same reversal: the people who condemned the righteous man are made to stand before him, recognize him, and confess in his presence that their earlier judgment was wrong. The Toledot Yeshu, built to prove the sages' judgment of Jesus correct, supplies no such scene — its disciples claim only that God rescued Jesus by raising him to heaven, and the sages who condemned him are never made to recognize their error. The Wisdom of Solomon in the Palestinian-Syriac Scriptural Contact Zone A comparison of this kind depends on Wisdom of Solomon having a plausible route into the Qur'an's late antique environment. The book's transmission history supplies one. Wisdom of Solomon began as a Greek Jewish composition from Hellenistic Alexandria, written in a monotheistic, Exodus-centered idiom for a Greek-reading Jewish community for whom the Septuagint already functioned as scripture. This Palestinian-Syriac contact zone already carries weight elsewhere in the study of the Qur'an's Jesus and Mary traditions. Stephen Shoemaker has argued that the nativity scene in Q 19, with Mary sent to a remote place, resting beneath a palm, and given water from a spring, intersects with Palestinian local tradition connected to the Kathisma church between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, where late antique Christian memory had already linked Mary's rest, a spring, and a palm tree at a single site. The Kathisma church supplies the material anchor for that intersection: built in the mid-fifth century on the Jerusalem–Bethlehem road and enlarged with an octagonal plan in the sixth, it commemorated the tradition that Mary rested there during her journey to Bethlehem, and Byzantine pilgrim accounts and liturgical calendars associate the same location with a spring and, eventually, a palm tree said to have bent down to offer her its fruit. Conclusion Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 satisfies, in a single continuous unit, all five criteria drawn from the Qur'an's own account of Jesus's end. The wicked plot against the righteous man. They test whether his claim to be God's son is genuine by condemning him to insult, torture, and a shameful death. They believe, once he is gone, that they have destroyed him. The text answers them from outside their own perspective, placing the righteous man's soul in God's hand and describing his removal as protection rather than defeat. Q 3:54–55, Q 4:157–159, and Q 5:117 move through the same sequence: hostile plotting, a claim of killing and crucifixion, the exposure of that claim as conjecture rather than knowledge, and God's own taking and raising of Jesus. The Toledot Yeshu supplies a hostile narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel directly, scene by scene, and it is this narrative, or something like it, that the Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 appear to be citing. Wisdom of Solomon supplies the older interpretive grammar that had already shaped how a scene of that kind could be told and understood, since it is Wisdom 2's mockery of a righteous son of God that stands behind Matthew's own account of the taunting at the cross. What the Qur'an adds to this inherited grammar is its own account of what Jesus was in the first place. Wisdom lets its righteous man call God his father and claim sonship as his own boast; the Qur'an gives Jesus none of that language, having the wicked in the text say only that they killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God. The wicked in Wisdom are wrong to think a righteous son of God can be destroyed by a shameful death. The Qur'an's opponents are wrong for the same reason and for a further one — even if a death had occurred, it would have marked the end of a servant's mission rather than the defeat of a divine son. title: The First Revelation Story: A Zubayrid Call Narrative?
description: A hadith-critical and source-critical study of the iqraʾ narrative, its Zubayrid transmission setting, the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr, al-Zuhrī’s canonical stream, Ibn Isḥāq’s Rayy-recension stream in al-Ṭabarī, and the Cædmon comparison.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.text: The famous story of the first revelation is usually told as if it were direct memory. Muhammad withdraws to Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel appears. The angel commands him, “Read.” Muhammad says, “I cannot read.” The command is repeated. The opening verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are revealed. Muhammad returns to Khadījah in fear. Khadījah consoles him. Waraqah b. Nawfal, the learned Christian relative, confirms that the visitor is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. The story is powerful. It explains the beginning of revelation, the first Qurʾānic words, Khadījah’s role, Waraqah’s scriptural validation, and Muhammad’s first confrontation with the terror of prophecy. But the question for a historian is not whether the story is powerful. The question is where the story becomes visible, what its transmissions look like, and why its narrative structure resembles a known Christian call-story so closely. The goal here is not to deny that Muhammad had a revelatory beginning. The goal is narrower. The polished “Read!” story, as it survives in hadith and sīrah, looks like a crafted call narrative. It has an isnād history. It has a literary shape. It has Qurʾānic interests. And it has a striking parallel in Bede’s story of Cædmon.

sections.heading: The Canonical Hadith Form
sections.text: The most influential form is the ʿĀʾishah report. Its upper route is: ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī. After al-Zuhrī, the report spreads through later transmitters and compilers. One early witness is ʿAbd al-Razzāq through Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Isḥāq b. Rāhawayh preserves the same broad form through ʿAbd al-Razzāq. Bukhārī then gives the version that becomes the standard form at the opening of his Ṣaḥīḥ. The report then gives the famous scene. This version is not simply a memory of a cave. It is a structured call narrative. It begins with true dreams, moves to seclusion, brings an angelic command, repeats the refusal, attaches the scene to Qurʾān 96:1–5, and ends with Khadījah and Waraqah validating the experience.

sections.heading: The Rayy Recension in al-Ṭabarī
sections.text: The most important source for the storyteller hypothesis is the Rayy-recension material preserved in al-Ṭabarī. The practical way to find this material is by filtering for the isnād: Ibn Ḥumayd → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Isḥāq. In the first-revelation passage, Ṭabarī gives the chain: Muḥammad b. Ḥumayd al-Rāzī → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Muḥammad b. Isḥāq → Wahb b. Kaysān, mawlā of the House of al-Zubayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. That chain matters because it does not merely transmit the story. It frames the story as a Zubayrid court event. Wahb b. Kaysān says that he heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr ask ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to tell them how the Messenger of God first began prophethood when Gabriel came to him. This is the core of the argument. The dramatic iqraʾ story is not merely floating in Ibn Isḥāq. In this stream, it is attached to a Meccan storyteller, in a Zubayrid court setting, transmitted by a client of the House of al-Zubayr.

sections.heading: The Two Zubayrid Exits
sections.text: The diagram below shows the two major exits from the Zubayrid memory world. One stream goes through ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr’s court to Wahb b. Kaysān and Ibn Isḥāq. The other goes through ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr to al-Zuhrī and then into the hadith collections. For a lay reader, the important point is simple. The story does not appear as a broad Companion memory with many independent early roots. Its most influential forms concentrate around Zubayrid-linked transmitters. ʿUrwah is a central figure of the Zubayrid household. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr is the Zubayrid claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān is attached to the House of al-Zubayr. ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr is the Meccan storyteller in the scene.

sections.heading: Why ʿĀʾishah Is Not an Eyewitness Here
sections.text: The ʿĀʾishah attribution is important, but it must be handled carefully. ʿĀʾishah was not present at Ḥirāʾ. She was not an eyewitness to the first revelation. The report attributed to her is therefore not a direct memory of the event. It is a report about the event transmitted through family and teaching networks. That does not make the report worthless. But it changes the question. We are not asking, “What did ʿĀʾishah see?” We are asking, “What form of the first-revelation story circulated through ʿUrwah and al-Zuhrī under ʿĀʾishah’s authority?” That distinction matters. A report can carry an early Companion name while still being a later household narrative, shaped by theological, Qurʾānic, and literary needs.

sections.heading: The Meccan Storyteller Hypothesis
sections.text: The strongest candidate for the narrative crystallizer is ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. That does not mean he definitely fabricated the story. It means he fits the social role better than almost anyone else in the surviving record. He is not merely a transmitter. He is a qāṣṣ, a storyteller-preacher. His function was to narrate sacred material in public, to make hidden beginnings vivid, and to turn religious memory into memorable moral instruction. The first-revelation story has exactly that kind of shape. It dramatizes an otherwise hidden event. It turns the first revelation into dialogue. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with iqraʾ. It gives Muhammad fear, crisis, and validation. It brings in Khadījah as moral witness and Waraqah as scriptural witness. Schoeler’s reconstruction is important here. He argues that ʿUbayd combined a set of motifs that circulated around the beginnings of revelation: Ḥirāʾ devotion, Khadījah, iqraʾ, the horizon vision, and Waraqah. In that reconstruction, the result was a coherent, edifying, and entertaining story. As a qāṣṣ, ʿUbayd may have embellished and extended some elements. The story then spread through the Zubayrid family as a family tradition.

sections.heading: The Source-Critical Debate
sections.text: The qāṣṣ hypothesis is not just a modern suspicion. Görke and Schoeler explicitly discuss the possibility that ʿUrwah’s source was the same family tradition that Ibn Isḥāq transmits through Wahb b. Kaysān from ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. They point out that ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, ʿUrwah’s elder brother, asks ʿUbayd in a meeting to report the Prophet’s first revelation. They then state that the al-Zuhrī / Hishām b. ʿUrwah tradition from ʿUrwah and the Ibn Isḥāq tradition from Wahb b. Kaysān and ʿUbayd are so close that they must have the same origin.

sections.heading: Ibn Isḥāq’s Dramatic Form
sections.text: The Ibn Isḥāq / Ṭabarī form is more vivid than the shorter canonical hadith form. Muhammad is at Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel comes while he is asleep. The angel brings a written object. The command is “Read.” Muhammad resists. The words of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are placed into his heart. He wakes frightened and considers whether he is a poet or possessed. He thinks of throwing himself from the mountain, until Gabriel appears again and confirms his prophethood. This version matters because it is the form most closely resembling the Cædmon pattern. The visitor comes in sleep. There is a command. There is an inability response. Sacred speech follows. The content concerns creation. The experience is later validated by authorities.

sections.heading: The Cædmon Story
sections.text: Bede’s story of Cædmon appears in the Ecclesiastical History of the English People. Cædmon is an unlearned man who cannot sing. At feasts, when the harp is passed around, he leaves in shame because he has no song. One night, after leaving a feast, he goes to the cattle stable and falls asleep. In a dream, someone calls him by name and commands him to sing. Cædmon says he cannot sing. The figure insists. Cædmon asks what he should sing about. The answer is: sing about the beginning of created things. He then sings verses praising God the Creator, words he had never learned before. In the morning, he remembers the song and is taken to religious authorities who test and validate the gift. The resemblance to the iqraʾ narrative is not just one shared motif. It is a sequence. This is why the comparison matters. Both stories are about an unprepared recipient who receives a supernatural command to perform sacred speech in his own language and then has the experience validated by religious authorities. The exact theological setting differs, but the narrative skeleton is strikingly similar.

sections.heading: The Similarities
sections.text: This is not a loose comparison between two religious people receiving inspiration. It is a specific story type. The recipient cannot perform sacred speech. A visitor commands it anyway. The inability is overcome by divine gift. The first speech concerns creation. A community authority confirms the gift afterward.

sections.heading: Which Direction Did the Influence Run?
sections.text: The direction is debated. Older comparisons often raised the possibility that the Islamic iqraʾ narrative and the Cædmon story share a direct relationship. Some scholars argued for Muhammad’s call influencing Cædmon. Others were more cautious and preferred a shared call-story pattern. Richard North has recently argued directly for the direction Muhammad story → Bede’s Cædmon story. His model is that Arculf heard the Muhammad call story around Jerusalem around 680, transmitted it to Adomnán in Iona in 683–686, and Adomnán passed it to Bede with De locis sanctis in Jarrow in 688.

sections.heading: The Qurʾānization of the Story
sections.text: The iqraʾ story is also exegetical. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with the command iqraʾ. The Qurʾānic word becomes the engine of the narrative. Gabriel says “iqraʾ.” Muhammad replies with a phrase built from the same root. The repeated command becomes the dramatic setup for the revelation of 96:1–5. This matters because the first-revelation story may not simply preserve the first moment of revelation. It may be a narrative built around a Qurʾānic opening. Anthony notes that the iqraʾ narrative claims Q. 96 is the first revelation, but modern Qurʾānic chronology has often rejected that claim on internal literary grounds. He treats the iqraʾ narrative as early and valuable for studying how sīrah traditions formed, but not as historically trustworthy for reconstructing the earliest Qurʾānic revelation.

sections.heading: Khadījah and Waraqah
sections.text: Khadījah and Waraqah are not decorative figures. They solve the narrative problem. Muhammad is terrified and uncertain. Khadījah provides moral reassurance. Waraqah provides scriptural validation. He is the learned figure who says that the being who came to Muhammad is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. Waraqah then moves the experience into biblical history. This is exactly what a call narrative needs. The chosen figure does not understand the event at first. A recognized authority interprets it. The frightening experience becomes a prophetic mission.

sections.heading: The Attempted-Suicide Motif
sections.text: One of the most striking features of some versions is Muhammad’s crisis after the first encounter. In Ibn Isḥāq’s version, he fears that he is a poet or possessed and considers throwing himself from the mountain. In some al-Zuhrī-related biographical variants, the attempted-suicide motif appears in connection with the lapse of revelation. In the canonical hadith collections, the most troubling forms are softened or excluded. This pattern matters. It suggests that the story circulated in more dramatic forms before later tradition stabilized the more acceptable version. The raw literary form includes fear, doubt, and a near-catastrophic crisis. Later hadith transmission preserves a cleaner version: terror, yes, but not the same full dramatic despair.

sections.heading: What the Corpus Shows
sections.text: The available corpus supports a two-stream model. The first stream is the canonical hadith family: ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī → Maʿmar / Yūnus / later transmitters. This stream gives the form that becomes dominant in hadith. It contains true dreams, seclusion, Ḥirāʾ, the angelic command, the refusal, the pressing, Q. 96:1–5, return to Khadījah, reassurance, and Waraqah’s validation. The second stream is the Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq family preserved in al-Ṭabarī: ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb b. Kaysān → Ibn Isḥāq → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Ḥumayd → al-Ṭabarī. This stream gives the dramatic storyteller form. It explicitly places the story in a Zubayrid court context. It contains the sleep setting, the written object, the repeated command, the “What shall I read?” reply, the placing of the words into Muhammad’s heart, and the mountain-crisis motif.

sections.heading: Why the Zubayrid Setting Matters
sections.text: The Zubayrid household was not just a private family. It was one of the major memory-making circles of early Islam. ʿĀʾishah was a central transmitter of prophetic household memory. ʿUrwah, her nephew, became one of the great early authorities for sīrah and maghāzī material. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr was a political claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān was attached to the House of al-Zubayr. This is a powerful social setting for the formation of early prophetic biography. Anthony stresses that the Ibn Isḥāq frame places the story during the Second Civil War, when ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr and the Zubayrids were competing with the Umayyads for the leadership of the early Islamic polity.

sections.heading: Why the Story Looks Literary
sections.text: A historical memory can be literary, but this story is highly literary. It has repeated dialogue. It has a threefold pressure scene. It has dramatic fear. It has a return home. It has a wise spouse. It has a learned scriptural interpreter. It has a prediction of rejection and victory. It has a Qurʾānic keyword turned into the center of the plot. That is not how raw memory usually survives. It is how a community tells the origin of revelation. The comparison with Cædmon makes this clearer. Bede’s story is not about Islamic history. It is a Christian hagiographical call story. Yet its structure matches the Ibn Isḥāq iqraʾ narrative at too many points: sleep, inability, command, sacred speech, creation theme, miraculous vernacular performance, validation. This does not prove a simple line of borrowing in every detail. But it does show that the iqraʾ story belongs to a recognizable literary world.

sections.heading: What Would Change the Analysis?
sections.text: This analysis would be weakened if we found many independent early Companion-level routes for the iqraʾ story that did not pass through ʿUrwah / al-Zuhrī or the Zubayrid storytelling environment. It would also be weakened if Ibn Isḥāq’s Zubayrid court frame were isolated and unrelated to the larger narrative shape. It would be weakened further if Cædmon only shared one generic motif, such as “a holy person receives inspiration.” But that is not what we have. The canonical hadith form concentrates through ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī. The Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq form is tied to ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr, ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, and Wahb b. Kaysān. The Cædmon comparison is not one shared idea but a shared narrative sequence. The result is a strong cumulative case.

sections.heading: Final Verdict
sections.text: The famous first-revelation story is best understood as an early Islamic call narrative, not as a direct transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Its most influential hadith form runs through ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr, and al-Zuhrī. Its most dramatic sīrah form, preserved in the Rayy-recension material inside al-Ṭabarī, is explicitly tied to a Zubayrid court setting: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr asks the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to narrate the beginning of prophecy, and Wahb b. Kaysān, a client of the House of al-Zubayr, transmits the scene. The matn is also not neutral. It is shaped around Qurʾān 96:1–5. The word iqraʾ becomes a scene. Gabriel commands. Muhammad refuses. The command is repeated. The revelation is attached to the first verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq. Khadījah and Waraqah then validate the experience. The story explains revelation, scripture, prophethood, and biblical attestation all at once. The Cædmon parallel shows why the story cannot be treated as simple memory. Bede’s Cædmon and Ibn Isḥāq’s Muhammad both receive a nighttime visionary command to perform sacred speech despite claiming inability. Both are given a creation-themed utterance. Both are validated afterward by religious authorities. Whether one follows North’s proposal that Bede modelled Cædmon on the Muhammad story, or the more cautious view that both stories belong to a shared late antique call-story repertoire, the conclusion is similar: the iqraʾ narrative is literary and comparative, not raw cave-memory. So the strongest conclusion is careful but pointed: the iqraʾ narrative is early, Zubayrid-linked, Qurʾānized, and literary. It may preserve the memory that Muhammad’s prophetic career began with a terrifying revelatory experience. But the polished story of Gabriel saying “Read,” as preserved in the canonical hadith and sīrah tradition, is a crafted origin narrative shaped by household transmission, Meccan storytelling, scriptural exegesis, and the wider call-story patterns of the late antique world.

fullText: The Problem The famous story of the first revelation is usually told as if it were direct memory. Muhammad withdraws to Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel appears. The angel commands him, “Read.” Muhammad says, “I cannot read.” The command is repeated. The opening verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are revealed. Muhammad returns to Khadījah in fear. Khadījah consoles him. Waraqah b. Nawfal, the learned Christian relative, confirms that the visitor is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. The story is powerful. It explains the beginning of revelation, the first Qurʾānic words, Khadījah’s role, Waraqah’s scriptural validation, and Muhammad’s first confrontation with the terror of prophecy. But the question for a historian is not whether the story is powerful. The question is where the story becomes visible, what its transmissions look like, and why its narrative structure resembles a known Christian call-story so closely. The goal here is not to deny that Muhammad had a revelatory beginning. The goal is narrower. The polished “Read!” story, as it survives in hadith and sīrah, looks like a crafted call narrative. It has an isnād history. It has a literary shape. It has Qurʾānic interests. And it has a striking parallel in Bede’s story of Cædmon. The Canonical Hadith Form The most influential form is the ʿĀʾishah report. Its upper route is: ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī. After al-Zuhrī, the report spreads through later transmitters and compilers. One early witness is ʿAbd al-Razzāq through Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Isḥāq b. Rāhawayh preserves the same broad form through ʿAbd al-Razzāq. Bukhārī then gives the version that becomes the standard form at the opening of his Ṣaḥīḥ. The report then gives the famous scene. This version is not simply a memory of a cave. It is a structured call narrative. It begins with true dreams, moves to seclusion, brings an angelic command, repeats the refusal, attaches the scene to Qurʾān 96:1–5, and ends with Khadījah and Waraqah validating the experience. The Rayy Recension in al-Ṭabarī The most important source for the storyteller hypothesis is the Rayy-recension material preserved in al-Ṭabarī. The practical way to find this material is by filtering for the isnād: Ibn Ḥumayd → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Isḥāq. In the first-revelation passage, Ṭabarī gives the chain: Muḥammad b. Ḥumayd al-Rāzī → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Muḥammad b. Isḥāq → Wahb b. Kaysān, mawlā of the House of al-Zubayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. That chain matters because it does not merely transmit the story. It frames the story as a Zubayrid court event. Wahb b. Kaysān says that he heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr ask ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to tell them how the Messenger of God first began prophethood when Gabriel came to him. This is the core of the argument. The dramatic iqraʾ story is not merely floating in Ibn Isḥāq. In this stream, it is attached to a Meccan storyteller, in a Zubayrid court setting, transmitted by a client of the House of al-Zubayr. The Two Zubayrid Exits The diagram below shows the two major exits from the Zubayrid memory world. One stream goes through ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr’s court to Wahb b. Kaysān and Ibn Isḥāq. The other goes through ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr to al-Zuhrī and then into the hadith collections. For a lay reader, the important point is simple. The story does not appear as a broad Companion memory with many independent early roots. Its most influential forms concentrate around Zubayrid-linked transmitters. ʿUrwah is a central figure of the Zubayrid household. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr is the Zubayrid claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān is attached to the House of al-Zubayr. ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr is the Meccan storyteller in the scene. Why ʿĀʾishah Is Not an Eyewitness Here The ʿĀʾishah attribution is important, but it must be handled carefully. ʿĀʾishah was not present at Ḥirāʾ. She was not an eyewitness to the first revelation. The report attributed to her is therefore not a direct memory of the event. It is a report about the event transmitted through family and teaching networks. That does not make the report worthless. But it changes the question. We are not asking, “What did ʿĀʾishah see?” We are asking, “What form of the first-revelation story circulated through ʿUrwah and al-Zuhrī under ʿĀʾishah’s authority?” That distinction matters. A report can carry an early Companion name while still being a later household narrative, shaped by theological, Qurʾānic, and literary needs. The Meccan Storyteller Hypothesis The strongest candidate for the narrative crystallizer is ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. That does not mean he definitely fabricated the story. It means he fits the social role better than almost anyone else in the surviving record. He is not merely a transmitter. He is a qāṣṣ, a storyteller-preacher. His function was to narrate sacred material in public, to make hidden beginnings vivid, and to turn religious memory into memorable moral instruction. The first-revelation story has exactly that kind of shape. It dramatizes an otherwise hidden event. It turns the first revelation into dialogue. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with iqraʾ. It gives Muhammad fear, crisis, and validation. It brings in Khadījah as moral witness and Waraqah as scriptural witness. Schoeler’s reconstruction is important here. He argues that ʿUbayd combined a set of motifs that circulated around the beginnings of revelation: Ḥirāʾ devotion, Khadījah, iqraʾ, the horizon vision, and Waraqah. In that reconstruction, the result was a coherent, edifying, and entertaining story. As a qāṣṣ, ʿUbayd may have embellished and extended some elements. The story then spread through the Zubayrid family as a family tradition. This is the most careful way to state the theory: ʿUbayd is not proven to be the inventor, but he is the best candidate for the narrative organizer of the dramatic form. The Source-Critical Debate The qāṣṣ hypothesis is not just a modern suspicion. Görke and Schoeler explicitly discuss the possibility that ʿUrwah’s source was the same family tradition that Ibn Isḥāq transmits through Wahb b. Kaysān from ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. They point out that ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, ʿUrwah’s elder brother, asks ʿUbayd in a meeting to report the Prophet’s first revelation. They then state that the al-Zuhrī / Hishām b. ʿUrwah tradition from ʿUrwah and the Ibn Isḥāq tradition from Wahb b. Kaysān and ʿUbayd are so close that they must have the same origin. That is the key. The two streams are not identical, but they are too close to be treated as fully independent. One can debate where the Qurʾānic elements entered. They may come from ʿUbayd, Wahb, Ibn Isḥāq, al-Zuhrī, or several stages together. But the broad conclusion remains: the story is a Zubayrid-linked call narrative, not a simple transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Shoemaker is the main methodological counterweight. He argues that many attempts to reconstruct ʿUrwah’s sīrah push the evidence too far. In his view, al-Zuhrī and sometimes figures of his generation can be linked to traditions, but the reach back to ʿUrwah is often less secure. The command is “Read.” Muhammad resists. The words of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are placed into his heart. He wakes frightened and considers whether he is a poet or possessed. He thinks of throwing himself from the mountain, until Gabriel appears again and confirms his prophethood. This version matters because it is the form most closely resembling the Cædmon pattern. The visitor comes in sleep. There is a command. There is an inability response. Sacred speech follows. The content concerns creation. The experience is later validated by authorities. The Cædmon Story Bede’s story of Cædmon appears in the Ecclesiastical History of the English People. Cædmon is an unlearned man who cannot sing. At feasts, when the harp is passed around, he leaves in shame because he has no song. One night, after leaving a feast, he goes to the cattle stable and falls asleep. In a dream, someone calls him by name and commands him to sing. Cædmon says he cannot sing. The figure insists. Cædmon asks what he should sing about. The answer is: sing about the beginning of created things. He then sings verses praising God the Creator, words he had never learned before. In the morning, he remembers the song and is taken to religious authorities who test and validate the gift. The resemblance to the iqraʾ narrative is not just one shared motif. It is a sequence. This is why the comparison matters. Both stories are about an unprepared recipient who receives a supernatural command to perform sacred speech in his own language and then has the experience validated by religious authorities. The exact theological setting differs, but the narrative skeleton is strikingly similar. The Similarities This is not a loose comparison between two religious people receiving inspiration. It is a specific story type. The recipient cannot perform sacred speech. A visitor commands it anyway. The inability is overcome by divine gift. The first speech concerns creation. Yet its structure matches the Ibn Isḥāq iqraʾ narrative at too many points: sleep, inability, command, sacred speech, creation theme, miraculous vernacular performance, validation. This does not prove a simple line of borrowing in every detail. But it does show that the iqraʾ story belongs to a recognizable literary world. What Would Change the Analysis? This analysis would be weakened if we found many independent early Companion-level routes for the iqraʾ story that did not pass through ʿUrwah / al-Zuhrī or the Zubayrid storytelling environment. It would also be weakened if Ibn Isḥāq’s Zubayrid court frame were isolated and unrelated to the larger narrative shape. It would be weakened further if Cædmon only shared one generic motif, such as “a holy person receives inspiration.” But that is not what we have. The canonical hadith form concentrates through ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī. The Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq form is tied to ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr, ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, and Wahb b. Kaysān. The Cædmon comparison is not one shared idea but a shared narrative sequence. The result is a strong cumulative case. Final Verdict The famous first-revelation story is best understood as an early Islamic call narrative, not as a direct transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Its most influential hadith form runs through ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr, and al-Zuhrī. Its most dramatic sīrah form, preserved in the Rayy-recension material inside al-Ṭabarī, is explicitly tied to a Zubayrid court setting: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr asks the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to narrate the beginning of prophecy, and Wahb b. Kaysān, a client of the House of al-Zubayr, transmits the scene. The matn is also not neutral. It is shaped around Qurʾān 96:1–5. The word iqraʾ becomes a scene. Gabriel commands. Muhammad refuses. The command is repeated. The revelation is attached to the first verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq. Khadījah and Waraqah then validate the experience. The story explains revelation, scripture, prophethood, and biblical attestation all at once. The Cædmon parallel shows why the story cannot be treated as simple memory. Bede’s Cædmon and Ibn Isḥāq’s Muhammad both receive a nighttime visionary command to perform sacred speech despite claiming inability. Both are given a creation-themed utterance. Both are validated afterward by religious authorities. Whether one follows North’s proposal that Bede modelled Cædmon on the Muhammad story, or the more cautious view that both stories belong to a shared late antique call-story repertoire, the conclusion is similar: the iqraʾ narrative is literary and comparative, not raw cave-memory. So the strongest conclusion is careful but pointed: the iqraʾ narrative is early, Zubayrid-linked, Qurʾānized, and literary. It may preserve the memory that Muhammad’s prophetic career began with a terrifying revelatory experience. But the polished story of Gabriel saying “Read,” as preserved in the canonical hadith and sīrah tradition, is a crafted origin narrative shaped by household transmission, Meccan storytelling, scriptural exegesis, and the wider call-story patterns of the late antique world. title: The “People of the Canyon” in Q85: A Case For The Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna)
description: A comparative reading of Q85 that challenges the traditional Najrān and Daniel explanations and argues that the “people of the canyon” are best understood against the biblical Valley of Hinnom, the site whose name became Jahannam.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Early in the Meccan period, when the Prophet’s followers were small in number and faced beatings, boycotts, and resentment for their faith, a short surah arrived that opened with an oath sworn on the stars, then turned to a scene of fire.

sections.heading: I. The Oaths (vv. 1–3): What the Surah Swears By
sections.text: The surah opens with three oaths, and they are not decorative. It swears by the sky and its burūj—a word usually translated as “great stars” or “constellations”—and by “the promised Day,” and then, third, by “the witness and what is witnessed” (wa-shāhidin wa-mashhūd). Commentators have long treated this as a standalone cosmic flourish, an appeal to the grandeur of the heavens before the main event begins. But the pairing of star-imagery with a valley-fire narrative two verses later has a precise biblical antecedent, and it is not a one-off.

sections.heading: II. The Scene (vv. 4–7): What Happened in the Canyon
sections.text: Let’s turn to the seven verses in question, because the argument depends on noticing what is present and what is missing: There is no mention of who built the ukhdūd, when, or why. The text simply names a group of people after a feature of the landscape: “the people of the ukhdūd.” Everything else—the identity of the persecutor, the location, the century—comes from the exegetical tradition layered on top of these seven verses, not from the verses themselves. That gap between text and tradition is where this argument lives.

sections.heading: III. The Pivot (vv. 8–9): Why They Burned
sections.text: The scene shifts abruptly from narrative to theology. “They hated them for no other reason than believing in God, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy. To Him belongs the kingship of the heavens and the earth. And God witnesses all things.” This is the theological heart of the surah. The persecutors are not rival monotheists with a doctrinal dispute. They are idolaters who hate believers for their allegiance to the one God. The dominion belongs to God alone. And God is witness—not the human spectators around the fire, but the divine witness who sees all. The witnessing motif, introduced in verse 3, now returns. The surah surrounds its judgment scene with the language and imagery of witnessing. An unidentified ‘witness’ and ‘witnessed’ at the opening, human spectatorship at the center, and divine witnessing at the conclusion. The specific biblical parallel may lie in the Josiah narrative. When Josiah undertakes his reform, he first gathers the elders and then all the people, reads the Book of the Covenant aloud, and only after this public covenantal act does he proceed to destroy the religious order that has been condemned. It’s not simply that both passages contain witnesses. In Josiah’s narrative, the destruction of the Hinnom cult is itself embedded within a publicly witnessed act of religious judgment. Jeremiah then supplies the other side of the Hinnom tradition. The elders and priests brought to the valley in Jeremiah 19 are summoned to hear the indictment and witness Jeremiah’s symbolic breaking of the potter’s jug. The significance of the passage demonstrates that the site of Hinnom could function as a deliberately staged site of public judgment. Jeremiah declares that the place has been filled with the blood of the innocent and announces that it should be called the “Valley of Slaughter.” The judgment reverses the meaning of the site. The valley where innocent blood was shed becomes the place where judgment falls upon the society responsible for it. The same Hinnom tradition appears in Jeremiah 7, where Topheth is associated with the burning of sons and daughters and is again destined to become the Valley of Slaughter: In the Hinnom tradition, the powerful use fire against the innocent; the same place is then transformed into an image of punishment awaiting those responsible. Q85 follows the same movement. The persecutors sit around the fire while believers are burned, but the surah then declares that God witnesses all things.

sections.heading: IV. The Reversal (v. 10): Gehenna and the Gardens
sections.text: The fire the persecutors lit becomes their own inheritance. The word the Quran uses is Jahannam (Gehenna/Hell) and that word is not a native Arabic coinage. Its lineage is uncontroversial in reference scholarship: Hebrew Gēʾ (ben-) Hinnōm, “the Valley of (the son of) Hinnom,” passes into Aramaic as Gēhinnām, then into Greek and Syriac as Gehenna, and finally into Arabic as Jahannam.

sections.heading: V. Summary
sections.text: Q85 describes persecutors who dig a fire filled trench, sit around it, and watch believers burn inside. Muslim tradition has offered two explanations for this scene. The massacre at Najran and the furnace from the Book of Daniel each solve only part of the puzzle. Najran supplies a real trench, but the wrong kind of persecutor, since Dhu Nuwas was a monotheist rather than an idolater. Daniel supplies the right kind of persecutor, but the wrong kind of fire, since every version of that story describes an oven rather than a valley. This article proposes a different source for the scene. It points to the Valley of Hinnom outside ancient Jerusalem, where kings once burned children as offerings to a fire god the Bible calls Molech. That valley’s Hebrew name passed through Aramaic and Greek into Arabic as Jahannam. The Quran’s own word for Hell already points back to this specific place. In summary, several threads tie Q85 to this tradition of The Valley of Slaughter: Twice in the Hebrew Bible, a king who revives the Hinnom fire cult is shown worshipping the sun, moon, and stars immediately before the fire ritual. Q85 opens with an oath on the sky and its constellations followed immediately by a valley fire. The valley’s fire cult is explicitly associated with children being made to pass through fire as an offering to Molech. Q85 opens on persecutors igniting a blazing fire and sitting around it to watch the burning of the believers. Jeremiah and Isaiah transform the valley of innocent bloodshed into a place associated with judgment against those responsible. Q85 declares that those who persecute believers have incurred the punishment of Gehenna. and burning. Josiah gathers the people publicly before dismantling the fire cult, making the destruction itself a witnessed act of religious judgment. Q85 opens with the enigmatic “witness and what is witnessed,” then develops a scene centered on watching and divine witnessing. The biblical “Molech” tradition preserves the consonantal root m-l-k , associated with melekh , “king.” The Quran names the guardian of Hell Mālik , from the same Semitic root and the same core sense of rulership.

Muslim commentaries since the eighth century identified this scene with one of two events: either the massacre of Christians at Najrān in 523 CE, or Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace from the Book of Daniel. I. The Oaths (vv. 1–3): What the Surah Swears By The surah opens with three oaths, and they are not decorative.
